A feature list ranked by customer request volume
quiz.explanation: Under high uncertainty, a Now/Next/Later view built around outcomes shows priorities without committing to dates the team is unlikely to hit. A dated quarterly timeline would be revised constantly and would set expectations the startup cannot meet.

quiz.question: Your B2B team uses a Now/Next/Later roadmap. A regulatory change means one compliance feature must ship by a fixed legal deadline. How should you show it?
options: Keep Now/Next/Later and show the fixed date on that one item
Convert the whole roadmap to a dated timeline for consistency
Omit the deadline so the roadmap avoids any date precision
Put the item in Later, since dates do not belong on roadmaps
quiz.explanation: "Direction, not dates" is a guideline against false precision, not a ban on real constraints. A hard external deadline should be shown on the item it applies to. Hiding the deadline would mislead stakeholders about a real commitment, and switching the whole roadmap to dates would add false precision everywhere else.

keyTakeaways: Roadmaps communicate direction, not dates
Outcome-based > feature-based
Now/Next/Later reduces false precision

lessons.title: Feature Prioritization Frameworks
lessons.description: Master RICE, MoSCoW, and Kano frameworks to make data-driven prioritization decisions.
learningObjectives: Calculate RICE scores accurately
Apply MoSCoW for release planning
Use Kano for UX prioritization
Combine frameworks for complex decisions

readingArticles.title: RICE Prioritization Framework
keyPoints: RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort
Reach: users affected per quarter
Impact: 3=massive, 2=high, 1=medium, 0.5=low, 0.25=minimal
Confidence: 100%=high, 80%=medium, 50%=low
Effort: person-months

readingArticles.title: Feature Prioritization: RICE, MoSCoW, Kano
keyPoints: MoSCoW: Must/Should/Could/Won't
Kano: Basic/Performance/Delighter needs
Combine: Kano for discovery, RICE for scoring, MoSCoW for release

videos.title: RICE Framework Explained
videos.creator: Product School
keyPoints: Walk through RICE calculation
Compare features with different scores
Make trade-offs visible

practicalTools.name: RICE Prioritization Spreadsheet
practicalTools.description: Prioritize features using RICE scoring
practicalTools.exercise: You have 5 features for an e-commerce app: (1) One-click checkout, (2) Product recommendations, (3) Dark mode, (4) Wishlist sharing, (5) Live chat support. Calculate RICE scores for each using: Reach (users/quarter), Impact (0.25-3), Confidence (50-100%), Effort (person-months). Rank and justify top 3.
practicalTools.deliverable: RICE scoring spreadsheet with rankings

quiz.question: What does RICE stand for?
options: Risk, Impact, Cost, Effort
Revenue, Investment, Customer, Engagement
Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort
Results, Input, Control, Execution
quiz.explanation: RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort. It helps compare features with a normalized score.

quiz.question: Your team must agree on scope for a fixed-date release in two weeks, and stakeholders need a simple shared language for trade-offs. Why might MoSCoW fit better than RICE here?
options: It produces a more precise ranking across a large backlog of ideas
It discounts each item by how confident the team is in its estimates
It shows which features delight users and which ones they simply expect
It sorts items into clear release buckets quickly, without numeric estimates
quiz.explanation: MoSCoW is fast and easy for stakeholders to discuss, which makes it a good fit for scoping a fixed-date release. Precise ranking across a large backlog and confidence-weighting are strengths of RICE, not MoSCoW, and separating delighters from expected features is what Kano does.

quiz.question: A feature reaches 2,000 users per quarter, has Impact 2 (high), Confidence 80%, and Effort of 4 person-months. What is its RICE score?
quiz.explanation: RICE = (2,000 × 2 × 0.8) / 4 = 800. 3,200 forgets to divide by Effort, 1,000 skips Confidence, and 400 leaves out Impact.

quiz.question: In the Kano model, what type of need is clean bed sheets in a hotel room?
options: Basic (must-be) need
Performance need
Delighter (attractive) need
Indifferent need
quiz.explanation: Guests expect clean sheets. Having them does not delight anyone, but missing them causes strong dissatisfaction, which makes them a basic need. It is not a performance need, because satisfaction does not keep rising the cleaner the sheets get.

quiz.question: You are scoping the MVP release of a new checkout flow with MoSCoW. Which item best qualifies as a Must have?
options: Payment processing so users can complete a purchase
Saved addresses so repeat buyers can check out faster
Order notes so buyers can add delivery instructions
Gift wrapping so buyers can send items as presents
quiz.explanation: A Must have is something the release cannot work without. Checkout with no payment processing fails its purpose. Saved addresses are valuable but have a workaround (typing the address again), so they are a Should have, not a Must.

quiz.question: You have 40 ideas from discovery and a fixed launch date in 8 weeks. Which sequence is a common way to combine prioritization frameworks?
options: RICE to classify needs, MoSCoW to score ideas, Kano to scope the release
Kano to classify needs, RICE to score ideas, MoSCoW to scope the release
MoSCoW to classify needs, Kano to score ideas, RICE to scope the release
Kano to score ideas, MoSCoW to classify needs, RICE to scope the release
quiz.explanation: Each framework does one job well. Kano shows what kind of need an idea meets, RICE compares many ideas by score, and MoSCoW turns the ranking into scope for a fixed release. The other orders give a framework a job it was not designed for, such as using MoSCoW to score 40 ideas.

quiz.question: A feature tops your RICE ranking, but its Reach and Impact estimates rest on one senior stakeholder's hunch with no supporting data. What should you do?
options: Keep Confidence at 100% since the stakeholder knows the market well
Score Confidence at 50% and run a quick test to firm up the estimates
Leave Confidence at 80% as the standard medium value for new ideas
Remove the feature from scoring until full user research is complete
quiz.explanation: The Confidence factor is how RICE accounts for weak evidence. An estimate backed only by one person's hunch deserves low confidence, and a cheap test is the right next step. Taking the feature out of scoring overreacts: RICE is built to score uncertain ideas and discount them, not to skip them.

quiz.question: RICE ranks a new AI recommendation widget above fixing inaccurate delivery-time estimates. Kano analysis says users treat accurate estimates as a basic need. What is the best call?
options: Follow the RICE ranking, since its score already accounts for Impact
Build the widget first, since delighters create the most differentiation
Fix delivery estimates first and revisit their RICE Impact score
Mark both as Should haves and let engineering decide the order
quiz.explanation: When a basic need goes unmet, users become dissatisfied, and a delighter cannot make up for that. A low RICE score here probably means its Impact was underestimated. Simply following the RICE ranking is tempting, but RICE scores are only as good as their inputs, so combine them with Kano instead of following them blindly.

quiz.question: In RICE scoring, how is Effort typically measured, and how does it affect the score?
options: In person-months, dividing the score so costlier work ranks lower
In person-months, subtracted from the score as a fixed cost penalty
In calendar weeks to launch, used to discount Reach for later launches
In dollar cost, used only as a tiebreaker between equal scores
quiz.explanation: In Intercom's RICE, Effort is estimated in person-months and is the denominator: (Reach × Impact × Confidence) / Effort. That makes the score a measure of value per unit of work. Subtracting Effort would mix units and would not scale the cost against the size of the value.

quiz.question: Two years ago, live order tracking delighted users of your food delivery app. Now every competitor has it, users barely notice it when it works, and they complain loudly when it breaks. In Kano terms, what happened?
options: It shifted from a delighter to a performance need
It shifted from a basic need to an indifferent feature
It shifted from a performance need to a reverse feature
It shifted from a delighter to a basic expectation
quiz.explanation: Delighters wear off over time. Once users take a feature for granted, it adds no satisfaction when it works but causes strong dissatisfaction when it fails, which is the mark of a basic need. It is not a performance need, because for a performance need satisfaction keeps rising as the feature gets better, and here users barely notice it.

keyTakeaways: RICE for data-driven comparison
MoSCoW for release scoping
Kano for UX prioritization
Combine frameworks for best results

lessons.title: Competitive Analysis
lessons.description: Analyze competitors systematically to identify opportunities, threats, and differentiation strategies.
learningObjectives: Conduct SWOT analysis
Create competitive feature matrices
Identify market gaps
Develop differentiation strategies

readingArticles.title: How to Do a Competitive Analysis
keyPoints: Identify direct and indirect competitors
Analyze features, pricing, positioning
Find gaps and opportunities
Update quarterly

readingArticles.title: SWOT Analysis: How To Do It Right
keyPoints: Strengths: internal advantages
Weaknesses: internal disadvantages
Opportunities: external favorable factors
Threats: external unfavorable factors

videos.title: Competitive Analysis Framework
videos.creator: Product School
keyPoints: Direct vs indirect competitors
Feature comparison matrix
Positioning map (price vs value)
Identify white space opportunities

practicalTools.name: Competitive Analysis Matrix
practicalTools.description: Analyze 3 competitors for a chosen product
practicalTools.exercise: Choose a market (e.g., project management tools). Pick 3 competitors (e.g., Asana, Monday.com, ClickUp). Create: (1) Feature matrix with 10 key features (2) Pricing comparison (3) SWOT for each (4) Positioning map: Price vs Functionality (5) Identify 2 opportunities for a new entrant.
practicalTools.deliverable: Competitive analysis document

quiz.question: What is a positioning map used for in competitive analysis?
options: Comparing competitor features in a table
Ranking competitors by total market share
Mapping each stage of the user journey
Plotting competitors on two key dimensions
quiz.explanation: A positioning map plots competitors on two key dimensions (e.g., price vs. functionality) to show how the market is positioned and where white space may exist. A side-by-side feature table is a feature comparison matrix, a different tool.

quiz.question: As a common practice, how often should a full competitive analysis be formally refreshed?
options: Every week
Every quarter
Every two years
Only once, before launch
quiz.explanation: A quarterly refresh is a common cadence that keeps the analysis current without turning it into a distraction. Weekly full rewrites are too frequent, although watching for major competitor moves between refreshes is still sensible.

quiz.question: In a SWOT analysis, what separates Strengths and Weaknesses from Opportunities and Threats?
options: S/W describe the present; O/T describe the future
S/W are internal to the company; O/T are external factors
S/W come from customer data; O/T come from competitor data
S/W are quantitative measures; O/T are qualitative judgments
quiz.explanation: Strengths and Weaknesses are internal advantages and disadvantages. Opportunities and Threats are external factors in the market or environment. The present-vs-future split is tempting, but an external threat such as a competitor's price cut can already be happening today.

quiz.question: You are the PM for a meal-kit subscription service. Which of these is an indirect competitor?
options: A food delivery app that solves dinner without any cooking
Another meal-kit service with similar recipes and pricing
A rival meal-kit brand launching in your city at a lower price
A meal-kit startup targeting the same busy-professional segment
quiz.explanation: Indirect competitors meet the same customer need (getting dinner sorted) with a different kind of solution, as a food delivery app does. The other three offer the same kind of product to the same need, so they are direct competitors, even if they differ on price or market.

quiz.question: Your feature matrix shows a competitor has 40 features to your 25. What is the best way to interpret this?
options: It shows gaps, but not which features your customers value
Build the 15 missing features first to reach feature parity
It shows the competitor's product is better for most users
Drop the matrix and compare the products on price alone
quiz.explanation: A feature matrix shows where products differ, but feature count is not customer value. You still need to validate which gaps matter to your target users. Rushing to reach parity is the tempting mistake: it leads to copying rather than differentiating, and can bloat the product.

quiz.question: A competitor launches a popular feature and Sales asks you to copy it right away. What is the best response?
options: Build a matching version fast so Sales has no gap to explain
Ignore it, since reacting to competitors always dilutes strategy
Build it only if it is table stakes for your target segment
Wait a quarter and copy it if the competitor's adoption grows
quiz.explanation: Know your competitors, but don't copy them: match a feature only when your target customers expect it as table stakes, and otherwise invest in what differentiates you. Building it fast lets the competitor set your roadmap. Ignoring it on principle can lose deals when the feature really is expected.

quiz.question: On a price-vs-functionality positioning map, no competitor sits in the mid-price, high-functionality area. What should you do next?
options: Treat it as a hypothesis and validate real customer demand
Target that area right away, since no rivals means easy share
Assume the area is empty because the segment is unprofitable
Reposition near the market leader, where demand is proven
quiz.explanation: White space on a map is a possible opportunity, not proof of demand. The gap may exist because few customers want that combination, or because it is hard to deliver profitably. Targeting it immediately is the tempting error, and assuming it is unprofitable is an equally unvalidated guess.

quiz.question: You are the PM for a payments app doing a SWOT analysis. Which item belongs under Threats?
options: Your app's slow onboarding flow, which causes sign-up drop-off
Your small team size, which limits how fast you can launch
A rival's new zero-fee plan aimed at your core user segment
Rapidly growing UPI adoption among first-time digital users
quiz.explanation: A competitor's move in your core segment is an external, unfavorable factor, so it is a Threat. Slow onboarding and a small team are internal problems, so they are Weaknesses. Growing UPI adoption is an external, favorable trend, so it is an Opportunity.

quiz.question: You are launching a new project management tool against Asana, Monday.com and ClickUp, which are all feature-rich and similarly priced. Which strategy is most defensible?
options: Match all their core features and undercut them on price
Ship more features than ClickUp to win on functionality
Target large enterprises, the most lucrative customer segment
Serve an underserved niche whose needs incumbents miss
quiz.explanation: A new entrant usually wins by differentiating: it owns an underserved segment where incumbents are weak instead of competing head-on. Matching features at a lower price is tempting, but it invites a price war with well-funded rivals and gives customers no real reason to switch. Large enterprises are lucrative, but that is where incumbents are strongest and switching costs are highest.

quiz.question: Your feature matrix shows you are at parity with a key competitor, yet you keep losing deals to them. What should you analyze next?
options: Add more granular features to the rows of the matrix
Compare how each product is priced and positioned
Benchmark your engineering velocity against theirs
Run a larger satisfaction survey of current users
quiz.explanation: A competitive analysis covers pricing and positioning as well as features. If features are at parity, the difference is often price, packaging or who each product says it is for. Adding more feature rows is tempting, but it keeps you looking only at features when that may not be why you are losing.

keyTakeaways: Know your competitors, but don't copy them
Identify white space opportunities
Update competitive analysis quarterly

lessons.title: North Star Metric & Product Analytics
lessons.description: Define your North Star Metric, build metrics frameworks, and use analytics to drive product decisions.
learningObjectives: Define a North Star Metric
Build a metrics framework
Choose the right analytics tools
Use data to inform decisions

readingArticles.title: Choosing Your North Star Metric
keyPoints: North Star = single metric that captures core value
Input metrics drive the North Star
Should reflect user value, not just revenue
Examples: Airbnb=nights booked, Slack=messages sent

readingArticles.title: Everything a PM Needs to Know About Analytics
keyPoints: A single measurement isn't analytics - trends and comparisons are
Segmentation reveals what averages hide
Funnels find drop-offs; cohorts track change over time
Plan top-down: vision to KPIs to metrics to data points

videos.title: How to Define Your North Star Metric
videos.creator: Reforge
keyPoints: North Star reflects product's core value
Decompose into input metrics
Align team around metric
Review and evolve over time

practicalTools.name: North Star Metrics Canvas
practicalTools.description: Define metrics framework for a product
practicalTools.exercise: For a meditation app: (1) Define North Star Metric (e.g., total meditation minutes) (2) Identify 3-4 input metrics that drive it (e.g., sessions/user, avg session length, DAU, new user activation) (3) Draw the metrics tree showing relationships (4) Define 2 counter-metrics to guard against gaming.
practicalTools.deliverable: Metrics framework with tree diagram

quiz.question: What makes a good North Star Metric?
options: It directly measures the company's monthly revenue
It captures the core value users get from the product
It counts the total number of registered users
It tracks how many features the team has shipped
quiz.explanation: A good North Star Metric captures the core value users get from the product, so when it grows, users are getting more value. Revenue is the tempting choice, but it is a business outcome that should follow from delivered value, and on its own it can rise while user value falls.

quiz.question: What are input metrics in a North Star framework?
options: Lagging business outcomes such as revenue and profit
Metrics added to stop the North Star from being gamed
Metrics teams can directly influence that drive the North Star
Raw event data collected by the analytics tool
quiz.explanation: Input metrics are the levers teams can move, such as sessions per user, and together they drive the North Star. Metrics that guard against gaming are counter-metrics, which is a separate part of the framework.

quiz.question: You are the PM for a music streaming app with free and paid tiers. Which is the strongest choice of North Star Metric?
options: Number of paid subscribers at month end
Songs added to playlists each week
Weekly hours listened by active users
Daily active users opening the app
quiz.explanation: Hours listened is the closest measure of the core value users get from the app (listening to music), and it tends to lead to conversions and retention. Paid subscribers is tempting, but it is a revenue outcome. Playlist adds and app opens are inputs or proxies that can grow without real listening.

quiz.question: A grocery delivery app's North Star is weekly orders delivered. Which is the best input metric for the checkout team to own?
options: Total weekly orders delivered
Cart-to-order conversion rate
Quarterly gross merchandise value
Average app store rating
quiz.explanation: Cart-to-order conversion is a lever the checkout team can move directly, and it feeds the North Star. Weekly orders delivered is the North Star itself, and many other teams also affect it, so it is too broad to serve as one team's input metric.

quiz.question: A news app's North Star is articles read per week. The team starts writing sensational headlines, and the metric jumps. Which counter-metric best guards against this kind of gaming?
options: Article read-completion rate
Click-through rate on headlines
Articles opened per session
Daily active readers
quiz.explanation: Read-completion rate shows whether people actually read the articles they open. Clickbait raises clicks but lowers completion, so this metric exposes the gaming. Headline click-through and articles opened are the very numbers the clickbait inflates, so they cannot act as a check on it.

quiz.question: Your app's overall week-4 retention has been flat at 40% for three months. What should you do first to find out whether anything underneath is changing?
options: Set a team goal to lift the average to 45%
Add more tracked events to the analytics setup
Run a satisfaction survey across all users
Segment retention by platform, channel and cohort
quiz.explanation: Segmenting shows what an average hides. For example, one platform may be getting worse while another improves, and the blended number stays flat. Setting a goal on the average skips the diagnosis, so you still would not know what to change.

quiz.question: You want to know whether users who signed up after a new onboarding flow launched are better retained at week 4 than users who signed up before it. Which analysis fits best?
options: Cohort analysis grouped by sign-up week
Funnel analysis of the onboarding steps
Overall daily active users trend
Feature usage breakdown by screen
quiz.explanation: Cohort analysis groups users by when they signed up and tracks how each group's behavior changes over time, which is exactly this question. Funnel analysis finds drop-offs between onboarding steps, but it does not compare later retention across sign-up groups.

quiz.question: A stakeholder reports, "We got 12,000 sign-ups this week." What would most help turn this number into a useful insight?
options: Feature it as a headline tile on the dashboard
Restate it as a share of all registered users
Compare it with previous weeks and the target
Celebrate it in the weekly team update email
quiz.explanation: A single measurement is not analytics. Comparing it with a trend or a target shows whether 12,000 is good, bad or unusual. Showing it as a share of all users is just one more snapshot, with no baseline to judge whether it changed.

quiz.question: You are setting up analytics for a new feature. Which approach to planning what to track is most sound?
options: Capture every possible event first, then look for useful metrics
Start from the goal, define KPIs and metrics, then the events
Pick an analytics tool first, then rely on its default reports
Copy a competitor's dashboard, then map events to its charts
quiz.explanation: Planning top-down, from vision to KPIs to metrics to data points, means every tracked event answers a question that matters. Capturing everything first is a common shortcut, but it produces noisy data that nobody has tied to a decision.

quiz.question: A B2B collaboration tool's North Star is weekly active users. WAU keeps rising, but retention and paid conversion have stalled, and many users only log in to clear notifications. What should the PM do?
options: Keep WAU and add more notification nudges to keep it growing
Replace the North Star with quarterly revenue to tie it to business
Drop the North Star and let each team choose its own KPI
Redefine the North Star around meaningful team collaboration
quiz.explanation: A North Star should be reviewed and updated when it stops tracking real user value. Here WAU counts shallow logins, so a metric closer to the actual collaboration value is needed. Switching to revenue is tempting, but it measures business results instead of user value and gives teams little guidance on what to improve.

keyTakeaways: North Star reflects core user value
Decompose into actionable input metrics
Add counter-metrics to prevent gaming

lessons.title: WEEK 2 REVIEW & EXAM
lessons.description: Comprehensive review and exam covering product strategy, OKRs, roadmapping, prioritization, competitive analysis, and metrics.
learningObjectives: Review all Week 2 concepts
Pass the Week 2 comprehensive exam
Synthesize strategy into actionable plans

readingArticles.title: What is a Product Strategy? (+How to Build One)
keyPoints: Vision is the destination; strategy is the route
Build it: research → competitive analysis → measurable goals → roadmap
Prioritize by customer needs and business goals, not feature requests
Strategy is living — monitor and adapt

readingArticles.title: 10 Steps to a Killer Product Strategy Framework
keyPoints: Start from vision, ground it in customer needs
Define measurable KPIs while creating strategy, not after
Translate strategy into roadmap work with feedback loops

videos.title: How to Create Your Product Strategy
videos.creator: Dan Olsen (Lean Product Playbook)
keyPoints: Product-Market Fit Pyramid: customer → needs → value prop → features
Vision (why) vs strategy (how you win) vs tactics (what you ship)
Prioritize with importance-vs-satisfaction analysis
Week 2 consolidation from the author of The Lean Product Playbook

practicalTools.name: Week 2 Capstone: Strategy Document
practicalTools.description: Create a complete product strategy
practicalTools.exercise: For a habit-tracking app: (1) Write 1-sentence vision (2) Define 3 strategic pillars (3) Write 2 OKRs with 3 KRs each (4) Create Now/Next/Later roadmap (5) RICE-score 5 features (6) Identify North Star and 3 input metrics.
practicalTools.deliverable: Complete product strategy document

quiz.question: Which sequence best describes how Vision, Strategy, Roadmap, and Backlog relate, from most long-term to most detailed?
options: Strategy → Vision → Roadmap → Backlog
Vision → Roadmap → Strategy → Backlog
Vision → Strategy → Roadmap → Backlog
Roadmap → Strategy → Vision → Backlog
quiz.explanation: Vision defines the destination, strategy defines how you will win, the roadmap shows the near-term steps, and the backlog details the work. Putting the roadmap before strategy is a common mistake: it lets a feature list set direction instead of the strategy.

quiz.question: What does the C in RICE stand for?
options: Cost
Customer
Confidence
Conversion
quiz.explanation: RICE (popularized by Intercom) = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort, where Confidence discounts scores for uncertain estimates. Cost is a tempting guess, but cost is already captured by Effort in the denominator.

quiz.question: For ambitious (stretch) OKRs, what average achievement rate typically suggests the goals were set at the right level?
quiz.explanation: Stretch OKRs should be ambitious, so a common heuristic is that landing around 60-70% means the targets were challenging but realistic. Hitting 95-100% every time usually means the targets were too safe. Committed OKRs are different and are expected to be fully delivered.

quiz.question: In MoSCoW prioritization, what does the 'W' stand for?
options: Worth having (if time)
Wanted (by stakeholders)
Won't have (this time)
Weighted (by value)
quiz.explanation: MoSCoW = Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (this time); the W explicitly records what is out of scope for this release. 'Worth having if time allows' is tempting, but that describes Could have, not W.

quiz.question: Your North Star is messages sent per week, and you also track spam-report rate as a counter-metric. What role does the counter-metric play?
options: An input metric the team pushes to grow messages sent
A guardrail that catches harm from over-optimizing messages sent
A benchmark comparing your messaging volume with competitors
A lagging indicator that confirms message growth weeks later
quiz.explanation: A counter-metric is a guardrail. It shows when pushing the North Star causes harm, for example growing message volume through spammy behavior. It is not an input metric, because the team is not trying to increase spam reports to move the North Star.

quiz.question: You are the PM for a habit-tracking app. Which metric is the strongest candidate for your North Star Metric?
options: Total app downloads since the product launched
Weekly users who complete three or more habit check-ins
Monthly revenue from premium subscription plans
Average time spent in the app per user per day
quiz.explanation: A North Star should capture the core value users get, and for a habit app that value is actually completing habits regularly. Revenue is a tempting choice, but it is a business outcome that lags user value. Downloads and time in app don't show whether users are building habits.

quiz.question: A sales lead asks you for firm delivery dates on every roadmap item for the next 12 months to share with a large prospect. What is the best response?
options: Share a Now/Next/Later view and commit only to near-term items
Give quarter-level dates for every item, padded with a buffer
Share the internal roadmap with every date marked as an estimate
Commit dates only for the items this prospect has asked about
quiz.explanation: Roadmaps communicate direction, not dates, and a Now/Next/Later view avoids false precision while still showing where the product is heading. Quarter dates with a buffer look safer, but they still turn uncertain long-term bets into commitments that sales will repeat to customers.

quiz.question: Your Objective is 'Make habit-building effortless for new users.' Which of these is the best-written Key Result?
options: Launch streak reminders and a redesigned onboarding flow
Make onboarding simple and delightful for every new user
Ship twelve onboarding improvements before quarter end
Raise day-30 retention of new users from 18% to 25%
quiz.explanation: A Key Result should be a measurable outcome with a baseline and a target. Launching reminders and onboarding is a tempting choice, but it is a list of outputs (tasks), not a measure of whether habit-building actually got easier.

quiz.question: In your habit app, RICE ranks new social challenges well above fixing unreliable reminders, which users expect to just work. What should you prioritize?
options: Fix reminders first, since a broken basic need drives churn
Build social challenges first, since RICE is the more objective method
Re-score both using stakeholder votes and follow the majority
Split capacity evenly so that neither item is fully deprioritized
quiz.explanation: In the Kano model, reminders are a basic expectation: when they fail, users become dissatisfied whatever the new features offer. This is why prioritization needs judgment as well as a score. Following RICE alone is the tempting mistake, because the scores can understate the cost of a broken basic need.

quiz.question: A rival habit app launches an AI coach and your CEO asks you to match it. Which response best reflects sound competitive strategy?
options: Match it quickly so you do not fall behind on the feature matrix
Ignore it, since competitor launches should not shape your roadmap
Add it to Next by default and refine the scope once it is built
Check whether it serves your target users' unmet needs before deciding
quiz.explanation: Know your competitors, but don't copy them: judge a competitor's move against your strategy and your users' needs, and look for gaps you could win in rather than chasing parity. Ignoring it is also wrong, because the launch may reveal a real customer need worth analyzing.

keyTakeaways: Strategy connects vision to execution
Prioritization requires data + judgment
Metrics should guide, not dictate

lessons.title: Writing Product Requirements Documents (PRDs)
lessons.description: Master the art of writing clear, actionable PRDs that align teams and reduce development churn.
learningObjectives: Write clear problem statements
Define user stories and acceptance criteria
Include relevant context without over-specifying
Create PRDs that engineers love

readingArticles.title: How to Write a Product Requirements Document
keyPoints: PRD includes: goals, background, assumptions, user stories, design, questions
Keep it scannable
Include success metrics
Write with engineering and design

readingArticles.title: PRD Templates: What to Include
keyPoints: Product details, objectives, features, personas
Release criteria, scope, open questions
Status tracking, timeline

videos.title: How to Write a PRD (with template)
videos.creator: Product School
keyPoints: Start with problem, not solution
Define success metrics
Include user stories
Keep it concise

practicalTools.name: PRD Template Exercise
practicalTools.description: Write a complete PRD for a feature
practicalTools.exercise: Write a PRD for 'Social Login' feature in a fitness app. Include: (1) Problem statement (2) Goals and success metrics (3) User stories with acceptance criteria (4) Out of scope items (5) Open questions (6) Assumptions. Use the format: As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit].
practicalTools.deliverable: Complete PRD document (1-2 pages)

quiz.question: What should a PRD always include?
options: Detailed technical architecture and database design
Final pixel-perfect mockups for every screen
Problem statement and success metrics
A fixed delivery date for each feature
quiz.explanation: A PRD must state the problem being solved and how success will be measured. Technical architecture is tempting, but engineering defines it; designs and dates can be linked or tracked, but they are not the core of the PRD.

quiz.question: What is the format of a user story?
options: As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit]
The system shall [function] when [condition]
Given [context], when [action], then [outcome]
As a [team], we will build [feature] by [date]
quiz.explanation: The standard user story format centres on the user and their motivation: 'As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit].' 'Given/when/then' is a common format for acceptance criteria, not for the story itself.

quiz.question: You are writing a PRD for Social Login in a fitness app. Which opening problem statement is strongest?
options: Add Google and Apple sign-in to onboarding so new users can register in a single tap
Our top three competitors already offer social login, so we risk losing sign-ups to them
Users expect a modern, frictionless sign-up experience, and ours now feels dated to them
Many new users quit at the email/password step; exit surveys cite password creation
quiz.explanation: A strong problem statement describes a user problem and the evidence for it, without choosing a solution in advance. The competitor option is tempting, but it argues for a solution (parity) rather than describing a user problem. The first option is already a solution, and the last is too vague to act on.

quiz.question: Which is the best primary success metric for the Social Login PRD, whose goal is to reduce sign-up friction?
options: Number of taps on the new Google sign-in button
Social login shipped on iOS and Android by quarter end
Sign-up completion rate compared with the pre-launch baseline
Number of social login providers supported at launch
quiz.explanation: The goal is less sign-up friction, so the completion rate compared with a baseline measures the outcome directly. Button taps are tempting, but they measure activity and can rise even if total sign-ups do not.

quiz.question: Your Social Login PRD names the OAuth library, the database schema and exact pixel layouts. The engineering lead pushes back. What is the best response?
options: Keep the details, since more specificity always reduces rework later
Remove all technical content, including the requirement to support existing accounts
Ask the engineering manager to confirm that the PM owns the final technical decisions
Move the implementation details out and keep the problem, requirements and constraints
quiz.explanation: A good PRD gives enough context and constraints and leaves the 'how' to engineering and design. Removing everything technical goes too far, because real constraints, such as supporting existing accounts, belong in the PRD.

quiz.question: Why does a PRD include user stories rather than only a list of features?
options: They give engineers the exact implementation steps to follow
They tie each requirement to who needs it and why it matters
They replace the need for acceptance criteria and design review
Scrum requires every backlog item to be written as a story
quiz.explanation: User stories link what is built to a real user need and its benefit, which helps the team make good trade-offs. The Scrum option is a common misconception: Scrum does not require the user story format.

quiz.question: During review of the Social Login PRD, a stakeholder asks about importing Facebook friends. The team has already decided it will not be in v1. How should the PRD handle this?
options: List it under Out of Scope, noting it was considered and deferred
List it under Open Questions so it can stay up for discussion
Leave it out entirely, since the PRD only covers what will be built
List it under Assumptions, since the team assumes users won't need it
quiz.explanation: Writing decided exclusions in Out of Scope prevents scope creep and repeated debates. Open Questions is tempting, but it is for items still undecided, and this one is already decided.

quiz.question: Your Social Login PRD says 'Most of our users already have a Google or Apple account,' but no one has checked this. Where should it go?
options: Under Background, stated as fact since it is true for most phone users
Under Assumptions, flagged so the team can check it before relying on it
Under Goals, since it describes the user base the feature targets
Under Out of Scope, since checking it is not part of building the feature
quiz.explanation: An unchecked belief that the plan depends on belongs under Assumptions, where it is visible and can be validated. Stating it as fact under Background is tempting, but it hides a risk that could undermine the feature.

quiz.question: For the story 'As a new user, I want to sign up with Google so that I can start a workout without creating a password,' which acceptance criterion is best?
options: Google sign-up should feel fast, simple and intuitive to every new user who tries it
Use the Google Identity SDK and store the returned tokens in the existing users table
Google sign-up is fully built and passes all QA regression checks before the release date
A user with no account who signs in with Google gets an account and sees onboarding
quiz.explanation: Good acceptance criteria describe specific, testable user-facing behaviour, such as what happens when a new user signs in with Google. 'Fast, simple and intuitive' is tempting but cannot be verified objectively. The SDK option is an implementation decision, and the QA option is a release gate, not a criterion for this story.

quiz.question: Your PRD is 15 pages long. Engineers say they skim it and still miss key requirements. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Make it concise and scannable, with goals and key requirements first
Add more detail so that every edge case is fully documented
Keep the document as is and walk the team through it in a meeting
Turn it into a slide deck so it is quicker to present to the team
quiz.explanation: PRDs that engineers value are concise and scannable, with the problem, goals and prioritized requirements easy to find and details linked elsewhere. A walkthrough is tempting, but the document stays hard to use as a reference afterwards.

keyTakeaways: Start with problem, not solution
Include clear success metrics
User stories connect user needs to development

lessons.title: User Stories & Acceptance Criteria
lessons.description: Write effective user stories with clear acceptance criteria that drive quality development.
learningObjectives: Write INVEST-quality user stories
Define clear acceptance criteria
Split epics into manageable stories
Connect stories to user value

readingArticles.title: INVEST in Good User Stories
keyPoints: I=Independent, N=Negotiable, V=Valuable, E=Estimable, S=Small, T=Testable
Stories are promises for conversation, not contracts
Slice vertically, not horizontally

readingArticles.title: Acceptance Criteria: Purposes, Formats, and Best Practices
keyPoints: Given/When/Then (Gherkin) format, with worked examples
How acceptance criteria differ from user stories and Definition of Done
Define criteria during backlog grooming, before the sprint starts

videos.title: How to Write User Stories
videos.creator: Atlassian
keyPoints: Focus on user value
Keep stories small
Use acceptance criteria
Slice vertically

practicalTools.name: User Story Breakdown Exercise
practicalTools.description: Break an epic into user stories
practicalTools.exercise: Epic: 'Users can purchase premium subscription.' Break into 5-7 user stories following INVEST: (1) User can view pricing plans (2) User can select a plan (3) User can enter payment info (4) User can apply discount code (5) User receives confirmation (6) User can cancel subscription. Write acceptance criteria for story #3 using Given/When/Then.
practicalTools.deliverable: Epic breakdown with 5-7 stories + acceptance criteria

quiz.question: What does INVEST stand for in user stories?
options: Important, Necessary, Valuable, Estimated, Small, Tested
Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Intuitive, New, Verified, Easy, Simple, Timely
Integrated, Noted, Validated, Executed, Scaled, Tracked
quiz.explanation: INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. Good stories have all these qualities.

quiz.question: What is vertical slicing of stories?
options: Splitting work by technical layer (UI, API, database)
Cutting scope so the story fits a fixed deadline
Prioritizing the highest-value stories in the backlog first
Delivering a thin, end-to-end slice of user functionality
quiz.explanation: Vertical slicing delivers a thin but complete piece of user functionality across all technical layers, so it can be tested end to end. Splitting by technical layer is horizontal slicing, and a layer on its own gives the user nothing they can use.

quiz.question: In the story format 'As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit]', what does the 'so that' clause do?
options: It specifies the technical approach the team should use
It states the user benefit the story is meant to deliver
It lists the conditions the story must meet to be done
It identifies which user persona the story is written for
quiz.explanation: The 'so that' clause ties the story to user value by stating why the user wants it. The conditions for being done belong in the acceptance criteria, not in the story statement.

quiz.question: Your team wants to add 'code is peer-reviewed and unit tests pass' to the acceptance criteria of every story. What is the best response?
options: Add it to each story's acceptance criteria so QA can check it per story
Write it as a Given/When/Then scenario inside each individual story
Put it in the team's Definition of Done, since it applies to all stories
Leave it out of the backlog, since code quality is engineering's concern
quiz.explanation: The Definition of Done holds quality standards that apply to every story, while acceptance criteria describe the behavior one particular story must show. Copying a team-wide standard into every story's criteria creates duplication and mixes the two up.

quiz.question: For the story 'User can enter payment info', which acceptance criterion is best written?
options: Given valid card details are entered, when the user taps Pay, then a confirmation screen appears
Given the payment page, when the user taps Pay, then the backend calls the charge API
Given any card, when the user pays, then the checkout should feel quick and simple
Given a declined card, when the user taps Pay, then the error is handled appropriately
quiz.explanation: Good acceptance criteria are specific and testable, and they describe what the user experiences. The backend-API option describes how to build the feature rather than how it should behave, and 'feel quick' and 'handled appropriately' are too vague to verify.

quiz.question: You are splitting the epic 'Users can purchase a premium subscription'. Which first story best reflects good story splitting?
options: Build all pricing tables and payment APIs first; build the checkout UI next
Design every checkout screen first, then build them, then QA and launch
Subscribe to one plan by card end to end; later stories add plans and coupons
Keep it as one story but raise the estimate so it fits a longer sprint
quiz.explanation: Starting with the simplest complete path delivers testable user value early, and later stories add the variations. Building all the APIs first is a horizontal split, so the user gets nothing they can use until every layer is finished.

quiz.question: Engineers cannot estimate a story because it depends on a third-party payment API nobody on the team has used. What should the PM do?
options: Give it a large estimate and start it, refining the estimate as the team learns
Run a short time-boxed spike on the API, then split and estimate the story
Split it by technical layer so each part is small enough to fit in a sprint
Leave it unestimated and let the team decide its scope during the sprint
quiz.explanation: The story fails the 'Estimable' test because of uncertainty, and a time-boxed spike reduces that uncertainty so the story can be split and sized. Guessing a large estimate and starting anyway brings the unknown into the sprint and puts the commitment at risk.

quiz.question: A stakeholder hands you a story that specifies the exact screen layout, button colors and database fields. Engineers push back. What is the best PM move?
options: Refocus the story on the user need and agree on details with the team
Keep the detailed spec, since precise stories reduce rework later on
Move the layout and field details into the acceptance criteria instead
Let engineering rewrite the story however they prefer to build it
quiz.explanation: Stories are a promise of a conversation, not a contract (the 'Negotiable' in INVEST), so they should state the user need and leave design details to collaboration. Moving implementation details into the acceptance criteria still dictates the solution instead of describing testable behavior.

quiz.question: Stories keep failing QA because developers and testers interpret them differently. Which change most directly fixes this?
options: Agree acceptance criteria with dev and QA during refinement, before the sprint
Have QA write detailed test cases after development of each story is complete
Add more technical detail to each story description before it is assigned
Let each developer define what done means when they pick up the story
quiz.explanation: Defining shared, testable acceptance criteria during backlog refinement aligns developers and testers before any work starts. Writing test cases after development only finds the mismatch later and does not prevent it.

quiz.question: The story 'User can apply a discount code' cannot be built or tested until 'User can enter payment info' ships. Which INVEST quality is weakest here?
options: Negotiable
Estimable
Valuable
Independent
quiz.explanation: A story that depends on another story shipping first is not Independent, which limits how freely it can be prioritized and released. The dependency does not stop the team from estimating it, so Estimable is not the main issue.

keyTakeaways: INVEST makes stories actionable
Acceptance criteria define 'done'
Vertical slices deliver user value faster

readingArticles.title: What Is the Agile Manifesto? 4 Values & 12 Principles Explained
keyPoints: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan
12 principles: early and continuous delivery, welcome changing requirements, sustainable pace, reflect and adjust

readingArticles.title: Scrum Guide 2020
keyPoints: 3 roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers
4 ceremonies: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective
3 artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment
Sprints are 1-4 weeks

videos.title: Scrum in 10 Minutes
videos.creator: Axosoft
keyPoints: Scrum roles and responsibilities
Sprint ceremonies
Backlog management
Increment delivery

practicalTools.name: Sprint Planning Simulation
practicalTools.description: Plan a sprint as a Product Owner
practicalTools.exercise: You have a team of 5 developers with 20 velocity points/sprint. Plan the next sprint: (1) Review 8 backlog items with story points (2) Select items fitting velocity (3) Define sprint goal (4) Identify risks. Items: User profile (5pts), Push notifications (8pts), Dark mode (3pts), Search filters (5pts), Analytics dashboard (13pts), Social sharing (3pts), Email verification (2pts), API integration (8pts).
practicalTools.deliverable: Sprint plan with selected items, goal, and rationale

quiz.question: According to the Scrum Guide, what is the maximum length of a Sprint?
options: 1 week
2 weeks
1 month
3 months
quiz.explanation: The Scrum Guide says Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less. Two weeks is a popular choice for faster feedback, but it is a common practice, not the upper limit.

quiz.question: Who is responsible for maximizing product value?
options: Scrum Master
Product Owner
Developers
Stakeholders
quiz.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team. The Scrum Master is accountable for the team's effectiveness, not for product value.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the four value statements of the Agile Manifesto?
options: Comprehensive documentation over working software
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Following a plan over responding to change
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
quiz.explanation: The Manifesto values individuals and interactions over processes and tools. The other three reverse the real values: it actually values working software, responding to change and customer collaboration more than the items they are paired with.

quiz.question: Three department heads each insist their request must be at the top of the Product Backlog. In Scrum, how should this be resolved?
options: Stakeholders vote, and the request with the most votes goes first
The Scrum Master decides, since they are neutral across departments
The Product Owner orders the backlog by value, using stakeholder input
Developers order it by which requests are quickest to build
quiz.explanation: The Product Owner is accountable for ordering the Product Backlog to maximize value. Stakeholders influence it by convincing the PO, not by owning the order. A vote feels fair, but it replaces a value-based decision with a popularity contest and leaves no single person accountable.

quiz.question: Your team has finished a sprint and wants stakeholders to see what was built and give feedback that may change upcoming priorities. Which Scrum event is designed for this?
options: Sprint Retrospective
Sprint Planning
Sprint Review
Daily Scrum
quiz.explanation: The Sprint Review is where the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog. The Retrospective is the tempting mix-up, but it looks at how the team works (people, process, tools), not at the product with stakeholders.

quiz.question: As Product Owner, you notice the Daily Scrum has turned into developers reporting their status to you one by one. What is the best way to reset it?
options: Keep it as is, since you need daily status to update stakeholders
Remind the team it is for Developers to inspect progress and adapt their plan
Replace it with a written status update that you review each morning
Move it to once a week so it takes up less of the team's time
quiz.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event where Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their own plan. It is not a status report to the PO. Keeping it as a status meeting may look harmless, but it shifts ownership away from the Developers and undermines self-management.

quiz.question: Daily Scrums routinely run 40 minutes, and the team is often blocked by another team's dependencies. In Scrum, who is primarily accountable for helping the team fix these issues?
options: The Product Owner
The engineering manager
The most senior Developer
The Scrum Master
quiz.explanation: The Scrum Master is accountable for the Scrum Team's effectiveness, which includes getting impediments removed and making sure events are productive and kept within their timebox. The Product Owner focuses on maximizing product value through the backlog, not on fixing the team's process.

quiz.question: An engineer cites "working software over comprehensive documentation" to argue the team should write no requirements at all. What is the best response?
options: Agree, since the Manifesto says documentation adds no value in Agile teams
Disagree, and require a full specification signed off before any coding starts
Agree for now, and write complete documentation once the product has launched
The Manifesto values documentation less, not zero; keep it lightweight and useful
quiz.explanation: The Manifesto says that while there is value in the items on the right, the items on the left are valued more. So documentation still matters when it builds shared understanding. Requiring a full signed-off spec swings to the opposite extreme, slowing feedback and working against the Agile value.

quiz.question: Which of these teams is the best fit for Scrum's sprint-based structure?
options: A team building a new product where needs and solutions are still uncertain
A team running a repeatable monthly payroll export with well-known steps
A support team handling unpredictable tickets that need same-day fixes
A team doing a fully specified migration with fixed scope and known steps
quiz.explanation: Scrum is built on empiricism (transparency, inspection, adaptation) for complex work where requirements and solutions are uncertain. The support team is the tempting choice because its work is unpredictable, but it is continuous interrupt-driven work that a flow approach such as Kanban usually handles better than fixed sprint commitments.

quiz.question: Mid-quarter, user research shows the next roadmap feature solves a low-priority problem, while a bigger customer pain point has emerged. What best reflects Agile values?
options: Share the evidence with stakeholders and reorder the backlog toward the bigger problem
Keep building the planned feature, since the roadmap was already committed to leadership
Finish the planned feature first, then revisit priorities at the next annual planning
Add the new problem to the current sprint without changing anything else in the plan
quiz.explanation: Agile values responding to change over following a plan, and the PO maximizes value by reordering the backlog as new evidence arrives, while keeping stakeholders informed. Sticking to the committed roadmap feels safe, but it knowingly spends capacity on lower-value work.

keyTakeaways: Agile values adaptation over planning
PO maximizes value through backlog
Scrum provides structure for complex work

practicalTools.name: Backlog Refinement Session
practicalTools.description: Refine a sample product backlog
practicalTools.exercise: You have 10 raw backlog items for a food delivery app. Refine them by: (1) Rewriting vague items into clear user stories (2) Adding acceptance criteria to 3 items (3) Estimating with story points using planning poker (4) Identifying dependencies (5) Marking top 5 as 'ready for sprint'.
practicalTools.deliverable: Refined backlog with 10 properly written stories

quiz.question: A common rule of thumb says backlog refinement should take no more than what share of a team's sprint capacity?
quiz.explanation: The 2013 and 2017 Scrum Guides said refinement usually takes no more than about 10% of the team's capacity. The 2020 guide dropped the number, but 10% is still a common rule of thumb. 25% or more cuts heavily into delivery time, and 5% is usually too little to keep the top items ready.

quiz.question: In Scrum sprint planning, who selects the work for the sprint?
options: Product Owner assigns tasks
Scrum Master decides
Manager allocates work
Developers select items
quiz.explanation: The Product Owner presents and clarifies the priorities, and the Developers select how much of the backlog they can take on, based on their capacity and the sprint goal. The PO sets the order of the backlog but does not assign work to people.

quiz.question: What should a team come out of a well-run sprint planning session with?
options: A finalized quarterly roadmap with committed release dates
Signed-off requirement documents for every backlog item
A list of tasks the Product Owner has assigned to each developer
A sprint goal and a sprint backlog with a plan to deliver it
quiz.explanation: Sprint planning covers WHAT the team will deliver and HOW it will do it, and it ends with a sprint goal and a sprint backlog (the selected items plus a plan). Assigning tasks to individuals is the most tempting wrong answer, but the team plans and organizes its own work.

quiz.question: During planning poker for a food delivery app story, one engineer votes 3 points and another votes 13. What should the team do next?
options: Have the high and low voters explain their reasoning, then re-vote
Take the average of about 8 points so the meeting keeps moving
Go with the most senior engineer's estimate, since they know best
Ask the Product Owner to choose the final estimate for the story
quiz.explanation: A wide spread in votes usually means people understand the story differently, so the outliers should explain their reasoning before the team votes again. Averaging hides that disagreement instead of resolving it, so the estimate stays unreliable.

quiz.question: A five-developer team averages 30 story points per two-week sprint. Next sprint, two developers are on leave for one week each. How much should the team plan to take on?
options: 30 points, because velocity is the team's average
About 24 points, scaled down to the reduced capacity
About 36 points, adding stretch work to catch up
About 15 points, halving the plan to be safe
quiz.explanation: Capacity falls by about 20% (10 of 50 developer-days), so planning about 24 points uses past velocity adjusted for availability. Planning the usual 30 ignores the reduced capacity and almost guarantees the team will overcommit.

quiz.question: Midway through a sprint, a sales VP asks your team to build a new feature for a prospect demo next month. As PM, what should you do?
options: Swap it in for a similar-sized story so the sprint's total points stay the same
Add it to the current sprint and ask the team to absorb it with extra hours
Add it to the product backlog and weigh it against other priorities before next planning
Cancel the current sprint and replan the work around the new request
quiz.explanation: The demo is a month away, so the request can go through normal prioritization without disrupting the current sprint. Swapping in a story of the same size keeps the point total level, but it still disrupts the team's plan and focus mid-sprint when nothing urgent justifies it, and it skips weighing the request against other priorities.

quiz.question: Halfway through a sprint, the team realizes it cannot finish every item it planned. What is the best response?
options: Extend the sprint by a few days so every planned item can be finished
Work with the PO to drop items that aren't essential to the sprint goal
Shorten testing on the remaining items so that everything still fits
Keep all items in scope and let unfinished ones roll into next sprint
quiz.explanation: The sprint goal stays fixed, but scope can be renegotiated with the PO as the team learns more, so the team protects the goal and drops less important items. Extending the sprint is tempting, but it breaks the fixed sprint length that makes delivery predictable.

quiz.question: Your sprint planning meetings keep running long because the team spends them debating what stories mean and splitting large epics. What is the best fix?
options: Make sprint planning a full-day session so there is time for the debate
Have the PO write detailed specs alone and assign stories to developers
Hold regular backlog refinement so top items arrive clarified and sized
Skip estimation in planning and let developers size stories during the sprint
quiz.explanation: Ongoing refinement clarifies, splits and estimates the top backlog items before planning, so the planning meeting can focus on choosing work and defining the sprint goal. A longer meeting treats the symptom but still leaves the items unready.

quiz.question: A food delivery app's backlog has the vague item "Make search better." Which rewrite is most ready for a sprint?
options: As a customer, I want to filter restaurants by delivery time; done when only places under 30 min show
As a user, I want a much better search experience so the app feels faster, smarter and more modern
Rebuild the search service on a new engine and add fresh indexes for restaurants, dishes and cuisines
As a user, I want search, filters, sorting, saved searches and personalized recommendations in one place
quiz.explanation: The first option is a small, user-focused story with a testable acceptance criterion, which makes it ready to estimate and build. The 'better search experience' option looks like a user story but has no measurable acceptance criteria, so the team cannot tell when it is done.

quiz.question: Leadership wants to compare two teams' velocity to decide which team is more productive. As PM, how should you respond?
options: Agree, as long as both teams estimate using the same Fibonacci point scale
Agree, and set a velocity growth target for each team to drive productivity
Explain that story points are team-relative and propose outcome metrics instead
Compare only teams that share the same sprint length and team size
quiz.explanation: Each team calibrates its story points relative to its own past work, so velocity helps a team forecast but cannot be compared across teams. Using the same Fibonacci scale is the tempting answer, but the same numbers still mean different amounts of work to each team, and velocity targets tend to cause point inflation.

keyTakeaways: Team selects work, not PO assigns
Refine 10% of capacity
Sprint goal aligns the team

practicalTools.name: Stakeholder Map & RACI Matrix
practicalTools.description: Map stakeholders and define roles
practicalTools.exercise: For a new checkout feature: (1) List 8 stakeholders (Engineering Lead, Designer, QA, Marketing, Sales, Customer Support, Legal, CFO) (2) Plot on Influence/Interest matrix (3) Create RACI for 5 key activities (Requirements sign-off, UX review, Launch approval, Marketing messaging, Post-launch review).
practicalTools.deliverable: Stakeholder map + RACI matrix

quiz.question: In RACI, what does 'Accountable' mean?
options: The person who carries out the work itself
Someone whose input is sought before deciding
Someone kept updated on progress afterwards
The person who ultimately owns the outcome
quiz.explanation: Accountable = the ONE person who ultimately owns the decision/outcome. Responsible = those doing the work. Only 1 Accountable per task.

quiz.question: How should you handle a high-influence stakeholder who disagrees with your roadmap?
options: Proceed as planned and explain your rationale at the next roadmap review
Add their requested items to the roadmap to protect the working relationship
Escalate to your own manager so leadership can make the final call
Meet one-on-one to understand their concerns, then align using data and trade-offs
quiz.explanation: High-influence stakeholders need to be managed closely. Seek to understand their perspective, share data, and find win-win solutions. Simply adding their requests gives up prioritization discipline, and escalating before you understand the concern damages trust.

quiz.question: On an Influence/Interest matrix for a new checkout feature, Legal has high influence but low day-to-day interest. What is the usual approach for this stakeholder?
options: Manage closely with frequent working sessions
Keep informed through regular broad status updates
Monitor with minimal effort until they show interest
Keep satisfied with targeted check-ins on key decisions
quiz.explanation: High-influence, low-interest stakeholders are usually kept satisfied: involve them on the decisions that affect them (e.g., compliance) without flooding them with detail. 'Manage closely' is for high-influence, high-interest stakeholders, and minimal monitoring risks a late veto.

quiz.question: In a RACI matrix, what is the key difference between 'Consulted' and 'Informed'?
options: Consulted give input before a decision; Informed are updated after it
Consulted are senior leaders; Informed are junior team members
Consulted approve the work; Informed carry out the work
Consulted are internal teams; Informed are external customers
quiz.explanation: Consulted is two-way: their input is sought before the decision or the work is done. Informed is one-way: they are told about progress or outcomes. RACI roles depend on involvement in a task, not on seniority, so the 'senior vs junior' option is wrong.

quiz.question: In your RACI for 'Launch approval', the Engineering Lead, Head of Marketing, and you (the PM) are all marked Accountable. Launch decisions keep stalling. What is the best fix?
options: Name a single Accountable owner and make the others Consulted
Mark all three as Responsible so the work is shared equally
Add the CFO as a further Accountable to break any ties
Drop the RACI and decide launch approval by majority vote
quiz.explanation: Common RACI practice is exactly one Accountable per activity, so there is a clear decision owner. Others can be Consulted for input. Adding another Accountable to break ties makes the shared ownership worse, which is the cause of the stalling.

quiz.question: Midway through building a checkout feature, Sales insists a discount-code field was 'already agreed' and must be added. What would most likely have prevented this scope creep?
options: A longer PRD listing every feature that might be requested
A RACI naming who is Accountable for requirements sign-off
Inviting Sales to every daily standup for full visibility
Letting engineering finalize scope during each sprint planning
quiz.explanation: A RACI makes decision ownership explicit. If Sales is Consulted and one person is Accountable for sign-off, late asks go through a deliberate change decision instead of being 'agreed' informally. Inviting Sales to standups adds visibility, but it does not settle who decides scope.

quiz.question: You need to tell the CFO that the checkout launch will slip by two weeks. Which update is most appropriate for this audience?
options: Lead with the business impact, a one-line cause, and any decision you need
Walk through the technical root cause and open bug list to show rigor
Forward the detailed update you already sent to the engineering channel
Share the sprint burndown chart so they can see where the slippage began
quiz.explanation: Tailor communication to the audience: executives need impact, cause, and the decision or ask, not implementation detail. Forwarding the engineering update looks efficient, but it buries what the CFO cares about under technical detail.

quiz.question: You discover a dependency risk that will probably delay a launch date you committed to a high-influence VP. What should you do?
options: Wait for the monthly review so you can raise it with complete data
Ask the team to work extra hours to protect the date before raising it
Raise it with the VP now, with the likely impact and the options you see
Share it only with the engineering lead until a fix plan is confirmed
quiz.explanation: Transparency builds trust. Flag risks early, along with impact and options, so the stakeholder can help or adjust plans. Waiting for complete data is tempting, but a late surprise does more damage to trust than an early heads-up on an incomplete picture.

quiz.question: Marketing wants the new checkout live before a festive sale. Legal says the compliance review needs three more weeks, which misses the sale. As PM, what is the best next step?
options: Launch on Marketing's date, as the sale revenue outweighs a short compliance gap
Move the launch three weeks and tell Marketing that Legal's view takes priority
Explore options like a reduced-scope launch and bring trade-offs to the decision owner
Ask Marketing and Legal to resolve the conflict directly and report back to you
quiz.explanation: In a difficult conflict between stakeholders, the PM frames options and trade-offs, such as a compliant reduced-scope or phased launch, and takes them to the Accountable decision-maker. Delaying immediately respects compliance but skips options that might meet both needs. Launching with a compliance gap is not acceptable.

quiz.question: Two weeks before launch, Customer Support learns about the new checkout flow and says they have no help articles or training. What is the best response?
options: Keep the date and let Support build articles from the first week of incoming tickets
Agree on the minimum Support needs for launch and add them to the RACI as Consulted
Postpone launch until Support has completed full training on every edge case
Log it as low-influence feedback and revisit it in the post-launch review
quiz.explanation: Support was missed when stakeholders were mapped. The fix is to close the critical gap now and give them a defined role so it does not happen again. Launching and learning from tickets pushes the cost onto customers, and a full training program over-corrects with an unnecessary delay.

keyTakeaways: Not all stakeholders are equal—prioritize
RACI prevents confusion and scope creep
Transparency builds trust

practicalTools.name: A/B Test Design Exercise

practicalTools.exercise: Design an A/B test for a checkout button color change: (1) Write hypothesis (2) Define primary metric (3) Define 2 guardrail metrics (4) Calculate required sample size (5) Set test duration (6) Define stopping criteria (7) Plan result analysis (segment by device type).
practicalTools.deliverable: Complete A/B test design document

quiz.question: What does p<0.05 mean in A/B testing?
options: The test has run long enough to reach its planned sample size
With no real difference, results at least this extreme occur under 5% of the time
The variant has at least a 95% chance of being better than control
The observed lift is accurate to within plus or minus 5 percent
quiz.explanation: A p-value is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the null hypothesis (no real difference) were true; p<0.05 means that probability is under 5%. It is not the probability that the variant is better, which is the most common misreading.

quiz.question: What is a guardrail metric?
options: A metric we monitor to ensure we're not causing harm
The primary metric we're trying to improve
A secondary metric we hope also improves alongside the primary
A leading indicator used to predict the primary metric early
quiz.explanation: Guardrail metrics protect against unintended negative consequences. For example, when testing a faster signup flow (primary: conversion rate), retention could be a guardrail so that faster signup does not lower user quality. A secondary metric is something you hope improves, while a guardrail is something you must not harm.

quiz.question: Before a checkout redesign test, the team proposes declaring a winner if any of conversion, order value, click-through, or time on page improves significantly. What is the best response?
options: Pick one primary metric up front and treat the others as secondary or guardrails
Accept it, since more success metrics give a fuller picture of impact
Require all four metrics to improve significantly before shipping
Wait for the results and use whichever metric moved the most as the primary
quiz.explanation: If you count any of several metrics as a win, the chance of a false positive goes up and you invite cherry-picking, so you should set one primary decision metric before the test starts. Requiring all four to improve swings too far the other way: real wins on the metric that matters would get rejected.

quiz.question: Why should a PM calculate the required sample size before launching an A/B test?
options: So the test can stop as soon as the result first looks significant
So the test is powered to detect the smallest lift worth acting on
So each variant receives an identical number of visitors every day
So the p-value threshold can be adjusted to match available traffic
quiz.explanation: Sample size comes from the minimum detectable effect, the baseline rate, the significance level and the power, so the test can reliably detect a lift that matters. Fixing it in advance also removes the temptation to stop when the result first looks significant, which inflates false positives.

quiz.question: On day 3 of a test planned for 14 days, the dashboard shows the variant ahead with p=0.03. A stakeholder wants to ship now. What should you do?
options: Keep running to the planned sample size before deciding
Ship now, since p<0.05 means the result is already reliable
Roll the variant out to half of users and keep monitoring
Stop the test and restart it with a fresh sample to confirm
quiz.explanation: Checking results early and stopping on the first significant reading ('peeking') inflates the false-positive rate well above 5%, so the decision should wait for the pre-planned sample size. A p-value read early in the test does not have the reliability it has at the planned endpoint.

quiz.question: A one-click checkout test lifts conversion by 4% (statistically significant), but the refund-request guardrail rises 12%. What is the best next step?
options: Ship it, since the primary metric was pre-registered as the decision rule
Ship it now and open a separate ticket to reduce refunds later
Hold the launch and investigate whether the refund rise erases the gain
Rerun the test with refund requests as the new primary metric
quiz.explanation: Guardrails exist to catch harm the primary metric cannot see. A large refund increase may cancel out the conversion gain or point to accidental purchases, so you should understand it before launching. Shipping and fixing later exposes every user to a harm you already know about.

quiz.question: A test shows no overall change, but after the fact you notice mobile users improved 6% while desktop dropped 5%. Device was not a pre-planned segment. What should you do?
options: Ship the variant to mobile users only, since that lift is real
Conclude the variant has no effect, since the overall result was flat
Keep slicing by other segments until one reaches significance
Treat it as a hypothesis and run a follow-up test powered for mobile
quiz.explanation: Segmenting can reveal effects that cancel out in the overall number. But a segment you found after the fact is exploratory and could be noise, so you should confirm it with a properly powered follow-up test. Shipping to mobile now treats an unplanned, underpowered slice as a confirmed result.

quiz.question: A designer wants to test 8 button colours at once on a low-traffic page. What is the main risk?
options: Users will notice the different colours and behave unnaturally
Each variant would need its own primary metric to be valid
Random assignment stops working once there are over two groups
Traffic is split thinly and many comparisons raise false-winner odds
quiz.explanation: With many variants, each one gets less traffic, so the test needs far longer to reach adequate power. Each extra comparison also adds a chance of finding a false winner. Randomisation still works fine with more than two groups; the problem is statistical power and multiple comparisons.

quiz.question: A test reports a 2% lift in conversion with a 95% confidence interval of -0.5% to +4.5%. How should you read this?
options: The variant has a 95% chance of lifting conversion by exactly 2%
The lift is significant because most of the interval is positive
Not significant at the 5% level, since the interval includes zero
The variant is likely harmful, since the interval dips below zero
quiz.explanation: Because the 95% interval includes zero, the data are consistent with no effect, so the result is not significant at the 5% level. Most of the interval being positive does not make it significant, and the small negative tail does not show harm either; it only means you cannot rule out zero or a small negative effect.

quiz.question: Your sample size calculation says the checkout test needs 4 days of traffic, and checkout behaviour differs a lot between weekdays and weekends. How long should you plan to run it?
options: Exactly 4 days, stopping the moment the sample size is reached
At least one full week so every day of the week is represented
Four weekdays only, excluding the less typical weekend traffic
Until the p-value first drops below 0.05, however long it takes
quiz.explanation: A common rule is to run for at least one full weekly cycle so the result reflects how all users behave, not only weekday users. Stopping at exactly 4 days meets the sample size but over-represents some days, which is the 'running too short' pitfall.

keyTakeaways: One primary metric per test
Calculate sample size before starting
Guardrail metrics protect users
Segment results for deeper insights
