quiz.question: A ride-hailing company is launching in a new city. Driver onboarding, payments, regulatory approvals and marketing are separate projects run by different teams, and all of them must land in the same week. Which role is mainly accountable for coordinating the dependencies across these projects?
options: The product manager for the rider app, who owns the rider experience
The Scrum product owner for the payments team, who orders its backlog
A program manager, who coordinates related projects toward one goal
The project manager for the marketing campaign, who owns its timeline
quiz.explanation: Coordinating several related projects toward one shared objective is the program manager's job. The rider-app PM is the tempting choice, but that PM owns what the rider app builds and why, not the delivery dependencies across payments, regulatory and marketing.

quiz.question: According to the Scrum Guide, what is the product owner accountable for?
options: Facilitating the daily stand-up and removing the team's impediments
Estimating story points on behalf of the developers each sprint
Approving the team's technical architecture before sprint planning
Maximising the product's value, including ordering the product backlog
quiz.explanation: The Scrum Guide makes the product owner accountable for maximising value and for managing the product backlog effectively (see Day 17). Removing impediments and making sure the Daily Scrum happens is the Scrum Master's area, and estimating belongs to the developers.

quiz.question: You join a fintech lending app as a PM. Illustrative data: loan applications have grown 15-20% month on month for six months, and early cohorts retain well. Crash rates and support tickets are rising with load, and onboarding drop-off has crept up. What stage is the product in, and what should you prioritise?
options: Growth stage: invest in reliability and onboarding so quality keeps pace with demand
Introduction stage: slow growth and rerun discovery to confirm product-market fit
Maturity stage: shift focus to cutting costs and raising margin on existing borrowers
Decline stage: plan to move borrowers onto a new lending product line instead
quiz.explanation: Sustained fast growth with healthy early retention means product-market fit is found and the product is scaling. The job now is to keep reliability and onboarding up with demand. Going back to discovery is tempting because problems are rising, but retention already shows fit. These are scaling problems, not fit problems.

quiz.question: You are a PM for a food delivery app in a large metro. Illustrative data: order growth has flattened to about 1% a quarter, most of the target customers already use the app, and competitors match most features within weeks. Which set of priorities fits best?
options: Raise acquisition spend to restart top-of-funnel growth in the same metro
Grow retention and order frequency and improve unit economics on each order
Build an MVP and test new value propositions with a small group of early adopters
Stop new feature work and run the app in maintenance mode to harvest cash
quiz.explanation: Saturation and feature parity point to maturity. Here the PM defends the base and gets more value from it through retention, order frequency and margin. More acquisition spend is the tempting carry-over from the growth stage, but with most target users already on the app it buys very little. Maintenance mode is a decline-stage response, and it is too early while order volume is stable.

quiz.question: Company A, a bank, is hiring a 'Product Owner' who writes user stories, refines the backlog and attends sprint ceremonies, while a 'Head of Digital Product' sets strategy. Company B, a startup, is hiring a 'Product Manager' who interviews users, sets the quarterly roadmap, owns the activation metric and also writes stories. Which reading is most accurate?
options: A is mostly about executing the backlog, while B combines strategy and backlog ownership
A is the more senior role, because product owners rank above product managers in agile
Both are effectively the same job, because both roles write user stories for the team
B is really a project management role, because it involves setting a roadmap with dates
quiz.explanation: Titles vary, so judge each role by what it owns. A executes strategy that someone else sets, while B owns the problem, the roadmap and the outcome as well as the backlog. Treating them as the same job because both write stories confuses a shared task with shared accountability.

quiz.question: Your self-assessment: Discovery 4, Strategy 3, Prioritization 3, Metrics & Unit Economics 2, Experimentation 2, Analytics 3, Launch/GTM 3, Technical 4, AI 3, Leadership 3, Case Studies 3. You are aiming for a growth PM role at an e-commerce company. Which 4-week plan is most defensible?
options: Experimentation in weeks 1-2, then Metrics & Unit Economics in weeks 3-4, each week ending with a written test or metric artefact
Metrics & Unit Economics in weeks 1-2, then Experimentation in weeks 3-4, each week ending with a written metric or test artefact
AI products for all four weeks, since it is a fast-growing specialisation, each week ending with a written AI feature brief
Discovery for all four weeks, to turn a 4 into a signature strength, each week ending with a written interview synthesis
quiz.explanation: Both weakest areas matter for a growth role, and Metrics comes before Experimentation in the path because you cannot design or read a test without the right success and guardrail metrics. Starting with Experimentation is tempting because testing feels like the core growth skill, but it would rest on a weak metrics foundation.

quiz.question: Your SaaS lead asks you to 'own the launch' of a new invoicing feature. The engineering manager assumes you are tracking the timeline, marketing assumes it owns launch messaging, and a PMO project manager also exists. Two weeks in, nobody has booked the partner bank's sandbox testing slot. What is the best first move?
options: Book the sandbox slot yourself now, and deal with the ownership confusion after launch
Escalate to your lead that the PMO project manager failed to track this dependency
Agree a RACI for launch tasks with the leads, starting by giving the sandbox an owner today
Ask marketing to track launch dependencies, since it already owns launch messaging
quiz.explanation: The root problem is unclear ownership. A RACI (Day 19) fixes it for this task and every later one, while the sandbox still gets an owner today. Booking the slot yourself closes this one gap but leaves ownership unclear until after launch, so the next dependency can be dropped the same way.

quiz.question: New-user growth for a subscription app has slowed for three straight quarters. Which additional finding most strongly suggests the product has moved from growth into maturity, rather than having a fixable problem or entering decline?
options: Activation of new sign-ups fell from 40% to 28% after an onboarding redesign last year
Total active users have fallen for three quarters as customers switch to a newer substitute
Sign-ups dropped for two quarters right after the paid acquisition budget was cut in half
Growth slowed across every acquisition channel while most of the target market is already active
quiz.explanation: A slowdown across every channel once most of the target market is already reached is structural saturation, which is the mark of maturity. The activation drop is tempting, but it points to a self-inflicted funnel problem the team can fix while still in growth. A shrinking active base as users move to a substitute signals decline, not maturity.

quiz.question: You have finished Discovery (Module 2) and run user interviews well. You now want to study Prioritization (Module 4), but you cannot yet state your product's goals for the year or explain where it should play and how it wins. Which module should you study first?
options: Metrics & Unit Economics (Module 5), because RICE scores need reliable impact numbers
Product Strategy (Module 3), because priorities are ranked against strategic goals
Leadership (Module 11), because prioritising is mostly about saying no to stakeholders
Experimentation (Module 6), because ideas should be tested before they are ranked
quiz.explanation: You can only rank work against goals, so Strategy is the prerequisite for Prioritization in the path. Metrics is tempting because frameworks like RICE need impact estimates, but it comes after Prioritization, and impact only means something relative to the goals the strategy sets.

quiz.question: You manage a legacy cash-on-delivery reconciliation tool for merchants on an e-commerce marketplace. Illustrative data: usage has fallen for six straight quarters as merchants move to prepaid and UPI, 8% of merchants still depend on the tool, it earns no direct revenue, and maintenance takes about a third of one team's capacity. The main payments dashboard could cover COD reconciliation with a small extension. What is the best course?
options: Invest in a redesign to improve the tool for the 8% of merchants still using it
Shut the tool down next week to free up engineering capacity as quickly as possible
Plan a phased sunset with a migration path, merchant communication and an end date
Freeze new features indefinitely and keep maintaining the tool exactly as it is today
quiz.explanation: The decline is long and structural, the tool earns nothing, and a migration destination exists, so a planned sunset protects the remaining merchants and frees capacity on a known date. Harvesting by freezing and maintaining is tempting because it is a valid decline strategy, but here it keeps paying a third of a team's capacity for no revenue, with no end date.

keyTakeaways: Product owns the why and what. Project owns the when, scope and budget of one effort. Program owns how related projects land together toward one shared goal. Product owner is a Scrum accountability for maximising value through the backlog, and the PM often holds it too.
Titles lie, ownership doesn't: Microsoft long used 'Program Manager' for product work, so in any team ask who decides what gets built and who answers for the outcome.
The lifecycle stage changes the job: find fit, then scale, then defend and extract value, then harvest, reposition or sunset with a plan.
Study your gaps in prerequisite order, and back every self-rating with evidence instead of a feeling.

lessons.label: Module 2
lessons.title: Continuous Discovery: Jobs To Be Done, Opportunity Solution Trees & Assumption Mapping
lessons.description: Learn to frame customer needs as jobs, map them in an Opportunity Solution Tree from a measurable outcome down to assumption tests, and pick the riskiest assumption to test first as part of a weekly discovery habit.
learningObjectives: Write a job story for a product (e.g. the food delivery app in the exercise) in the form 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [desired outcome]', and describe its functional, emotional and social dimensions
Use the four forces of progress (push, pull, anxiety, habit) to explain why a specific user segment does or does not switch, and name one product lever for each force
Build an Opportunity Solution Tree with a measurable product outcome, at least 3 opportunities written as customer needs, one chosen target opportunity and 3 competing solutions

List at least 6 assumptions behind a solution, tag each as desirability, viability, feasibility, usability or ethical, place them on an importance-vs-evidence map, and write a test plan for the riskiest one with success criteria set in advance

readingArticles.title: Opportunity Solution Trees: Visualize Your Discovery to Stay Aligned and Drive Outcomes
keyPoints: The tree runs from a desired outcome at the root, through the opportunity space (customer needs, pain points and desires), to solutions and then assumption tests

Starting from a desired outcome (ideally a product outcome the team can influence that drives a business outcome) keeps discovery commercially grounded, while the opportunity layer keeps it customer-centric
Before building a tree, the author recommends a clear target customer, a clearly defined outcome and a few story-based customer interviews
The tree is a living document. Update it as new interviews and assumption tests come in, not once a quarter

readingArticles.title: Assumption Testing: Everything You Need to Know to Get Started
keyPoints: Names five assumption categories: desirability, viability, feasibility, usability and ethical

Assumption mapping (a technique from David J. Bland that Torres uses) ranks assumptions by how important they are to the idea and how much evidence you already have, so the riskiest one is tested first
Describes test types: prototype tests, one-question surveys, data mining and research spikes
Advises comparing several solutions at once and not deciding based on a single assumption test

readingArticles.title: Unpacking the Progress Making Forces Diagram (Full Transcript)
readingArticles.source: Jobs-to-be-Done Radio (Bob Moesta & Chris Spiek, The Re-Wired Group)
keyPoints: Bob Moesta and Chris Spiek walk through the four forces: the push of the current situation and the pull of the new solution drive a switch, while the anxiety of the new solution and the habit of the present hold it back
A struggling moment creates the push, but push alone is not enough: people also need a concrete new option that pulls them
Customers rarely talk about anxiety and habit unprompted, yet these hidden forces explain why people who like a product still do not switch (and where non-consumption lives)
Switch interviews rebuild the timeline of a real decision so you can see where each force built up; most of the story is noise, and the useful part is the energy and effort behind the switch

videos.title: Build better products with continuous product discovery | Teresa Torres
videos.creator: Lenny's Podcast
keyPoints: Continuous discovery explained: the team building the product talks to customers at least weekly
How a product trio (PM, designer, engineer) shares discovery work instead of handing it off
Using Opportunity Solution Trees to connect business outcomes to customer opportunities
Testing assumptions instead of whole ideas, to learn faster and spend less

videos.title: Clay Christensen: The Jobs to be Done Theory
videos.creator: HubSpot Marketing
keyPoints: Clayton Christensen explains the idea that customers 'hire' products to get a job done
Why demographic and product-category views can hide the real job and the real competition
The well-known milkshake example: the same product can be hired for different jobs in different situations
Why the circumstances around a purchase matter more than the customer's attributes

practicalTools.name: Opportunity Solution Tree + Assumption Map
practicalTools.description: A fill-in worksheet that takes you from a job story and its four forces to one measurable outcome, a chosen target opportunity, three competing solutions, a ranked list of assumptions and one test plan. It builds on Day 4 (interviews) and Day 6 (problem statements), and does not repeat them. The 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [desired outcome]' job story format comes from Intercom/Alan Klement; Ulwick's Outcome-Driven Innovation writes job statements as verb + object + context (e.g. 'restock breakfast staples before the morning'). Both stay solution-free. Every job has a functional dimension (the practical task), an emotional one (how the person wants to feel) and a social one (how they want others to see them). The four forces of progress (Bob Moesta and Chris Spiek) are a widely used heuristic, not a law: push of the current situation and pull of the new solution drive a switch; anxiety about the new solution and habit of the present hold it back. A switch happens only when push + pull outweigh anxiety + habit. Opportunity sizing is covered in Day 6, ranking solutions with RICE/MoSCoW/Kano in Day 11, and opportunity scoring in Deep Dive 4. Experiment statistics are covered in Deep Dive 6.
practicalTools.exercise: Context (illustrative): you are the PM for a food delivery app. 30% of new users place a second order within 14 days, and the target is 36%. (1) In Part 0 of the template, write one job story for a new user in the form 'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [desired outcome]', and add one functional, one emotional and one social dimension. (2) Note one push, one pull, one anxiety and one habit that affects whether a new user comes back to your app instead of their usual option, and name one product lever that strengthens push/pull or reduces anxiety/habit for each. (3) Fill in Part A of the template. Write at least 3 opportunities of your own as customer needs (not features), break at least one into sub-opportunities, choose ONE target opportunity, and come up with 3 different solutions for it. (4) For your strongest solution, fill in Part B. Write at least 6 'We believe that...' assumptions covering at least 4 of the 5 types, score importance and evidence, and place them on the map. (5) Fill in Part C for the assumption in the 'test first' quadrant. Choose the cheapest test that measures behaviour, and set the pass or fail threshold before you run it. Time box: 60 minutes.
practicalTools.deliverable: A job story with functional, emotional and social dimensions, a four-forces table with one product lever per force, a one-page Opportunity Solution Tree (outcome, 3 or more opportunities, a chosen target opportunity, 3 solutions), an assumption table with 6 or more typed and scored assumptions, an importance-vs-evidence map, and a test plan for the riskiest assumption with pre-set success criteria

quiz.question: You are a PM on a grocery delivery app. Which of these is the best-formed Jobs To Be Done job story?
options: When I realise late in the evening that we're out of breakfast staples, I want to restock quickly so the morning isn't disrupted
Busy working parents aged 28-40 in metro cities who order groceries online about twice a week and value speed
I want a 'reorder last basket' button on the home screen so I can check out faster on busy weekday evenings
Users should be able to search, filter and add items to the cart in fewer taps than they can today in the app
quiz.explanation: A job story describes the situation, the motivation and the progress the customer wants, without naming a product. The 'reorder button' option is tempting because it sounds customer-centred, but it is a solution dressed up as a need. The first option is a persona or segment, not a job.

quiz.question: In Teresa Torres's Opportunity Solution Tree, what belongs at the root of the tree?
options: The highest-demand feature from support tickets and sales calls, so the tree starts from proven customer pull
A measurable outcome the team is asked to drive, such as the share of trial users who activate in week one
The company's long-term product vision, so every branch of the tree ladders up to the overall strategy
The primary persona the team serves, so every opportunity on the tree stays tied to one specific user
quiz.explanation: The tree starts from a desired outcome, then branches into opportunities, solutions and assumption tests. The vision is tempting because the tree should align with strategy, but it is too broad to measure progress against. A requested feature belongs at the solution level.

quiz.question: You are reviewing a ride-hailing team's Opportunity Solution Tree. Under the outcome 'increase rider ratings of trips', the opportunity branches read: 'Add in-app tipping', 'Add a driver photo on the pickup screen', 'Add a quiet-ride toggle'. What is the most important fix?
options: Add a RICE score to each branch so the team can rank the three ideas objectively before building any of them
Replace the outcome with trip revenue, because rider ratings are a vanity metric for a ride-hailing business
Add more branches so the tree covers at least five feature ideas before the trio commits to one of them
Rewrite the branches as rider needs, e.g. 'Is this the right car?', and move the features under them as solutions
quiz.explanation: These branches are solutions placed in the opportunity layer. That shuts down the problem space and makes it impossible to compare different solutions for the same need. Scoring them with RICE only ranks features before anyone has checked which customer needs matter.

quiz.question: Your fintech team mapped assumptions for a 'round-up savings' feature. Which assumption should you test first?
options: Users can find the round-up toggle in settings: medium importance, little evidence
Our payments partner supports micro-transfers: critical to the idea, confirmed in their API docs
Users like the savings jar illustration: low importance, no evidence yet
Users want to save spare change automatically: critical to the idea, almost no evidence
quiz.explanation: The riskiest assumption is the one that is both critical to the idea and least supported by evidence. The partner assumption is just as important, but you already have strong evidence for it, so testing it again teaches you little.

quiz.question: Your neobank sees many users open an account but not move their salary credit to it. In interviews about why they did or did not switch, users praise your features but keep saying 'What if my salary gets stuck during the change?' Using the four forces of progress, what is the best next move?
options: Strengthen the pull by adding more premium features, such as higher cashback and lounge access
Reduce the anxiety of the new with an assisted salary-switch flow and a clear guarantee if a credit is delayed
Increase the push by highlighting fees and pain points of users' current bank in ads
Accept the habit of the present and target only users who have never had a salary account
quiz.explanation: Users already feel the pull (they praise the features). What blocks the switch is anxiety about the transition, so reducing that anxiety is the lever most likely to work. Adding more pull is the common mistake: it does not remove the fear that is stopping them.

quiz.question: Leadership tells your food delivery team: 'Grow GMV 20% this year.' You are setting up an Opportunity Solution Tree. What is the best outcome to place at the root?
options: GMV itself, because it is the number leadership will judge the team on at year end
Launch a loyalty programme by Q3, because it is the initiative most likely to move GMV
Number of discovery interviews completed per week, because it measures discovery progress
The % of new users who place a second order within 14 days, a driver of GMV the team can directly influence
quiz.explanation: Torres recommends product outcomes: behaviour metrics the team can influence that drive the business outcome. GMV is tempting, but it is a lagging business outcome with too many inputs for one team to learn from week to week, and a launch date is an output, not an outcome.

quiz.question: A SaaS team runs one big round of 20 customer interviews each quarter, writes a report, and then builds for 12 weeks. They want to adopt continuous discovery. Which change best fits the practice?
options: The product trio holds small customer touchpoints every week, with recruiting automated so interviews keep happening
Double the quarterly study to 40 interviews and add a survey so the findings are statistically significant
Hire a dedicated research team to run interviews and send insights to the PM monthly
Replace interviews with weekly dashboard reviews, since behavioural data is more reliable than talk
quiz.explanation: Continuous discovery means the team building the product has at least weekly customer touchpoints tied to its outcome, and automated recruiting is what keeps that sustainable. A separate research team brings back the handoff problem, because the people making product decisions are no longer the ones hearing customers.

quiz.question: Your team has three solutions for the target opportunity 'new users don't trust delivery times'. The designer wants to fully test Solution A first, because it is the team favourite. What is the strongest approach?
options: Build Solution A as an MVP and A/B test it, since real usage data beats any other test
Ask users in the next interviews which of the three solutions they would prefer to use
Identify the riskiest assumptions behind all three and run quick assumption tests to compare them
Commit to Solution A, since the trio agrees on it, and test only its feasibility assumptions
quiz.explanation: Comparing several solutions on their riskiest assumptions avoids getting attached to one idea and is usually faster than building. Building an MVP of the favourite sounds rigorous, but it spends weeks learning about one option while the other two go untested.

quiz.question: On an e-commerce team's tree, the only opportunity under the outcome 'increase repeat purchase rate' reads: 'Shoppers want a better post-purchase experience.' The team is stuck choosing what to build. What should the PM do?
options: Run a brainstorm to generate 30 solutions for the broad opportunity, then dot-vote on the best five to build
Replace the outcome with a narrower one, since a broad outcome is what makes this tree so hard to act on
Break it into smaller child opportunities from interview stories, e.g. 'I can't tell when my order will arrive'
Score the broad opportunity with RICE so the team can decide whether it is worth investing in this quarter
quiz.explanation: Large opportunities are broken into child opportunities until a target is small enough to solve in a few weeks, which makes it clear what to build. Brainstorming solutions for a vague opportunity feels productive, but it produces scattered ideas that do not address a specific need.

quiz.question: The riskiest assumption behind your food delivery subscription idea is 'Repeat customers will pay a monthly fee for free delivery.' Which assumption test gives the most trustworthy evidence for the least effort?
options: Survey 500 users on whether they would pay a monthly fee for free delivery, and proceed if over 50% say yes
Interview 5 power users about the subscription idea, and proceed if most of them say they would sign up
Show a fake-door subscription offer at the real price to a small group, with the sign-up rate needed to proceed set in advance
Build the full subscription with billing, run it for a quarter, and proceed if uptake beats the plan's target
quiz.explanation: A fake-door test at the real price measures what people do rather than what they say, and fixing the pass mark in advance stops the team from explaining away the result. The survey is tempting because it is cheap and has a large sample, but stated willingness to pay is hypothetical and usually overstates real demand.

keyTakeaways: Customers do not buy products; they hire them to make progress on a job. Learn the job and you can see your real competition.
Start the tree with an outcome, not a feature: outcome -> opportunities -> solutions -> assumption tests.
Test the assumption that would kill the idea and that you have the least evidence for, and test it before you build.
Discovery is a weekly habit for the product trio, not a quarterly research project.

lessons.label: Module 3
lessons.title: Strategy Deep Dive: Business Models, Competitive Forces, Positioning & Moats
lessons.description: Go past vision and SWOT to test the economics, competitive forces, positioning and defensibility behind a product decision.
learningObjectives: Describe a product's business model in one line (value proposition, who pays for what, main cost drivers) and explain how a proposed feature changes each part.
Apply Porter's Five Forces to one specific product decision, rate each force Low/Medium/High, and name the force that most changes the decision.
Write a positioning statement covering target customer, competitive alternative, market category, differentiator, customer value and proof.
Score a product's defensibility 0-3 across network effects, switching costs, scale economies, brand and data, and test any 'data moat' claim with three questions.
Write one product principle and use it to settle a metric trade-off.

readingArticles.title: A quickstart guide to positioning
readingArticles.source: Lenny's Newsletter (guest post by April Dunford)
keyPoints: Positioning is not your tagline or messaging. It is the context that tells customers who you compete with, what you are good at and who should care.
Start from competitive alternatives: what customers would actually do without you, which is often a spreadsheet, a habit or doing nothing, not only rival brands.
Move from differentiated capabilities to customer value, then to the segment that cares most, then pick the market category that makes that value obvious.
Creating a brand-new category takes far more resources than winning inside an existing one, so pick your category deliberately.

readingArticles.title: The Empty Promise of Data Moats
readingArticles.source: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Martin Casado and Peter Lauten
keyPoints: Many claimed 'data network effects' are really scale effects: more data does not make the product better for other users the way a real network does.
The value of extra data often falls as you collect more, while the cost of getting new, unique data goes up.
Data tends to become a commodity as competitors build similar datasets, so any edge has to be kept up all the time.
Lasting defensibility usually comes from elsewhere, such as verticalization, go-to-market strength, proprietary data sources or execution, with data supporting those.

readingArticles.title: The Network Effects Manual: 16 Different Network Effects (and counting)
keyPoints: A network effect means the product becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it. This is different from being big or popular.
The manual sorts network effects into types such as direct, two-sided marketplace, data, tech-performance and social or belief-based. Their strength varies a lot.
Some marketplaces, such as ride-hailing, are 'asymptotic': past a certain point, more drivers add little value for riders.
Use the categories to say exactly which mechanism (if any) protects a product, rather than claiming 'we have network effects' in general.

videos.title: The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy
videos.creator: Harvard Business Review
keyPoints: Michael Porter explains why competition is wider than direct rivals: buyers, suppliers, new entrants and substitutes also squeeze profits.
Industry structure, not just how hot or fast-growing an industry is, determines how much value companies in it can keep.
The framework is meant to show where you can position yourself so the strongest forces affect you least.
Course note: as a PM, run it before a big bet (a new vertical, membership or market) to see which force could undermine the plan.

videos.title: a16z Podcast | Data Network Effects
videos.creator: a16z
keyPoints: a16z general partners Vijay Pande and Alex Rampell discuss when data creates a real network effect and when it is just 'data exhaust'.
Simply having a large corpus of data does not create a network effect. The data has to feed back into a better product.
Founders and PMs have to balance building a data team early against waiting until there is enough data to be useful.
The partners, who focus on bio and fintech, also discuss the ethical considerations that data advantages raise.

practicalTools.name: Consumer App Strategy Teardown
practicalTools.description: This exercise covers the strategy layer that sits underneath vision (Day 8) and competitor matrices (Day 12). (1) Business model: one widely used tool is the Business Model Canvas (Alexander Osterwalder / Strategyzer), but for a PM decision three answers are often enough: the value proposition, who pays for what (revenue model) and what drives cost (cost structure). (2) Five Forces (Michael Porter): rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Porter built it to explain an industry's profitability. As a PM, do the industry view first, then ask which force most affects one specific decision. In food delivery, for example, restaurants are suppliers and cooking at home is a substitute. On a two-sided platform one side can be both supplier and paying customer; restaurants supply meals and also pay commission. (3) Positioning: target customer, competitive alternative, category, differentiator, value and proof. (4) Moats: network effects, switching costs, scale economies, brand and data. A useful test, adapted from Casado and Lauten (a16z), is to treat a 'data moat' as weak unless more data still improves the product, rivals cannot easily get similar data, and the advantage grows faster than it goes stale. (5) Product principles, such as 'trust over speed' in a payments app, give the team an agreed tie-breaker when metrics conflict.
practicalTools.exercise: Pick a real consumer app you use (e.g. a food delivery, ride-hailing, e-commerce or payments app). Use only public information plus your own experience as a user, and label anything you estimate as an assumption. Fill in Parts A to E of the template: a one-line business model; Five Forces applied to one concrete decision the app faces (e.g. launching a paid membership); a short positioning statement; a moat check that scores each moat type 0 to 3, runs the three-question data-moat test and says how each moat could fail; and one product principle the app seems to follow. Finish with a verdict: which moat (if any) the app has, and its biggest strategic risk.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page strategy teardown covering a business model line, a Five Forces table tied to one decision, a positioning statement with proof, a scored moat check with the data-moat test, one tie-breaker principle and a final verdict.

quiz.question: You are a PM at a food delivery app and you are mapping Porter's Five Forces. Which of these is a 'threat of substitutes' rather than another force?
options: A well-funded new aggregator announcing a launch in your city
A rival aggregator that already operates in all your cities
Large restaurant chains pushing to lower your commission rate
Customers cooking at home with quick-commerce groceries
quiz.explanation: A substitute meets the same need (getting a meal) in a different way, and cooking at home with fast grocery delivery does that. A new aggregator is tempting, but it is the threat of new entrants, because it offers the same kind of product.

quiz.question: A junior PM drafts this positioning for a fintech app: 'For everyone who wants to save money, PayFast is the best savings app.' What is the biggest weakness?
options: It targets 'everyone' and has no differentiator or proof
It does not state the app's pricing or fees anywhere
It does not name a specific competitor brand to beat
It is too short to use as a landing-page headline
quiz.explanation: Positioning needs a narrow target customer, a specific differentiator and proof, and this draft has none of them. Not naming a rival is a weaker criticism, because the competitive alternative can be a habit (such as a bank FD or doing nothing) rather than a brand.

quiz.question: You manage a SaaS invoicing tool for small businesses. A cheaper rival is winning some of your customers. Which investment most legitimately raises switching costs?
options: Deep integrations with customers' accounting and bank tools
Removing CSV export so invoice history is harder to move out
A one-time 20% discount for customers who prepay annually
More frequent reminder emails in the weeks before renewal
quiz.explanation: Integrations put your product inside the customer's workflow, so leaving means rebuilding real value they rely on. Blocking export does raise friction, but it damages trust and can run into data-portability expectations or rules. It is a lock-in trick, not a moat.

quiz.question: A ride-hailing startup's pitch says 'our trip data is our moat' because it powers ETA predictions. Which question best tests that claim?
options: Would more trips still improve ETAs, or have the gains flattened?
Do we hold more trip data today than any rival in our cities?
Is our ETA accuracy currently better than our main rival's?
Is our trip data stored securely so it cannot be copied or leaked?
quiz.explanation: A data moat holds only if more data keeps improving the product. If ETA gains have flattened, a rival with less data can match you, so this tests the claim directly. Having more data or a better ETA score today is tempting, but a lead in volume or accuracy says nothing about diminishing returns, and rivals can catch up by buying mapping and traffic data.

quiz.question: At your food delivery app, about 20 restaurant chains drive roughly a third of orders (illustrative). Several are now launching their own ordering apps. Which force is rising, and what is the best product response?
options: Buyer power; cut delivery fees for all users to protect order volume
Threat of substitutes; launch a grocery vertical to diversify revenue
Rivalry; match the biggest competitor's discount campaign immediately
Supplier power; widen long-tail selection and build restaurant tools
quiz.explanation: Restaurants supply the meals (and also pay you commission). When a few of them control a large share of demand and can go direct, their bargaining power rises, so you need to depend on them less and give them value beyond demand alone. Cutting user fees is tempting, but it addresses buyers, not the supplier concentration causing the risk.

quiz.question: Your payments app has the principle 'Trust over speed'. An experiment shows that removing the confirmation screen raises completed transfers by 3% but also increases transfers sent to the wrong person. What should you do?
options: Ship the one-tap flow, since completed transfers are the north star
Let users pick either flow in settings and keep both live indefinitely
Keep a confirmation step and look for a faster design that keeps trust
Escalate to leadership, since principles cannot settle metric trade-offs
quiz.explanation: Product principles exist to settle exactly this kind of conflict. Here the principle says not to trade away trust for speed, but you can still try to make the safe step faster. Shipping for the north star is tempting, but wrong-recipient errors cause harm and erode trust in ways a short experiment will not show.

quiz.question: Your ride-hailing app dominates City A. Leadership says 'our network effect will let us win City B quickly', where a rival holds about 70% share (illustrative). What is the best response?
options: Agree: our total rider base across cities shortens wait times in every city
Agree: brand awareness from City A will pull riders over and tip B's network
Disagree: liquidity is local, so City A density barely cuts wait times in B
Disagree: ride-hailing has no real network effects, only price competition
quiz.explanation: Ride-hailing network effects are mostly local. Riders in City B gain nothing from drivers in City A, so you still face the chicken-and-egg problem in B, now against an incumbent with 70% share. Brand carry-over is tempting, but riders who come for the brand still leave if there are not enough drivers nearby, and claiming there are no network effects ignores how local driver density cuts wait times.

quiz.question: Your VP wants a quick-commerce app to promise free 10-minute delivery to win customers. Viewed through the business model, what is the strongest concern?
options: Value proposition: many shoppers plan weekly shops and may not value 10 minutes
Customer segments: speed offers attract deal-seekers who churn once offers end
Key partners: FMCG brands may resist the narrower range dark stores can stock
Cost structure: more dark stores and idle riders per order, no fee to offset
quiz.explanation: A faster promise improves the value proposition, but it changes the cost structure the most: more dark stores and idle rider capacity per order. Because delivery is free, no fee offsets that extra cost, which threatens unit economics. Doubts about whether customers value speed are tempting, but quick-commerce demand for urgent top-up orders is well established, so that risk is smaller than a structurally higher cost per order.

quiz.question: You run a home-services marketplace in Bengaluru. A well-funded rival copies your top features in two months and launches in the city. Which of your current advantages is most likely to last?
options: Your team currently ships releases faster than the rival's team
Top-rated local professionals already get steady jobs through you
Reviewers consistently praise your cleaner, simpler booking flow
You are spending more on city marketing than the rival is this year
quiz.explanation: Supply density is a local two-sided network effect. Customers get faster, better-rated matches, which keeps professionals busy and loyal, and copying features does not recreate that. Shipping speed is tempting, but it is execution: a better-funded rival can hire to match it, so on its own it does not protect you.

quiz.question: You are evaluating entry into peer-to-peer payments, where transfers are free, users can switch at almost no cost and three large incumbents hold most of the market. Your Five Forces analysis shows weak standalone profits. What is the best implication?
options: Enter with a small per-transfer fee so payments are profitable on their own
Enter only as a wedge into credit or merchant services where you can earn
Stay out, since weak standalone profits mean the market is not worth entering
Enter and win share with heavy cashback first, then monetize transfers later
quiz.explanation: High buyer power and intense rivalry mean payments alone are unlikely to earn money, so entry makes sense only as a way into something monetizable, such as credit or merchant services, where you can differentiate. Staying out is tempting, but it treats the payments market as the whole opportunity and ignores the adjacent profit pools that frequent payments use opens up. Adding fees later fails because users can switch to free rivals at almost no cost.

keyTakeaways: A quick business-model check needs three answers: what value you create, who pays for it, and what it costs to deliver. Use the full Canvas when partners or channels matter.
Use Five Forces as a decision tool: find the one force that changes your choice instead of filling in five boxes for a slide.
Positioning starts from what the customer would really do without you, and every differentiator needs proof.
Many claimed 'data moats' are scale effects with diminishing returns. Check that more data still improves the product, rivals cannot easily get it, and the edge grows faster than it goes stale.

lessons.label: Module 4
lessons.title: Advanced Prioritization: ICE, Opportunity Scoring, Cost of Delay & WSJF
lessons.description: Go beyond RICE and MoSCoW: learn when ICE is good enough, how opportunity scoring finds underserved needs, how Cost of Delay and WSJF bring time into prioritization, where every scoring model breaks, and how to explain the trade-offs you make.
learningObjectives: Choose between ICE, opportunity scoring, a value/effort matrix and WSJF for a given backlog, and justify the choice in one sentence based on decision stakes, data available and time sensitivity

Calculate opportunity scores (importance + max(importance - satisfaction, 0)) for a set of customer outcomes and identify underserved outcomes (high score) and overserved ones (satisfaction above importance)

Classify backlog items by urgency profile (expedite, fixed date, standard, intangible) and compute WSJF as Cost of Delay (business value + time criticality + risk reduction/opportunity enablement) divided by job duration

Identify at least three failure modes of scoring models (false precision, gaming, comparing unlike items) and write a one-paragraph trade-off note that states what was chosen, what was deferred and the cost of that delay

readingArticles.title: Cost of Delay
keyPoints: Cost of Delay combines value and urgency into one number: how much it costs (per week) to not have something yet
Introduces CD3 (Cost of Delay Divided by Duration), the idea behind WSJF, as a way to prioritise by value and urgency
Includes a worked industry example of how much a feature lost while waiting in queues
Argues that making value and urgency visible changes decisions about queues, WIP and release frequency

readingArticles.title: ICE Scoring Model
keyPoints: ICE = Impact x Confidence x Ease, each scored 1-10; the product of the three is the item's ICE score
Associated with Sean Ellis, who coined 'growth hacking', and suited to fast, experiment-driven growth teams that value failing fast
Strength: quick and simple, good enough when ideas are cheap to try and easy to reverse
Weaknesses: scores are subjective, scales get applied inconsistently, and the model favours low-effort items over bigger bets

readingArticles.title: Opportunity Scoring
keyPoints: Opportunity scoring comes from Tony Ulwick's Outcome-Driven Innovation and compares how important an outcome is with how satisfied customers are with it
Formula: opportunity = importance + max(importance - satisfaction, 0), so importance counts twice and the gap never goes negative
Important but poorly satisfied outcomes are the best opportunities; outcomes where satisfaction exceeds importance are overserved and candidates to simplify or make cheaper
Covers how to survey customers on a 1-5 or 1-10 scale for importance and satisfaction, and how to shift effort away from over-served features

videos.title: Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF) in SAFe
videos.creator: iZenBridge Consultancy
keyPoints: Why SAFe ranks work by the economics of delay instead of by value alone
The three Cost of Delay components and relative (modified Fibonacci) estimation
Computing WSJF by dividing Cost of Delay by job size, and how that changes the order
Why smaller jobs with high urgency tend to rise to the top

videos.title: How to Measure Customer Needs with Outcome-Driven Innovation
videos.creator: Tony Ulwick, Strategyn
keyPoints: Defining customer needs as measurable desired outcomes of a job
Surveying customers on the importance of each outcome and their satisfaction with it
Using importance and satisfaction to spot underserved and overserved outcomes
Turning that data into decisions about where to innovate

practicalTools.name: WSJF vs Value/Effort Ranking Lab
practicalTools.description: Day 11 ranked features with RICE. Here you rank the same kind of backlog two ways and see how adding time (Cost of Delay) and duration changes the order. You are the PM for a food delivery app with one squad and room for about 3 items next quarter. A short ICE warm-up and an opportunity-scoring block come first, so you practise all three tools. The scores in the template are illustrative. The three Cost of Delay columns use relative points on a modified Fibonacci scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20), scored one column at a time, as SAFe teams commonly do. Duration is the team's estimate in weeks. SAFe itself scores job size on the same relative Fibonacci scale as a proxy for duration; we use weeks here so the scheduling questions (step 6) can be checked.
practicalTools.exercise: 0) Score these 5 growth experiments with ICE (Impact, Confidence, Ease, 1-10 each; ICE = I x C x E), starting from the suggested scores in the template, rank them, and say in one line why ICE is enough here but not for items A-F. 1) For each backlog item, compute Cost of Delay = BV + TC + RR. 2) Compute WSJF = CoD / Duration (2 decimals). 3) Compute a simple value/effort ratio = BV / Duration and rank the items by it. 4) Rank the items by WSJF. 5) Compare the two rankings: which items moved the most, and which input caused each move? 6) Tag each item with an urgency profile using the legend (expedite, fixed date, standard, intangible) and check whether the WSJF order lets one squad meet C's fixed date; if it does not, re-sequence. 7) Find any near-ties and say what you would do instead of trusting the decimals. 8) Item E (group ordering) is the CEO's favourite and ranks near the bottom on WSJF. Propose a first slice of E and re-score it. 9) Write a 5-line trade-off note for your manager: what you are doing next quarter, what slips, why, and the cost of that delay. 10) For outcomes O1-O5, compute opportunity = Imp + max(Imp - Sat, 0). Above 10 = underserved (above 15 = strongly); Sat > Imp = overserved (simplify or cut cost). Ulwick treats these cut-offs as rules of thumb. Which outcome supports your slice of E? Check your work against the answer key at the bottom of the template.
practicalTools.deliverable: An ICE ranking of 5 experiments, opportunity scores and labels for 5 outcomes, a completed scoring table with both rankings, urgency tags and a deadline-safe schedule, one re-scored slice of item E, and a 5-line trade-off note ready to share with stakeholders.
