quiz.question: In SAFe's version of WSJF, how is the score calculated?
options: (Business value + time criticality + risk reduction/opportunity enablement) multiplied by job duration
(Business value x confidence + time criticality) divided by team capacity in story points
(Business value + time criticality + risk reduction/opportunity enablement) divided by job duration or size
(Reach x impact x confidence) divided by effort in person-months
quiz.explanation: WSJF divides Cost of Delay (the sum of business value, time criticality and risk reduction/opportunity enablement) by job duration or size, so short, high-CoD jobs rank first. Multiplying by duration does the opposite and favours big jobs; the last option is RICE, which divides by effort but has no time-criticality term.

quiz.question: A growth PM at a fintech app has 40 small ideas to improve referral sign-ups. Each takes 1-3 days to build and can be switched off with a flag. Which prioritization approach fits best?
options: Score each idea quickly with ICE, run the top few as experiments, and let results update the list
Build a full WSJF model with time criticality and risk reduction scored for every idea
Survey users on the importance of and satisfaction with each idea before building any of them
Have engineering estimate story points for all 40 ideas, then rank them on a value/effort matrix
quiz.explanation: When ideas are cheap, reversible and numerous, a light heuristic like ICE is good enough, because running the experiment is the best way to learn. A full WSJF model is the tempting distractor, but it adds scoring effort without improving a decision that is cheap to get wrong.

quiz.question: You surveyed ride-hailing riders; the share of riders rating each outcome 4-5 on importance and on satisfaction, scaled to 0-10, is shown below. Using Ulwick's opportunity formula, importance + max(importance - satisfaction, 0), which outcome is the biggest opportunity?
options: Minimize time to find the pickup point: importance 6, satisfaction 2
Minimize the cost of the ride: importance 9, satisfaction 8
Minimize steps to add a payment method: importance 4, satisfaction 1
Minimize uncertainty about the arrival time: importance 9, satisfaction 3
quiz.explanation: The scores are 10, 15, 10 and 7, so arrival-time uncertainty is the biggest opportunity. The pickup-point outcome is tempting because its satisfaction gap (4) looks large, but importance counts twice in the formula and it is less important.

quiz.question: An e-commerce PM must change the checkout to meet a payment-network rule that takes effect in 10 weeks. The work takes 3 weeks. Before the deadline, delay costs almost nothing; after it, transactions could be declined. What is the best way to schedule it?
options: Put it first in the queue now, because compliance work should always outrank feature work
Score its time criticality low for now and re-score it only if someone escalates the deadline
Start it exactly 3 weeks before the deadline, then expedite it ahead of all other work
Schedule it to finish a few weeks before the deadline as a buffer, using the earlier weeks for other work
quiz.explanation: This is a fixed-date urgency profile: the cost of delay jumps at the date, so the goal is to finish safely before it with a buffer, not necessarily first. Starting exactly 3 weeks out is tempting but leaves no room for estimation error; putting it first by default wastes weeks that could deliver other value.

quiz.question: In your WSJF ranking, 'Group ordering' has the highest business value on the backlog but ranks 5th of 6 because it takes 20 weeks. The CEO is unhappy. What is the strongest response?
options: Raise its time-criticality score so it reaches the top three and the CEO is satisfied
Split it into a smaller first slice that delivers part of the value, then re-score that slice
Keep the ranking as it is and commit to starting Group ordering once the four higher-ranked items ship
Replace WSJF with a pure business-value ranking for this quarter only
quiz.explanation: WSJF rewards small jobs, so splitting a large, valuable item into a thin first slice can raise its score honestly and deliver value sooner. Keeping the ranking unchanged is tempting because it respects the model, but it lets the most valuable item wait months without checking whether part of it could ship early. Inflating time criticality is gaming the score.

quiz.question: Each team at your SaaS company scores its own items for WSJF. After two quarters, most items score 13 or 20 on time criticality, and the ranking no longer separates anything. What is the best fix?
options: Cap time criticality at 8 for every team and require a director's sign-off for any item scored above it
Drop time criticality from the formula and rank all items on business value divided by job duration
Score all items together in one cross-team session, one column at a time, noting the reason for each high score
Have leadership assign every score centrally so that individual teams no longer have a chance to game them
quiz.explanation: Scoring relatively in one shared session, one column at a time, with the reasons written down, makes inflation visible and brings back the spread between items. A cap is tempting but just moves the clustering to 8. Dropping time criticality throws away the urgency signal, and central scoring loses the teams' knowledge without fixing the relative-scoring problem.

quiz.question: Two items score 1.40 and 1.31 on WSJF. Both inputs were relative estimates made in a 30-minute meeting. How should you treat this result?
options: Treat it as a tie and decide on other factors, such as dependencies, strategy fit or a cheap test
Pick the 1.40 item, because applying the model's rule consistently beats reopening the debate
Re-score both items using decimal values so the ranking has enough precision to separate them
Multiply both scores by a confidence factor, then pick whichever item comes out higher
quiz.explanation: The estimates are too rough to support a 0.09 difference, so reading meaning into it is false precision. Following the rule mechanically is tempting for consistency, but the rule is only as good as its inputs. Adding decimals or more multipliers makes the number look more exact without making the inputs any more accurate.

quiz.question: Your food delivery squad's backlog mixes revenue features, a database migration and support-ticket bugs. When everything is scored on one value scale, the migration never makes it in, even though the outage risk is growing. What is the best structural fix?
options: Give the migration the top business-value score so it is guaranteed to make it into the plan
Agree capacity shares first (e.g. some for platform work), then rank items within each share
Keep one ranked list, but re-score everything every two weeks instead of once a quarter
Postpone the migration until an incident proves its value with real outage data
quiz.explanation: Scoring unlike items on one scale keeps starving enabler work. Deciding capacity shares first, then ranking within each share, compares like with like. Inflating the migration's value is tempting, but it turns the score into fiction and teaches others to do the same.

quiz.question: On your ride-hailing value/effort 2x2, a 'fare breakdown screen' sits in the quick-win quadrant. What does this matrix leave out that Cost of Delay would capture?
options: Whether the item's value shrinks or disappears if it ships later
How many riders the feature would reach each month
How confident the team is in the effort estimate
Whether the feature is a basic expectation or a delighter in Kano terms
quiz.explanation: A value/effort matrix is static; Cost of Delay adds time by asking how value changes with delay (urgency). Reach is tempting, but reach can already be folded into 'value'; it is not what is missing.

quiz.question: Mid-quarter, your VP asks you to add a loyalty-points feature 'right away'. Your squad is at full capacity on three committed items. What is the best way to respond?
options: Accept it and ask the team to absorb it with extra hours, so that no committed item slips
Show which committed item would slip and what each delay costs, recommend one, and let the VP decide
Decline it, because the quarter's plan was already agreed and signed off with stakeholders
Add it to next quarter's backlog so the current plan stays intact, and revisit it then
quiz.explanation: Good trade-off communication makes the cost explicit: something has to give, and the decision-maker should see what and at what cost. Absorbing it quietly is tempting but hides the trade-off and usually leads to missed commitments or burnout. Declining or deferring without discussion skips the cost-of-delay comparison.

keyTakeaways: A score is a conversation starter, not a verdict: use it to surface assumptions, then decide with judgment.
Value/effort ignores time; Cost of Delay asks what it costs to wait, and WSJF asks what earns the most per week of team time.
WSJF rewards small jobs, so the best response to a big, valuable item that ranks low is usually to split it, not to inflate its score.
Every trade-off has a loser: name what slips, why, and what it costs, and the decision gets easier to defend.

lessons.label: Module 5
lessons.title: Unit Economics & Business Metrics for PMs
lessons.description: Learn the money math behind product decisions: ARPU, margins, CAC, LTV, payback, stickiness, and metric trees that connect a North Star to profit.
learningObjectives: Calculate ARPU, gross margin, contribution margin, blended vs paid CAC, simple LTV, LTV:CAC and CAC payback from a raw input table
Explain the assumptions behind LTV = ARPU x margin / churn (steady churn, stable ARPU and margin, no time value of money) and spot when it overstates value
Build a metric tree that breaks a North Star (see Day 13) into revenue, margin and engagement inputs, using DAU/MAU stickiness only where it fits the product's natural usage frequency

Decide whether a discount or free-delivery proposal is worth it by comparing the incremental customers' gross profit (net of their own discount) with the subsidy paid to customers who would have bought anyway

readingArticles.title: Startup Killer: the Cost of Customer Acquisition
keyPoints: CAC = total sales and marketing cost for a period divided by the customers acquired in that period
LTV should be measured in gross margin (after the costs of serving the customer), not revenue
Widely cited SaaS heuristics: LTV around 3x CAC or more, and win back CAC in under about 12 months
Shows how a long CAC payback period means the business needs a lot of cash to grow, even when LTV looks healthy

readingArticles.title: DAU/MAU is an important metric to measure engagement, but here's where it fails
keyPoints: DAU/MAU (stickiness) fits high-frequency products like social and messaging apps
Low-frequency products such as travel, e-commerce and many SaaS tools can be very valuable with low DAU/MAU
Pushing notifications often adds more monthly users than daily users, which can lower the ratio
Pick an engagement metric that matches how often your users naturally need the product

readingArticles.title: The Power User Curve: The Best Way to Understand Your Most Engaged Users
readingArticles.source: Andreessen Horowitz (Li Jin and Andrew Chen)
keyPoints: DAU/MAU squashes engagement into one average; the power user curve shows how many users were active on 1, 2, ... 30 days of the month
A 'smile' shape means a group of users comes back daily; a curve weighted to the left means most use it rarely
Compare curves across cohorts to see whether product changes create more power users
Measure a core action (an order, a trip, a post) instead of app opens

videos.title: Consumer Startup Metrics | Startup School
videos.creator: Y Combinator (Tom Blomfield)
keyPoints: Separates organic growth from paid growth, so you don't credit paid ads with users who would have come anyway
Explains cannibalization: paid spend that captures existing demand inflates paid results
Unit economics section: compare what a user costs to acquire with what they are worth
Also covers NPS and finding the 'magic moment' worth tracking in your product

videos.title: SaaS Metrics: LTV, CAC, CAC Payback Periods, and More
videos.creator: Mergers & Inquisitions / Breaking Into Wall Street
keyPoints: Why the lifetime value calculation is tricky and depends on its churn and margin assumptions
How to calculate CAC and which costs belong in it
Why LTV/CAC can mislead unless it is adjusted properly
Makes the case for CAC payback period as a more robust alternative

practicalTools.name: Unit Economics and Discount Decision Worksheet
practicalTools.description: A two-part worksheet. Part A: from raw inputs for an illustrative subscription app, calculate ARPU (per paying sub), gross margin, contribution margin, blended and paid CAC, simple LTV, LTV:CAC and CAC payback. Part B: decide whether a '50% off your first 3 months' campaign is worth it. The key is to count the discount given to subscribers who would have joined anyway, not just the extra sign-ups.
practicalTools.exercise: 1) Use the Part A inputs in the template to fill in every metric, including both gross margin and contribution margin, and write each formula next to your answer. 2) Write one sentence on what blended vs paid CAC tells you, and one on which LTV assumption (steady churn, stable price and margin, no time value of money) you trust least. 3) In Part B, work out B1-B8. Notice that paid CAC goes down while lifetime contribution barely moves, and explain why. 4) Find the break-even number of extra subscribers, then rerun the numbers with 14% churn for the deal-seekers. 5) Make a Go / No-go / Test call, and suggest one cheaper version of the campaign (e.g. smaller or targeted) plus the metric you would use as a guardrail. 6) Bonus: sketch a 3-level metric tree for PlanPlate's North Star 'weekly active paying subscribers', with a revenue branch and a margin branch, mark which input the discount campaign moves, and say whether DAU/MAU or WAU/MAU fits PlanPlate, and why. (Note: Day 22 used DAU/MAU as a retention proxy; it really measures frequency.) Only then compare with the answer key.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page decision memo with the completed Part A metrics table, your Part B calculations with break-even and sensitivity, a Go / No-go / Test recommendation with three reasons and one guardrail metric, and a simple metric tree sketch.
practicalTools.template:
ILLUSTRATIVE DATA - "PlanPlate", a meal-planning subscription app (India)
All numbers are invented for practice. Rs = rupees. 1 lakh = 1,00,000.

DEFINITIONS
Gross margin = (revenue - cost of serving) / revenue. Contribution margin
= revenue - ALL variable costs per unit (incl. fees, discounts, delivery).
In this worksheet, LTV and payback use contribution per sub per month.
"ARPU" here is per PAYING sub (ARPPU); ARPU across all users, including
free ones, would be lower.

PART A - INPUTS (last month, paid + organic)
Input                                       Value
------------------------------------------  ---------------
Average paying subscribers (month)          20,000
Subscription revenue (month)                Rs 60,00,000
Cost to serve per sub per month             Rs 60
  (servers, support)
Payment fees per sub per month              Rs 30
Monthly subscriber churn                    7%
Total sales & marketing spend               Rs 6,00,000
  of which paid ads                         Rs 5,00,000
New subscribers, all channels               1,500
  of which attributed to paid ads           1,000

PART A - CALCULATE
Metric                      Formula                            Answer
--------------------------  ---------------------------------  ----------
ARPU (per paying sub =      subscription revenue / paying subs ________
  ARPPU)
Gross margin %              (ARPU - cost to serve) / ARPU      ________
Gross profit per sub/month  ARPU - cost to serve               ________
Contribution margin/sub/mo  ARPU - all variable costs          ________
                              (incl. fees, discounts)
Blended CAC                 total S&M / all new subs           ________
Paid CAC                    paid spend / paid-attributed subs  ________
LTV (simple)                contribution per month / churn     ________
LTV:CAC (blended / paid)    LTV / CAC                          ___ / ___
CAC payback, months (b / p) CAC / contribution per month       ___ / ___

PART B - PROPOSAL: "50% off your first 3 months" for every new
subscriber who arrives via paid ads. Paid spend stays Rs 5,00,000.
Assumption (growth team forecast)           Value
------------------------------------------  ---------------
Paid new subscribers with the campaign      1,400 (+400)
Discount per subscriber (Rs 150 x 3)        Rs 450 (upper bound)
Churn of the 1,000 who would join anyway    7% (unchanged)
Churn of the 400 incremental deal-seekers   12%

PART B - CALCULATE
B1  Paid CAC with campaign (ad spend / 1,400)            ________
B2  LTV of a "would have joined anyway" sub: LTV - 450   ________
B3  LTV of an incremental sub: 210 / 12% - 450           ________
B4  Lifetime contribution, no campaign: 1,000 x LTV      ________
B5  With campaign: (1,000 x B2) + (400 x B3)             ________
B6  Difference B5 - B4                                   ________
B7  Break-even incremental subs: (1,000 x 450) / B3      ________
B8  Redo B3, B5, B6 with incremental churn at 14%        ________
B9  Decision: Go / No-go / Test, with 3 reasons

ANSWER KEY (try first!)
A:  ARPU (ARPPU) 60,00,000 / 20,000 = 300 | GM (300 - 60) / 300 = 80%
    GP/month 240 | CM 300 - 60 - 30 = 210 | blended CAC 400 | paid 500
    LTV 210 / 0.07 = 3,000 | LTV:CAC 7.5 / 6.0 | payback 1.9 / 2.4 months
B1  357 (looks 29% better, but avg LTV per paid sub also falls ~27%,
    to about 2,193, so total contribution barely moves - see B6)
B2  2,550   B3  1,750 - 450 = 1,300   B4  30,00,000
B5  25,50,000 + 5,20,000 = 30,70,000   B6  +70,000 (about +2%)
B7  4,50,000 / 1,300 = about 347 incremental subs needed
B8  1,500 - 450 = 1,050; B5 = 29,70,000; B6 = -30,000
B9  Not worth launching at full scale: the 4.5 lakh subsidy to people who
    would have paid full price almost cancels the gain, and a small miss
    on churn or lift turns it negative. Test it against a holdout, or
    shrink it (e.g. first month only, or only for lapsed users).

quiz.question: Illustrative food delivery order: the customer's basket is Rs 400. The platform earns a Rs 80 commission and a Rs 30 delivery fee. Its costs on this order are rider cost Rs 50, payment fee Rs 8 and a platform-funded discount of Rs 20. What is the contribution margin per order?
options: Rs 32
Rs 52
Rs 110
Rs 322
quiz.explanation: Platform revenue is 80 + 30 = 110. Subtract the variable costs of 50 + 8 + 20 = 78 and you get Rs 32. Rs 52 is the tempting answer, but it forgets that the platform-funded discount is a real cost on every order.

quiz.question: You are the PM of an expense-splitting fintech app with 30,000 average DAU and 300,000 MAU. Your manager asks what the 10% DAU/MAU ratio tells you. Which interpretation is best?
options: Only 10% of monthly users return next month, so retention work is the urgent priority
The app is unhealthy, because strong consumer apps typically need DAU/MAU of 50% or more
The average monthly user is active about 3 days; judge that against how often people split bills
About 90% of this month's users churned, so most of the acquisition spend was wasted
quiz.explanation: DAU/MAU measures how often monthly users show up (10% of about 30 days is roughly 3 days), not month-to-month retention. People split expenses only after shared events, so a low ratio may be natural. Reading the ratio as retention or churn is the common mistake; retention needs cohort analysis (Day 24).

quiz.question: Illustrative SaaS data: last quarter's sales and marketing spend was Rs 40 lakh, which brought 2,000 new customers. Rs 36 lakh went on paid ads, which brought 800 customers. The other Rs 4 lakh funded SEO content and the referral program, which brought 1,200 customers who would likely have arrived without ads. The CFO asks whether to scale paid ads. Which CAC should you use?
options: Blended CAC of Rs 2,000, because it covers every channel and is the official number
Fully loaded paid CAC of Rs 5,000, putting all Rs 40 lakh of spend on the 800 paid customers
Organic CAC of about Rs 333, because organic is the cheapest channel and should scale first
Paid CAC of Rs 4,500, dividing paid ad spend by the 800 customers that ads brought in
quiz.explanation: For a paid-ads decision, divide paid spend by the customers paid ads brought: 36 lakh / 800 = Rs 4,500. Blended CAC (Rs 2,000) looks efficient only because cheap organic customers pull the average down, and loading the SEO and referral budget onto paid customers (Rs 5,000) charges them for spend that drives a different channel. Treat Rs 4,500 as a floor, because the next rupee of ads usually buys customers at a higher marginal CAC.

quiz.question: Your subscription app's LTV is computed as ARPU x gross margin / monthly churn, using last month's overall churn of 2%. Most of the base are loyal subscribers who have stayed two years. New paid cohorts churn about 10% in month one and about 5% after that. What is the biggest problem with using this LTV to set the paid CAC budget?
options: The formula should use revenue rather than gross margin, so LTV is understated
Churn from a mature base hides how fast new cohorts leave, so LTV of bought users is overstated
Churn should be expressed annually rather than monthly, so the unit is inconsistent
LTV should subtract CAC first, so the ratio against CAC double counts spend
quiz.explanation: The simple formula assumes a steady churn rate that applies to the customers you are buying. Here, churn from loyal long-term subscribers makes new paid cohorts look far more valuable than they are, so you need cohort-based LTV. Using gross margin is correct, not a flaw.

quiz.question: Illustrative B2B SaaS data: CAC is Rs 60,000, ARPU is Rs 5,000 per month and gross margin is 80%. What is the CAC payback period?
options: 9.6 months
12 months
15 months
60 months
quiz.explanation: Payback = CAC / monthly gross profit per customer = 60,000 / (5,000 x 0.8) = 15 months. The tempting 12 months divides by revenue and ignores the cost of serving the customer.

quiz.question: You are a PM at a food delivery app. The proposal is free delivery on orders above Rs 299. Illustrative data: contribution is Rs 25 per order today, which includes a Rs 30 delivery fee, and 60% of orders are already above Rs 299. Growth forecasts +10% orders, with 60% still above Rs 299. Per 100 of today's orders, what is the best conclusion?
options: Falls to about Rs 770: all 66 qualifying orders lose the Rs 30 fee, so redesign the offer first
Rises to about Rs 2,750: 110 orders at Rs 25 each, so growth pays for the offer
Dips to about Rs 2,570: 10 extra orders add Rs 250 and only 6 new qualifying orders lose the fee
Falls to about Rs 950: 60 existing qualifying orders lose the fee, partly offset by 10 extra orders
quiz.explanation: Today: 100 x 25 = 2,500. After: 110 x 25 - 66 x 30 = 2,750 - 1,980 = Rs 770, because every qualifying order, old or new, loses the fee. The tempting Rs 2,570 counts the lost fee only on new orders and ignores the subsidy to the 60 orders that already qualified.

quiz.question: Your grocery delivery app's North Star is 'weekly orders delivered on time' (see Day 13). It has grown strongly, but the CFO says each extra order loses money. How should you change your metric tree?
options: Replace the North Star with revenue, so every team optimizes directly for money
Add engagement inputs such as app opens and sessions, since engagement eventually raises profit
Leave the tree alone and give a separate finance team cost targets so product stays on growth
Keep the North Star and add a contribution-per-order branch with owned inputs as a guardrail
quiz.explanation: A metric tree should show which inputs drive user value and which drive money. A contribution-per-order branch (AOV x take rate + fees - delivery, discounts, refunds) used as a guardrail stops growth that destroys value. Swapping the North Star for revenue loses the user-value focus and still ignores costs.

quiz.question: You are building a metric tree for an e-commerce app whose top business metric is monthly GMV. Which decomposition is well formed, with inputs that multiply back to the parent and that teams can own?
options: GMV = sessions x add-to-cart rate x average order value
GMV = monthly buyers x orders per buyer x average order value
GMV = monthly buyers x average order value x gross margin
GMV = new buyers x AOV + returning buyers x retention rate
quiz.explanation: Buyers x orders per buyer x AOV multiplies exactly to GMV, and each input maps to a lever (acquisition, frequency, basket size). The add-to-cart version is tempting but skips the step from cart to purchase, so it does not equal GMV.

quiz.question: A fintech app's paid channel shows LTV:CAC of 9:1 and a 2-month payback. Spend has been flat for a year. A common heuristic target is around 3:1. What is the most reasonable read?
options: Cut paid spend, because such a high ratio means marketing budget is being wasted
Hold spend flat, since the ratio already beats the 3:1 target and more spend adds risk
The channel may be under-invested; raise spend in steps and watch marginal CAC climb
Lower prices to pull the ratio toward 3:1 and convert more users at the margin
quiz.explanation: A very high LTV:CAC with fast payback often means you could profitably spend more. CAC usually rises with scale, so increase spend step by step and track marginal CAC. Holding flat treats 3:1 as a ceiling and leaves profitable growth unused.

quiz.question: E-commerce proposal (illustrative): 20% off the first order for all new buyers, a Rs 200 discount per order. Today 10,000 new buyers a month place a first order. With the offer, forecasts say 11,000. Each of the 1,000 extra buyers is worth Rs 600 of lifetime contribution before the discount. What is the net monthly impact?
options: About -Rs 16 lakh: Rs 22 lakh of discounts on all 11,000 orders vs Rs 6 lakh of new value
About +Rs 4 lakh: Rs 6 lakh of new value minus the discount on only the 1,000 extra buyers
About +Rs 6 lakh: the 1,000 extra buyers each add Rs 600 of lifetime contribution
About -Rs 22 lakh: the full discount cost, since discounted buyers bring no lasting value
quiz.explanation: The discount goes to all 11,000 first orders (11,000 x 200 = Rs 22 lakh), but only the 1,000 extra buyers create new value (Rs 6 lakh). The tempting +Rs 4 lakh ignores the subsidy to the 10,000 buyers who would have ordered anyway.

keyTakeaways: If every order loses money, more volume means bigger losses unless scale itself lowers the per-order cost. Check contribution margin before you celebrate growth.
LTV is a forecast and CAC is cash already spent. Treat LTV:CAC and payback as health checks, not proof.
A discount's real cost includes every customer who would have paid full price anyway.

A metric tree turns a North Star into levers teams can own, and shows which lever actually moves money. Match engagement ratios to the natural cadence: DAU/MAU for daily habits, WAU/MAU or DAU/WAU for weekly products like meal planning.

lessons.label: Module 6
lessons.title: Experimentation Deep Dive: Designing and Reading A/B Tests
lessons.description: Go past the A/B testing basics from Day 20 and learn how to design a test that can actually prove you wrong, size it properly, and read the results without fooling yourself or your stakeholders. It also refines Day 20's advice on segmenting results: segments you plan before launch can inform a decision, but segments found afterwards only suggest new hypotheses. Guardrail metrics are usually underpowered, so a guardrail breach that is not statistically significant is still a warning sign, not a pass.
learningObjectives: Write a falsifiable hypothesis for a product change that names the user group, the change, one primary metric, the expected direction and a minimum detectable effect, plus guardrail metrics with explicit thresholds that block a launch

Estimate sample size per variant for a conversion metric with the approximation n = 16 x p(1-p) / MDE^2 (alpha 0.05 two-sided, 80% power), turn it into a test duration in full weeks, and fix both before launch
Interpret a test readout correctly: say what a p-value and a confidence interval do and do not tell you, and tell a false positive (Type I) apart from a false negative (Type II) on a real decision
Find and handle four common ways to misread a test (peeking, novelty effects, sample ratio mismatch, segment over-slicing), and decide when an A/B test is the wrong tool

readingArticles.title: How Not To Run an A/B Test
keyPoints: If you check results repeatedly and stop as soon as they look significant, the real false positive rate can be far higher than the 5% you think you are running at
The fix is to set the sample size in advance and not act on interim results
Gives a simple rule of thumb for sample size: n = 16 x variance / delta^2
Sequential and Bayesian designs are the legitimate ways to look at results early

readingArticles.title: Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch in A/B Testing
keyPoints: A sample ratio mismatch (SRM) is when the user split between variants differs from the planned split by more than chance can explain
SRM usually means some users went missing in a biased way, so the result cannot be trusted, and the conclusion can even flip
Causes can come from assignment, execution (e.g. redirects), log processing or analysis filters
Run an SRM check before you interpret any result, and find the root cause instead of 'adjusting' the numbers

readingArticles.title: Patterns of Trustworthy Experimentation: Pre-Experiment Stage
keyPoints: The hypothesis must be falsifiable with the metrics you chose, including guardrail and data-quality metrics
Choose the randomization unit carefully: how stable the IDs are and whether users affect each other (network effects) both matter
Checking for pre-existing differences between groups (for example a retrospective A/A analysis) catches biased splits early
Ramp exposure gradually (for example 1% to 5% to 10%) so a harmful change is caught before many users see it

videos.title: Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments at Large Scale w/ Ronny Kohavi
videos.creator: Split (DECISIONS/Replay)
keyPoints: Why a result you can trust is worth more than running many tests
How large experimentation programmes pick their key metrics and guardrails
Why surprising results should be checked for errors before anyone celebrates
Practical lessons from running experiments at scale at large tech companies

videos.title: p-values: What they are and how to interpret them
videos.creator: StatQuest with Josh Starmer
keyPoints: A p-value measures how surprising the data would be if there were really no difference
The 0.05 threshold sets how often you accept a false positive
A small p-value does not tell you how big or important the difference is
Uses intuitive examples instead of heavy maths

practicalTools.name: Experiment Brief: One-Page Checkout Test
practicalTools.description: An experiment brief is a short document you fill in before launch. It fixes the hypothesis, metrics, sample size, duration and decision rules, so the result is read the way you planned and not the way you hoped. Use the template below. The worked numbers in it are illustrative only. The formula is a widely used approximation (often called Lehr's rule) for alpha 0.05 two-sided and 80% power: 2 x (1.96 + 0.84)^2 is about 15.7, which rounds to 16.
practicalTools.exercise: Scenario (illustrative): you are the PM for checkout in a food delivery app. Today checkout has three screens (address, payment, review). Design has built a single-page checkout that pre-selects the user's last-used payment method (for example UPI). Write an experiment brief for a 50/50 test. (1) Write a falsifiable hypothesis in the template's format. (2) Choose ONE primary metric and define it exactly (who counts, which event, which time window). (3) Choose 2-3 guardrail metrics with a threshold that would block launch, for example payment failure rate, refund or cancellation rate, or checkout page load time. (4) Use the baseline conversion from your own product, or the illustrative numbers in the template, and choose an MDE. Explain why that effect size would be worth shipping. (5) Calculate sample size per variant with n = 16 x p(1-p) / delta^2 and show your working. (6) Turn it into a duration in full weeks, using eligible traffic per day. (7) Write the decision rules: ship, iterate, or stop, including what you will do if the result is inconclusive or a guardrail is breached. (8) Name at most 2 segments you will look at, and why. Bonus: in two sentences, say how you would spot a novelty effect, and what would make you pause the test early (a safety stop, not a peek at results).
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page experiment brief, signed off before launch. It must include the hypothesis, primary metric, guardrails with thresholds, baseline, MDE, a sample size calculation that shows the formula, duration in full weeks, SRM check plan, pre-registered segments, and decision rules.
practicalTools.template:
EXPERIMENT BRIEF  (fill in before launch, freeze after sign-off)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Field              Your answer
-----------------  ---------------------------------------------------
Name / owner       
Change             Control sees: ...   Treatment sees: ...
Hypothesis         Because [evidence], we believe [change] for
                   [users] will [raise/lower] [primary metric] by at
                   least [MDE]. We are wrong if, at the planned sample
                   size, the 95% CI rules out an effect of [MDE] or more.
Unit and split     [user / device / order]   [50/50]
Eligibility        [who enters, e.g. users who open the cart]
Primary metric     [ONE metric, exact definition, time window]
Guardrails         Metric                    Blocks ship if
                   ------------------------  -------------------------
                   [e.g. payment fail rate]  [worse by > X pp]
                   [e.g. cancel/refund rate] [worse by > X pp]
                   [e.g. page load p75]      [slower by > X ms]
                   (breach = point estimate past X, or CI upper > X)
Baseline (p)       
MDE (delta)        [absolute pp]  =  [relative %]
Alpha / power      0.05 two-sided / 80%
Sample size        n per variant = 16 x p x (1 - p) / delta^2
Duration           (n x variants) / eligible users per day,
                   rounded UP to full weeks (aim for at least 2)
Trust checks       SRM chi-square daily, flag if p < 0.001; logging QA
Segments (max 2)   [pre-registered, with reason]
Safety stop        [e.g. guardrail breached by 2x -> pause]

DECISION RULES (agree before launch)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Result                                       Decision
-------------------------------------------  -------------------------
Primary sig. better, no guardrail breached   Ship, ramp 50% -> 100%
Primary sig. better, guardrail breached      Do not ship; find cause
Not sig., CI rules out effects >= MDE        Stop; pick next bet
Not sig., CI still includes MDE              Inconclusive; judgment
Primary sig. worse                           Stop; write learnings
SRM detected                                 Do not read; debug first

WORKED EXAMPLE  (ILLUSTRATIVE NUMBERS ONLY)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Baseline cart-to-order conversion   p     = 0.30  (30%)
MDE                                 delta = 0.015 (1.5 pp abs = 5% rel)
n per variant = 16 x 0.30 x 0.70 / 0.015^2
              = 3.36 / 0.000225
              = about 14,934 users per variant
New eligible users per day = 6,000  ->  3,000 per variant per day
Days needed = 14,934 / 3,000 = 5 days
Run for 14 days (2 full weeks, ~42,000 per variant): this covers
weekday/weekend cycles and gives a short novelty effect time to fade.
Freeze this end date and sample before launch; it is now the plan.
Note: halving the MDE to 0.75 pp needs about 4x the users (~59,700).

quiz.question: Your test of a new ride-hailing fare screen ends at the planned sample size. Bookings are up 2.1% with p = 0.03. Your manager asks what the p-value means. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 97% chance that the new fare screen really increases bookings
If the new screen truly had no effect, a difference at least this large would show up only about 3% of the time
There is a 3% chance that the 2.1% uplift will not repeat after a full rollout
The true uplift in bookings is 2.1%, with a 3% margin of error either way
quiz.explanation: A p-value is calculated assuming no real difference: it is how often data this extreme would appear by chance alone. The tempting '97% chance it works' reverses the logic. The p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

quiz.question: You are the PM for an e-commerce app and plan to test showing estimated delivery dates on product pages. Which hypothesis is best written for an A/B test?
options: For mobile shoppers, showing delivery dates will raise product-to-cart rate, checkout conversion and repeat orders by at least 2% relative
For mobile shoppers, showing delivery dates will raise product-to-cart rate by at least 2% relative, without return rate rising over 0.5 pp
For mobile shoppers, showing delivery dates will raise product-to-cart rate, measured on whichever platform shows the clearest effect
For mobile shoppers, showing delivery dates will improve product-to-cart rate, with return rates watched as a guardrail during the test
quiz.explanation: A testable hypothesis names the user group, the change, one primary metric, a direction, a minimum effect and a guardrail with a threshold, so the result can clearly prove it wrong. The three-metric option looks rigorous, but with several primary metrics and no single success test, almost any result can be called a win.

quiz.question: A food delivery checkout test was planned for 14 days to reach its sample size. On day 3 the dashboard shows +4% conversion with p = 0.02, and the growth lead wants to ship today. The test uses a standard fixed-horizon design. What should you do?
options: Keep running until the planned sample size, unless a guardrail safety stop is triggered
Ship now, because p = 0.02 is already below the 0.05 significance threshold
Stop the test and ship to 50% of users as a compromise while gathering more data
Lower the significance threshold to 0.01 and ship only if day 4 still meets it
quiz.explanation: With a fixed-horizon test, stopping the first time the result crosses p < 0.05 makes the real false positive rate much higher than 5%, because the result will drift above and below the threshold by chance. Changing the threshold mid-test is still peeking. Only a sequential design planned in advance allows valid early stopping.

quiz.question: A fintech app ran a 50/50 test of a new onboarding flow. The readout shows 50,000 users in control and 48,200 in treatment, and treatment has a much higher KYC completion rate. A chi-square test on the split gives p < 0.001. What is the right next step?
options: Report the KYC uplift, since a 1,800-user gap is small next to nearly 100,000 users
Re-weight the treatment group to 50,000 users so the two groups can be compared fairly
Compare only users who reached the KYC screen, so both groups start from the same point
Treat it as a sample ratio mismatch and trace the missing treatment users first
quiz.explanation: A split this far from 50/50 cannot be explained by chance. It usually means some treatment users were lost in a biased way (for example, early drop-offs were never logged), which can create a fake uplift. Re-weighting or filtering to users who reached the KYC screen keeps the same biased population, so it hides the problem without fixing it.

quiz.question: A ride-hailing app tests a redesigned home screen that moves the 'Saved places' shortcut to the top. Taps on Saved places are up 12% vs control in week 1 but only 3% in week 2. Which reading and action is most sound?
options: The shortcut is losing value quickly, so roll the test back now before the effect turns negative
Week 1 shows the true effect, so report +12% and treat week 2 as noise from lower traffic
This may be a novelty effect; compare new vs returning users over time and judge on the steady-state effect
Average the two weeks to +7.5% and use that as the expected long-term impact in the business case
quiz.explanation: A large early lift that fades is the classic sign of a novelty effect: returning users tap a changed element because it is new. Splitting by new vs returning users and watching the trend shows the lasting effect. Averaging the two weeks still overstates the long-run impact because the lift is still falling.

quiz.question: Your checkout test was sized to detect a 2% relative change in conversion. Leadership now wants it to detect a 1% relative change, with the same alpha and power. Roughly how many users per variant will you need compared with the original plan?
options: About half as many users
About twice as many users
About four times as many users
About eight times as many users
quiz.explanation: Sample size scales with 1 / MDE^2, so halving the MDE multiplies the required sample by about 4. 'About twice as many' is the intuitive mistake of assuming the relationship is linear.

quiz.question: A food delivery test of a new restaurant ranking shows no overall change in orders. An analyst then slices the results into 20 segments and finds iOS users in tier-2 cities up 9% (p = 0.04). The team wants to launch for that segment only. What is the best response?
options: Launch for that segment, because p = 0.04 is below 0.05 and the uplift is large
Launch for all users, because a strong segment shows the ranking works and will spread
Combine the segment with the overall result to raise the confidence of the overall test
Treat it as a new hypothesis and confirm it in a separate test where that segment is planned in advance
quiz.explanation: At alpha 0.05, checking 20 segments would be expected to produce about one 'significant' segment by chance even if there were no real effect. A segment found after the fact can only suggest a hypothesis; it needs its own pre-registered test. The low p-value is misleading because of how many comparisons were made.

quiz.question: A SaaS team ran a pricing-page test powered at 80% to detect a 5% relative uplift in trial starts. At the planned sample size the result is +1.0%, p = 0.58, with a 95% confidence interval of -2.5% to +4.5%. What is the most accurate conclusion?
options: The test proves the new page has no effect, so it should be removed from consideration
The test was underpowered, so it should be extended until p falls below 0.05
It rules out a 5%+ uplift but not a small effect, so decide on cost and strategy
The new page is probably better by 1.0%, so ship it given the positive direction
quiz.explanation: Not significant does not mean no effect. The confidence interval excludes the planned 5% MDE but cannot rule out small positive or negative effects, so the decision depends on cost and strategy. Extending the test until it turns significant is peeking under another name and inflates the false positive rate.

quiz.question: In which situation is a classic user-level A/B test the LEAST appropriate tool?
options: A food delivery app with 2 million weekly users testing a new cart upsell widget
An e-commerce site testing two versions of its free-shipping threshold banner on 500,000 daily visitors
A B2B SaaS tool with 300 enterprise accounts and about 10 contract signings a month testing a new sales demo flow
A ride-hailing app testing a new pickup-pin interaction in cities that have plenty of daily trips
quiz.explanation: With about 10 conversions a month, reaching any reasonable sample size would take years, and accounts are not independent users. Qualitative research, before/after analysis or expert judgment is a better fit. The free-shipping test looks risky because it touches money, but it has the traffic and reversibility that suit an A/B test.

quiz.question: Your fintech checkout test reaches its planned sample. Payment conversion is up 2.0% (significant). The pre-registered guardrail was 'payment failure rate must not rise by more than 0.2 pp'. It rose by 0.4 pp, and the whole 95% confidence interval sits above 0.2 pp. Leadership argues the conversion gain outweighs it. What should you do?
options: Hold the launch, find out why failures rose, fix the cause and retest the change
Ship the change, because the primary metric is significant and the guardrail is secondary
Ship to 50% of users, so the gain is captured while failures affect only half the base
Ship now with an alert that rolls back automatically if failures rise past 0.6 pp
quiz.explanation: Guardrail thresholds are set before launch so the team does not rationalise harm after a win, and here the breach is clear. Shipping with a new 0.6 pp rollback trigger is tempting, but it is just moving the pre-registered threshold after seeing the data, which is the post-hoc decision change the guardrail exists to prevent.

keyTakeaways: Decide everything before launch: hypothesis, primary metric, guardrails, MDE, sample size, duration and decision rules. If you change them after seeing data, you are no longer running an experiment.
A p-value tells you how surprising the data would be if the change did nothing. It is not the probability that your change works, and 'not significant' does not mean 'no effect'.
Check that the test can be trusted before you read the result: a sample ratio mismatch, a peeked-at stopping point or a lucky segment can make a wrong answer look convincing.
A/B tests are for reversible decisions with enough traffic. When traffic is low, the change is ethically or legally required, or the effect will take months to show up, use other evidence.

lessons.label: Module 7
lessons.title: Product Analytics & Root-Cause Analysis
lessons.description: A repeatable method for diagnosing why a metric moved: validate the data, decompose it, segment it, separate internal from external causes, then test hypotheses with SQL and a well-designed tracking plan and dashboard.
learningObjectives: Run the five-step diagnosis on a metric change (validate the data, decompose, segment, check internal vs external causes, form and test hypotheses) and explain why the order matters
Decompose a top-line metric (e.g. orders = sessions x conversion, or by funnel step) and calculate what share of a drop each segment owns
Write a tracking-plan entry with object-action event names and consistent properties, and sketch a dashboard that leads with headline metrics, comparisons and drill-downs
Write the SQL a PM needs for diagnosis (GROUP BY, JOINs, date bucketing, conversion rates) and spot common errors such as join fan-out

readingArticles.title: Mastering RCA Questions in Product Management Interviews: A Step-by-Step Guide
keyPoints: Clarify the metric definition, timeframe and affected segments before proposing any cause
Sort possible causes into system (logging or calculation changes), internal, external and out-of-control buckets
Work through the buckets in order, collecting evidence such as drop-off rates, load times and user feedback
Two worked examples (Zomato and Amazon) show the structure applied end to end

readingArticles.title: Naming conventions: why you need them for clean data
keyPoints: Use an object-action naming pattern for events, e.g. 'Product Viewed' or 'Order Completed'
Put variable details (product, city, dish) in properties, never inside the event name
Reuse the same property set across related events so you can segment them consistently
Pick one casing style (e.g. "Order Placed" or "order_placed") and never mix them; duplicates such as "Sign Up" vs "signup" quietly break funnels and dashboards

readingArticles.title: Dashboards: Making Charts and Graphs Easier to Understand
keyPoints: Readers judge length and 2D position fastest, so bar and line charts work best for comparisons
Area-based charts (pie, donut, treemap) and 3D effects make quantitative comparisons slower and less accurate
Use colour and shape to mark categories, not to encode quantities
Design for a quick glance: the key comparison should stand out without careful study

videos.title: PM School - How to Solve RCA questions | Problem Solving based questions in PM Interviews
videos.creator: PM School by NextLeap
keyPoints: Walks through a structured approach to root-cause-analysis questions
Useful for practising the clarify-then-segment habit under time pressure
Compare its structure with the internal vs external split taught in this module
Good for interview prep; then apply the same steps to the drill dataset

practicalTools.name: Metric-Drop Diagnosis Drill
practicalTools.description: A worked diagnostic exercise on an illustrative food delivery dataset. Day 6 introduced the 5 Whys, Day 13 covered choosing metrics, Day 22 funnel drop-offs, Day 24 cohorts and Day 31 the analytics tools and SQL basics. This drill practises the diagnostic method itself: confirm the drop is real, decompose orders into sessions x conversion, segment by platform, funnel step and app version, rule context items in or out, and turn what you find into testable hypotheses and a next query.
practicalTools.exercise: 1) Use the backend orders figures to confirm the drop is real and not a tracking change. 2) Fill in the W2 conversion rates in Table 1 and decide whether sessions or conversion moved. 3) Work out what share of the 8,400 lost orders each platform owns. 4) Fill in the Android W2 step conversion rates in Table 2 and find the step that diverges. 5) Use Table 3 to find which app version owns that divergence. 6) For each context item (release, fee experiment, rain), say whether the data fits it and why. 7) Write three hypotheses. Each must predict a specific pattern you could see in the data. 8) Write the SQL for your next query against the orders/events tables, using a JOIN between events and orders, GROUP BY, date bucketing and a conversion rate, and say which result would confirm or rule out H1. 9) Write a tracking-plan entry for the event that would have caught this drop fastest (event name, trigger, properties) and sketch a 4-tile dashboard: headline orders vs last week and target, orders = sessions x CR, funnel by platform, checkout->order CR by app version. Check your work against the self-check only after you finish.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page diagnosis note containing: the completed tables, a sentence stating where the drop is concentrated (for example, "about 80% of the loss is iOS, at menu to cart, among new users"), the context items you ruled out with reasons, three testable hypotheses with the pattern each predicts, one runnable SQL query with the result that would confirm or rule out your lead hypothesis, one tracking-plan entry and a dashboard sketch.
practicalTools.template:
METRIC-DROP DRILL  (all numbers are illustrative, not real company data)
Food delivery app. Weekly orders fell from 110,000 (W1) to 101,600 (W2).
W1 = 1-7 Sep 2025, W2 = 8-14 Sep 2025.

CONTEXT YOU ARE GIVEN
- Android app v5.2 (new checkout UI) rolled out from Mon 8 Sep and
  reached about 60% of Android users by Sun 14 Sep.
- A delivery-fee experiment runs on 10% of users, iOS and Android, since
  1 Aug (unchanged in W1 and W2).
- Heavy rain in one city on Sat 13 Sep.
- Backend orders table (source of truth): W1 110,000 | W2 101,600.

TABLE 1 - ORDERS = SESSIONS x CONVERSION, BY PLATFORM
Platform   W1 sessions  W1 orders  W1 CR   W2 sessions  W2 orders  W2 CR
Android        500,000     60,000  12.0%       505,000     52,000  ____
iOS            300,000     42,000  14.0%       298,000     41,700  ____
Web            100,000      8,000   8.0%        99,000      7,900  ____
Total          900,000    110,000  12.2%       902,000    101,600  ____

TABLE 2 - ANDROID FUNNEL (count of sessions reaching each step)
Step                    W1 count  W1 step CR   W2 count  W2 step CR
Session                  500,000          -     505,000          -
Menu viewed              300,000      60.0%     303,000      _____
Added to cart            120,000      40.0%     121,200      _____
Checkout started          80,000      66.7%      80,800      _____
Order placed              60,000      75.0%      52,000      _____

TABLE 3 - ANDROID W2, SPLIT BY APP VERSION
Version   Sessions  Checkout started  Orders  Checkout->Order CR
v5.1       205,000            32,800  24,600  _____
v5.2       300,000            48,000  27,400  _____

AVAILABLE TABLES FOR YOUR NEXT QUERY
orders(order_id, user_id, created_at, platform, app_version,
       payment_method, status)
events(event_id, user_id, event_name, event_ts, platform, app_version,
       properties)   -- e.g. event_name = 'checkout_started',
                     --      'payment_failed' (property: error_code)

WORKSHEET
1. Is the drop real? Evidence: ______________________________________
2. Decompose: did sessions or conversion move? ______________________
3. Share of the 8,400-order drop owned by each platform:
   Android ____  iOS ____  Web ____
4. Funnel step where Android W2 diverges from W1: ____________________
5. Version that owns the divergence: _________________________________
6. Which context items can you rule out, and why? ____________________
7. Hypotheses (each must be testable and predict a pattern in data):
   H1: _______________________________ Predicts: ____________________
   H2: _______________________________ Predicts: ____________________
   H3: _______________________________ Predicts: ____________________
8. Next query (write the SQL) and what result would confirm or kill H1:
   ___________________________________________________________________
9. Tracking-plan entry: event ________ trigger ________ properties ______
   Dashboard tiles: 1 ______ 2 ______ 3 ______ 4 ______

SELF-CHECK (read only after you finish)
Table 1 W2 CR: Android 10.3%, iOS 14.0%, Web 8.0%, Total 11.3%.
Sessions are flat (+0.2%); conversion fell. Shares: Android ~95%,
iOS ~4%, Web ~1%. The fee test is unchanged since 1 Aug and covers iOS
too, so it cannot explain an Android-only change. Rain on one day in one
city cannot explain a week-long, version-specific Android gap.
Android owns about 8,000 of the 8,400 lost orders. Its funnel is flat
until checkout -> order (75.0% to about 64.4%), and within W2 that step
is about 75.0% on v5.1 versus about 57.1% on v5.2.
Caveat: early updaters can differ from others; check v5.1 vs v5.2
users' W1 conversion to rule out a population difference.

One possible query (Postgres):
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', e.event_ts) AS day, e.app_version,
       COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_id) AS checkout_users,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS ordering_users,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id)
             / COUNT(DISTINCT e.user_id), 1) AS cr_pct
FROM events e
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.user_id = e.user_id
 AND o.created_at BETWEEN e.event_ts AND e.event_ts + INTERVAL '1 hour'
WHERE e.event_name = 'checkout_started' AND e.platform = 'android'
  AND e.event_ts >= '2025-09-01' AND e.event_ts < '2025-09-15'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;

quiz.question: You are a PM for a food delivery app. The dashboard shows orders down 8% week over week, while sessions are flat. What should you do first?
options: Send an in-app survey asking recent users why they ordered less often this week
Roll back the most recent app release and watch whether orders recover over the week
Check whether the drop also appears in the backend orders table, not just in client events
Compare this week's orders with competitors' download rankings to look for share loss
quiz.explanation: Confirming the data is real comes first. A logging or instrumentation change can create a 'drop' that never happened. Rolling back is tempting, but you do not yet know a release is involved, and a rollback costs time and adds risk.

quiz.question: Orders are down 8% week over week. You break weekly orders into sessions x conversion rate. Sessions are flat and conversion fell from 12.5% to 11.5%. What does this tell you?
options: Users are still arriving but fewer complete an order, so examine the funnel steps
The issue is in acquisition, so marketing spend and channel mix should be reviewed first
The cause must be seasonal, because traffic stayed steady while orders went down
The drop is probably a logging artifact, since a real demand drop would also cut sessions
quiz.explanation: Flat sessions with an 8% relative fall in conversion (12.5% to 11.5%) mean the loss happens after users arrive, so the next step is to find the funnel step where conversion fell. Acquisition is the tempting answer, but acquisition problems show up in sessions, which did not move.

quiz.question: At a ride-hailing company, completed rides fell 6%. You segment by city, platform, app version and new vs returning riders, and every segment is down by roughly the same amount. What does this pattern most suggest?
options: A bug in one app version that has not yet rolled out widely enough to stand out
A broad cause that touches every rider, such as pricing, driver supply or a shared backend
A mistake in the segmentation, because a real drop should be concentrated in one segment
A competitor launch in a single city that is pulling riders away from the platform
quiz.explanation: When every segment falls by about the same amount, look for causes that touch everyone at once. A bug in one version would make that version stand out, and a competitor in one city would make that city stand out. The data shows neither.

quiz.question: You are writing the tracking plan for an e-commerce checkout. Which event design will make later diagnosis easiest?
options: One 'Order Placed' event with properties such as order_value, payment_method, platform and app_version
One event per payment method, such as 'Order Placed UPI' and 'Order Placed Card', to compare methods
One generic 'checkout_action' event, with a free-text label describing what the user did
Separate events for each platform, such as 'checkout_android' and 'checkout_ios', to split traffic
quiz.explanation: An object-action event with consistent properties lets you segment by any dimension, such as platform or payment method, without changing the tracking. Splitting events by payment method or platform looks convenient, but it breaks one action into several names, so every funnel and dashboard has to stitch them back together.

quiz.question: An e-commerce site's overall conversion fell from 4.0% to 3.6%, but conversion within each traffic source (search, email, paid social, direct) is unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A tracking bug is undercounting orders equally across every traffic source this week
Random noise, because segment rates cannot all stay flat while the total moves
A checkout bug is lowering conversion by the same amount for every traffic source
Traffic mix has shifted toward a lower-converting source, such as a new paid social campaign
quiz.explanation: If every segment's rate is flat but the total falls, the mix of segments has changed. This is a mix-shift effect, the same mechanism behind Simpson's paradox. A tracking or checkout bug would lower the rate inside each source, and that has not happened.

quiz.question: To report sessions and orders by platform in one query, an analyst joins sessions (one row per session) to orders (one row per order) on user_id and counts sessions with COUNT(*) grouped by platform. The session total is about 40% higher than the dashboard. What is the most likely cause?
options: GROUP BY platform double-counts users who switch between Android and iOS during the week
DATE_TRUNC moved late-night sessions into the next day, inflating the weekly totals
A LEFT JOIN removed sessions that had no matching orders, distorting the totals
The join repeats each session row once per order the user has, inflating the count
quiz.explanation: Joining on user_id repeats each session once for every order that user placed (join fan-out), so COUNT(*) is inflated. The fix is to aggregate orders per user or session before joining, or to use COUNT(DISTINCT session_id). The LEFT JOIN option is wrong because a LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched sessions and could never push the count above the true total.

quiz.question: At a fintech app, UPI payment success fell from 96% to 91% on the day v8.0 began a staged rollout to 30% of Android users. What is the best next step to test whether v8.0 is the cause?
options: Roll back v8.0 for every user immediately and watch whether the success rate recovers
Compare this week's success rate with the same week last year to rule out seasonality
Compare v8.0 with older versions over the same days, split by bank and payment app
Ask engineering whether any of the code shipped in v8.0 touched the payment flow
quiz.explanation: Comparing versions over the same days controls for external factors such as a bank outage, so a gap between them points to the release. A rollback may be a sensible mitigation, but as a test it mixes up the version change with the passing of time, and it tells you little about which part broke. Check that v8.0 and older-version users had similar success rates before the release, since staged-rollout users are not always a random sample.

quiz.question: You are designing a weekly business dashboard for food delivery leadership. Which principle should guide the design?
options: Lead with the full funnel broken out by every city and platform, so no segment's problem is hidden
Lead with each team's own operational metrics, so every function sees its numbers on the first screen
Lead with the current value of each headline metric alone, keeping comparisons in a separate report
Lead with a few headline metrics, each with its week-over-week change and target, then allow drill-down
quiz.explanation: A leadership dashboard should answer 'are we on track, and what changed?' at a glance, so it needs a few key metrics shown against a comparison and a target, with detail one click away. Leading with the full segmented funnel looks thorough, but it buries the headline under detail that belongs in the drill-down.

quiz.question: Food delivery orders fell 12% on Sunday only. The drop affects every platform and app version, is concentrated in dinner hours in two cities, and app error rates were normal. What should you investigate next?
options: Check what changed in those two cities that evening, such as weather or rider supply
Audit every release from the past two weeks for regressions in the ordering flow
Launch a discount campaign in those two cities to win back the lost orders quickly
Re-cut the data by new vs returning users to find which cohort stopped ordering
quiz.explanation: A one-day drop confined to two cities and certain hours, across all platforms and versions and with normal error rates, points to something local: weather, a big event or a rider-supply shortfall. A release audit is tempting, but a release problem would normally show up by version or platform, not in two cities on one evening.

quiz.question: Your analysis shows the order drop is concentrated on Android v5.2, at the checkout-to-order step. Which hypothesis is the most useful to pursue next?
options: v5.2 users dislike the new checkout design, so a survey of v5.2 users will show lower satisfaction
v5.2 breaks one payment method, so payment_failed events on v5.2 will spike for that method only
v5.2 has a bug somewhere in the app, so engineering should review every change in the release
Android users are more price-sensitive, so last week's delivery-fee increase hit Android orders hardest
quiz.explanation: This hypothesis fits the pattern (v5.2 only, at the step where payment happens), makes a specific prediction, and one query on payment_failed by method and version can confirm or reject it. The price-sensitivity idea sounds plausible, but it cannot explain why Android users on other versions are converting normally.

keyTakeaways: Before you explain a drop, prove it is real: check instrumentation, logging and pipeline changes first.
Decompose, then segment: find which input moved and which segment owns the loss before you form theories.

A drop spread evenly across segments points to a broad cause (pricing, supply, seasonality, a shared outage or a tracking change); a drop concentrated in one segment points to something that touched only that segment, such as a release, a local event or a partner outage.
A good hypothesis predicts a specific pattern in the data and names the query that could prove it wrong.

lessons.label: Module 8
lessons.title: Launch & Go-To-Market: Release Management, Launch Plans and Post-Launch Reviews
lessons.description: Learn how to ship features safely with flags and staged rollouts, size the launch effort with tiers, prepare go-to-market and enablement, and run a blameless post-launch review.
learningObjectives: Design a staged rollout (internal, beta, percentage ramps, 100%) behind a feature flag, with written go/no-go and rollback thresholds for each stage agreed before stage 0 starts
Assign a launch tier (Tier 1/2/3) to any release and justify the matching level of marketing, sales and support effort in one sentence
Draft the go-to-market basics for a mid-sized feature: target segment, one-line positioning message, channels, pricing/packaging hand-off and a sales/support enablement plan with owners
Define a launch metric set (adoption, one primary outcome metric, 2+ guardrails, read-out dates) and run a 60-minute blameless post-launch review that ends in owned action items

readingArticles.title: Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags)
keyPoints: Separates deploying code from releasing a feature, so unfinished work can ship to production switched off
Sorts toggles into four types: release, experiment, ops (including kill switches) and permissioning (e.g. beta or premium users)
Classifies toggles by how long they live and how dynamic they are, which shapes how each should be managed
Warns that toggles carry cost: keep the inventory small and remove release toggles once a feature is fully rolled out

readingArticles.title: Chapter 16 - Canarying Releases (The Site Reliability Workbook)
keyPoints: A canary is a partial, time-limited deployment of a change that is compared against a control population running the current version
Judge a canary on a small set of user-facing signals such as error rate and latency, not on dozens of noisy metrics
Choose metrics that can be attributed to the change being tested, so a go/no-go call is not confused by unrelated noise
A small exposure limits the damage: a defect hitting a 5% canary affects far fewer users than a full release

readingArticles.title: How To Build a Product Launch Plan For SaaS
keyPoints: Splits a launch into pre-launch (research, personas, value proposition, KPIs, beta), launch and post-launch phases
Distinguishes soft, minimal and full-scale launches by audience and fanfare; this is related to, but not the same as, this module's Tier 1/2/3 effort sizing
Recommends a beta with a small group of key customers before a major release to catch edge cases
Treats post-launch as part of the plan: measure exposure, activation, retention and business impact over the following weeks

videos.title: Checklist for Successful Product Launch by Walmart PM Leader
videos.creator: Product School
keyPoints: An experienced PM's talk on what to prepare before a launch and who needs to be involved
Useful for comparing a practitioner's checklist with the template in this module's exercise
Shows that launch work reaches past engineering into marketing, support and operations
Watch for how the speaker sequences pre-launch, launch-day and post-launch activities

videos.title: Feature Toggles & Trunk Based Development | How To and How NOT To
videos.creator: The Theory Of Code
keyPoints: Explains why teams use trunk-based development instead of long-lived branches, and how flags make that possible
Shows how unfinished features can be merged and deployed while switched off
Covers static vs dynamic toggles and the life cycle of a toggle, from creation to removal
Gives a PM enough vocabulary to discuss rollout and kill-switch plans with engineers

practicalTools.name: Mid-Sized Feature Launch Plan
practicalTools.description: A one-page launch plan that ties release mechanics (flags, stages, rollback) to go-to-market (tier, segment, positioning, enablement) and to learning (metrics and a post-launch review). It reuses earlier course tools: the primary metric and guardrails from Day 13 and Day 20, the RACI from Day 19 for launch owners, and the PRD success metrics from Day 15. For the pricing/packaging line, reuse the value metric and good/better/best packaging from Day 34; this module covers only the launch hand-off. Deeper experiment design is covered in Module 6 (Deep Dives), and launching a whole new product is worked through as a case in Module 15.
practicalTools.exercise: Pick a mid-sized feature, either your own or this illustrative one: 'Scheduled lunch orders' for office workers in a food delivery app (order in the morning, choose a 15-minute delivery slot). Using the template: (1) Choose a tier and justify it in one sentence. It is meaningful for one segment but is not a new product or pricing change, so Tier 2 is the usual answer; argue for a different tier if you disagree. (2) Fill in the GTM basics: segment, a positioning line about the customer's outcome rather than the feature, channels, and whether pricing or packaging changes. If you use the illustrative feature, write your own lines rather than reusing the bracketed examples. (3) Define at least 4 rollout stages. Each stage needs an audience, a minimum bake time, a go criterion and a numeric rollback trigger, plus a named kill-switch owner and a date to remove the flag. (4) Build the enablement table for support, ops and marketing with owners. (5) Pick 1 adoption metric, 1 primary outcome metric and at least 2 guardrails (for example on-time delivery rate for scheduled orders, payment errors, support contacts), each with a baseline, target and read-out date, and decide whether to keep a holdout. (6) Complete the launch-day checklist, naming who confirms each item. (7) Adapt the 60-minute post-launch review agenda and list three questions you expect it to answer.
practicalTools.deliverable: A completed one-page launch plan (sections 1-7 of the template) with a tier and rationale, at least 4 rollout stages with a go criterion and a numeric rollback trigger per stage, an enablement table with owners, a metric table with at least 2 guardrails, a filled launch-day checklist and a dated post-launch review agenda.
