quiz.question: You are a PM at a ride-hailing app. A new fare-breakdown screen is shipping behind a feature flag with a 'kill switch'. Ops asks what the kill switch actually gives the team. What is the best answer?
options: It reverts the whole app to the previous app-store version within a few minutes
It automatically runs an A/B test comparing the new screen against the old one
It switches the feature off at runtime, without a new deploy or app-store release
It restricts the feature to internal employees until the launch is approved
quiz.explanation: A kill switch (an ops toggle) disables the feature at runtime, so turning it off needs no deploy or app-store release; reverting the binary is a much slower full rollback, and app-store releases cannot be pulled back instantly. It only works if the old code path still exists, and mobile clients may take a few minutes to fetch the new flag value.

quiz.question: Your B2B SaaS team ships three things this month: (a) a renamed label on the settings page, (b) bulk invoice export that many mid-market customers asked for, and (c) a new paid analytics add-on. Which launch tiering is most sensible?
options: (a) Tier 3 changelog, (b) Tier 1 full GTM because customers asked for it, (c) Tier 2 sales-led
(a) Tier 3 changelog, (b) Tier 3 changelog, (c) Tier 2 sales-led launch to existing accounts
All three as Tier 2 with an email and in-app note, to keep launch effort consistent
(a) Tier 3 changelog, (b) Tier 2 targeted in-app and CSM, (c) Tier 1 full GTM
quiz.explanation: Tiering matches launch effort to customer and business impact. A label change needs only a changelog entry. A requested feature for one segment gets targeted Tier 2 outreach. A new paid product needs full GTM, pricing and sales enablement. Treating the popular feature as Tier 1 and the paid add-on as Tier 2 gets this backwards, because new revenue and packaging changes carry the most impact and risk.

quiz.question: Your food delivery app's new checkout flow is at a 5% rollout. After 48 hours, conversion is flat versus control, support tickets are steady, but the payment error rate is 0.9% versus 0.4% for control. The pre-agreed rollback trigger was 'payment errors more than 0.2pp above control'. What do you do?
options: Expand to 25%, because flat conversion shows that users are not harmed overall
Turn the flag off for the 5% group and investigate the payment errors before re-ramping
Hold at 5% for another week to collect more data, then decide whether to roll back
Expand to 25% but ask the payments team to watch the error dashboard closely
quiz.explanation: The guardrail threshold was set in advance and has been clearly breached (+0.5pp), so the plan says roll back and then investigate. Holding at 5% keeps exposing users to a known failure and weakens the trigger you agreed on before the launch.

quiz.question: A fintech app is about to launch an 'auto-save spare change' feature for salaried first-time investors. You want the beta to give the most decision-useful feedback before the wider rollout. Which beta design is best?
options: An open beta that anyone can join from a home-screen banner, to get the most sign-ups
An employee-only dogfood period, since staff give fast and candid feedback
A beta limited to the highest-balance customers, since they matter most for revenue
A closed beta of recruited target-segment users, with a feedback channel and exit criteria
quiz.explanation: A useful beta represents the target segment and has clear success and exit criteria. An open opt-in beta tends to over-represent enthusiastic early adopters, which skews the signal; employees and high-balance users are not representative of salaried first-time investors either.

quiz.question: A new dispatch-matching change for a food delivery app ran cleanly at 1% for one day. Engineering proposes going straight to 100%. What is the strongest argument for adding intermediate stages, such as 10% and then 50%?
options: Each stage ships a smaller slice of the code, so reviews and deploys are easier to manage
Load, capacity and rare edge-case failures may only appear at higher traffic levels
A slow ramp lets the team skip pre-launch load testing, since real traffic will show the limits
Riders and couriers notice sudden matching changes, so a slow ramp prevents complaint spikes
quiz.explanation: Problems that depend on scale, such as load on dispatch services or rare edge cases, often cannot be seen at 1% of traffic over one day. Intermediate stages with bake time limit how many users are affected while those problems surface. Smaller code slices is wrong because the code is already deployed behind the flag, and a ramp only changes who sees it (deploy is not release).

quiz.question: Your SaaS company is moving existing customers onto a new usage-based pricing tier next week (a Tier 1 launch). With limited time, which enablement item is most critical to finish before launch day?
options: Sales and support have a pricing FAQ, objection handling and the billing migration steps
A press release and analyst briefing that position the new pricing model in the market
A launch webinar for prospects that compares the new tier with competitors' pricing
A live dashboard that tracks daily upgrades to the new tier against the revenue target
quiz.explanation: A pricing change affects existing customers' bills, so the teams who will field their questions must have answers and migration details on day one. A press release or a tracking dashboard is useful but can follow later, and neither prevents the churn and ticket spikes that an unprepared sales and support team causes.

quiz.question: Two weeks after launching 'Save for later' in an e-commerce cart, 18% of cart users have used it, which beats the adoption target. However, overall checkout conversion is 1.2pp lower than in the month before launch. A 10% holdout group never got the feature. What is the best read to bring to the post-launch review?
options: Call it a success, because adoption beat its target and conversion is a lagging metric
Compare conversion against the holdout and check whether saved items convert later
Recommend rollback, because the primary outcome metric fell after launch
Attribute the dip to seasonality, since adoption shows users clearly value the feature
quiz.explanation: A before/after comparison mixes the feature's effect with seasonality and other changes, and the holdout isolates the feature's effect. You also need to know whether saving delays purchases or replaces them. Recommending rollback on the before/after drop alone could kill a feature that is not actually causing the dip.

quiz.question: In a launch readiness review, the engineering lead says, 'We don't need rollback criteria; we'll know a problem when we see it.' As the PM, what is the best response?
options: Agree on numeric thresholds and an owner for each stage before any rollout begins
Agree, and define the criteria after stage 1, once real baseline data is available
Let the on-call engineer decide in the moment, since they have the best context
Use only the company-wide uptime SLO, since it already covers every feature launch
quiz.explanation: Writing thresholds and owners in advance makes the go/no-go call fast and protects it from launch pressure and sunk-cost bias. Deciding after stage 1 means users are already exposed with no agreed trigger, and a company-wide uptime SLO will not catch feature-specific harm such as payment errors.

quiz.question: A ride-hailing app's new driver-payout feature delayed payouts for six hours. The blameless review finds that a wrong config value caused it, no alert fired until drivers complained four hours in, and on-call then took two hours to find the feature's kill switch. You can fund two action items this sprint. Which pair would most shorten the next payout incident, whatever triggers it?
options: Two-person approval and a mandatory staging check on every payout config change
Extra review on the config author's changes, plus config-safety training for the team
An alert on payout delays past a short threshold, and the kill switch in the on-call runbook
A weekly payout-metrics review and a full audit of all past payout config changes
quiz.explanation: Four of the six hours went to detecting the problem and two to finding the off switch, so faster alerting and a documented kill switch shorten any future incident, whatever causes it. Approval and staging checks are worth doing, but they only make this particular config error less likely. They do not reduce detection or mitigation time when a different trigger hits.

quiz.question: You are launching scheduled lunch orders in a food delivery app for office workers. Which launch positioning message is strongest?
options: 'Order by 11, lunch lands in the slot you pick: no more lunch scrambles between meetings'
'Scheduled orders are here, with 15-minute slots powered by our new dispatch engine'
'Schedule any order up to 7 days ahead, from any restaurant, for any time of day'
'Get 20% off your first three scheduled orders this month only'
quiz.explanation: Good positioning speaks to the target segment's problem and the outcome they get. The 'any order, any time' message lists how broad the feature is instead of addressing the office worker's lunch problem. The feature-spec message describes what was built, and a discount is a promotion tactic, not positioning.

keyTakeaways: Deploy is not release: feature flags let you ship code dark, ramp it to 1%, 5%, 25%, 100%, and switch it off without a deploy, usually within seconds to minutes.
Write rollback criteria before you launch; in the middle of a launch, sunk cost and pressure make every red number look 'probably fine'.
Match launch effort to impact: in most teams the majority of releases are Tier 3 changelog items, and only a few earn a full Tier 1 go-to-market.
A launch is done when the post-launch review closes, not on launch day: compare results to targets, blame the process rather than people, and leave with owners and dates.

lessons.label: Module 9
lessons.title: Technical PM: How Systems Fit Together
lessons.description: Learn how the main parts of a modern product (apps, services, databases, queues, cloud and data pipelines) fit together, so you can sketch a system, spot where it can fail and talk trade-offs with engineers.
learningObjectives: Draw a text architecture diagram of a real order flow (client, backend services, database, third parties, queue, data pipeline) and label each arrow as synchronous (S), webhook (W), async job (A) or pipeline (P)
Tell apart authentication and authorization, webhooks and polling, relational and NoSQL storage, and batch and streaming pipelines, and pick the right one for a given product scenario

Explain the trade-offs between a monolith and microservices, and between managed cloud services and self-run infrastructure, including the main cloud cost drivers (compute, storage, data transfer, logging)
List at least 6 failure points in a food-delivery order flow and write one specific PM question for each, covering retries, timeouts, duplicates, fallbacks and data freshness
Turn a technical-debt or scalability request from engineers into product terms (incidents, delivery speed, user impact) so it can be prioritised against roadmap work

readingArticles.title: What's the Difference Between Monolithic and Microservices Architecture?
keyPoints: A monolith is one codebase that handles many business functions. Microservices split the product into small, independently deployable services that talk to each other through APIs (Day 32).
Monoliths are simpler to start with but get harder to change as they grow. Microservices need more upfront planning and operational maturity, such as DevOps practices and container tooling.
Microservices can be scaled and deployed one at a time, which can limit a bad release to one component, as long as safeguards like timeouts and circuit breakers stop failures from cascading.
AWS's own guidance (an opinion, from a vendor) is to choose a monolith for simple projects and microservices for complex systems that are evolving fast.

readingArticles.title: What is a Data Pipeline?
keyPoints: A data pipeline is a series of steps that moves data from sources (app events, databases) to a destination such as a data warehouse or data lake, cleaning and reshaping it along the way.
ETL (extract, transform, load) is one type of pipeline. ELT loads raw data first and transforms it later inside the warehouse.
Batch pipelines run on a schedule over large chunks of data. Streaming pipelines process events continuously and need reliable, low-latency infrastructure.
Dependencies between pipeline steps can delay data downstream, which is why dashboards can be stale or incomplete.

readingArticles.title: Technical Debt Quadrant
keyPoints: Fowler classifies technical debt on two axes, deliberate vs inadvertent and prudent vs reckless, which gives four kinds of debt.
Prudent, deliberate debt is a conscious trade-off, such as shipping for a deadline with a plan to pay it back. Reckless debt comes from ignorance or careless shortcuts.
Some debt is unavoidable: teams often understand the best design only after building the system for a while.
The debt metaphor is a useful way to explain design problems to non-technical stakeholders, PMs included.

videos.title: System Design Concepts Every Product Manager Should Know in 25 Minutes | Technical PM Interview Prep
videos.creator: Racheal Ou
keyPoints: High-level architecture concepts and database/storage choices at the depth a PM needs, not an engineer
Non-functional requirements: performance, scalability, reliability and availability, data consistency and security
How to talk about trade-offs between these requirements instead of treating any one as free
Framed for technical PM interviews, so it doubles as interview prep (see Day 25)

videos.title: 7 System Design Concepts Explained in 10 Minutes
videos.creator: ByteByteGo
keyPoints: System reliability, and what "eventually consistent" data means for what users see
Load balancing and consistent hashing as ways to spread traffic across servers
Circuit breakers that stop one failing dependency from taking down the whole system
Monitoring as the way a team finds out something is broken before users do (rate limiting is also covered and builds on Day 32)

practicalTools.name: Order-Flow Architecture & Failure Map
practicalTools.description: A fill-in text template for sketching how a food-delivery order moves through the system, then listing where it can fail and what the PM should ask. Day 32 taught you the individual API call. This exercise connects many calls into one system: client apps, backend services, a relational orders database, a third-party payment gateway that replies by webhook, a queue that feeds async dispatch and notification jobs, and an event pipeline that feeds a warehouse and dashboards. QUICK REFERENCE. Authentication = who you are (login). Authorization = what you are allowed to do (roles, permissions). OAuth = a standard that lets a user give one app limited access to their data on another service (e.g. letting a scheduling app read your Google Calendar) without sharing their password. 'Sign in with Google' uses OpenID Connect, a login layer built on top of OAuth 2.0. Session = server stores your login state and the browser keeps only an ID in a cookie. Token (e.g. JWT) = a signed credential the client sends with each request, so the server can check it without a lookup. Frontend = the UI running on the user's device. Backend = the services and databases behind it (see Day 32). Webhook = the other system calls you when something happens; polling = you keep asking. Webhooks can arrive late, twice or never, so handlers must be idempotent and verify the sender's signature. Queue = work saved for background workers so the user is not kept waiting. Relational (SQL, e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL) = tables with a defined schema, joins and multi-row transactions. A strong default for orders, payments and inventory. NoSQL = a family (document, key-value, wide-column, graph; e.g. MongoDB, DynamoDB, Redis, Cassandra) with flexible or denormalised data. It often scales out more easily, but consistency guarantees vary by product. Good for catalogues, caches, sessions, feeds and high-volume events. Managed service = the cloud provider runs it for you (e.g. a managed database). Less ops work, but higher unit cost and some lock-in. Self-run = more control and sometimes cheaper at scale, but your team handles patching, backups and on-call. Scaling up (vertical) = a bigger machine. Scaling out (horizontal) = more machines, which needs stateless services. Region = a geographic location of data centres. Choose one close to users, and note that data-residency rules (e.g. Indian payment data) can force a choice. Main cost drivers: compute, storage, data transfer (especially out of the cloud or across regions) and logging/monitoring volume. IDEAS TO CONSIDER for Part B: an auth token expiring mid-checkout; dispatch finding no rider or a job retried twice; a restaurant tablet offline so the order is never accepted; push notifications not delivered; the data pipeline dropping or duplicating events so dashboards disagree; dinner-peak traffic at 3-5x normal (illustrative).
practicalTools.exercise: 1) Copy Part A. Redraw it for one app you know (Swiggy, Zomato, Uber Eats or similar), adding any boxes it lacks, such as coupons, ETA prediction or a restaurant menu service. 2) Mark every arrow S (synchronous: the user waits), W (webhook), A (async job via a queue) or P (pipeline: batch or streaming). Two arrows are pre-labelled as examples. A rule of thumb (not a law): if the user does not need the result before the next screen, it can probably be async. 3) Fill Part B with at least 6 failure points. For each one, write what fails, what the user would see, and one specific question for engineers (retries? idempotency? timeout? fallback? how fresh is the data?). Rows 1-3 are examples. Your 6 rows must be your own, and at least 3 must cover boxes you added. 4) In Part C, pick your top 3 risks, rate likelihood and user impact (H/M/L), rank them, and propose one mitigation for each. 5) Optional: take your sketch to an engineer friend or colleague and ask "What did I get wrong?" Note their corrections. Those corrections are the real learning. 6) Pick one risk from Part C and write a 3-line debt case in Part D: 'Today this causes [N incidents / X hours of downtime / Y extra days per change]. Users feel it as [impact]. Fixing it costs [effort] and unblocks [roadmap item].' Use made-up but labelled numbers.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page text diagram of the order flow with each arrow labelled S/W/A/P, a failure table with 6 or more rows of your own (component, what fails, what the user sees, PM question), a ranked top-3 risk list with one proposed mitigation each, and a 3-line debt/scalability case in product terms.

quiz.question: You are the PM for a fintech app. An audit finds that any logged-in customer-support agent can open any customer's full profile, including unmasked card details. Which kind of problem is this, first and foremost?
options: Authorization: agent roles grant more access than the job requires
Authentication: agents should log in with a stronger password and 2FA
Encryption: card details should be encrypted while in transit
Session management: agent sessions should expire much sooner
quiz.explanation: The system already knows who the agent is (authentication works). The problem is what that identity is allowed to see, which is authorization (least-privilege roles, masking). Stronger login is tempting, but a perfectly authenticated agent would still see too much.

quiz.question: At checkout, your food-delivery app hands payment to a third-party gateway. An engineer's first draft has your server ask the gateway "is this order paid yet?" every 2 seconds for every open order. Which alternative should you raise?
options: Poll every 10 seconds instead, to reduce the load on the gateway
Mark the order paid right away and reconcile mismatches at month end
Have the gateway send a webhook on payment, with a periodic check as backup
Have the customer's app poll the gateway directly, to take load off your servers
quiz.explanation: Webhooks push the result to you as soon as payment happens, which avoids the waste and delay of constant polling. A periodic check catches webhooks that arrive late or not at all. Slower polling, or moving the polling to the client, keeps the same polling pattern: the user waits longer, and payment status comes from a device you cannot trust.

quiz.question: In your ride-hailing app, when a trip ends the server generates a PDF receipt, emails it, updates loyalty points, and only then shows the "Trip complete" screen. Riders wait about 8 seconds. What is the best change to propose?
options: Add a progress spinner with friendly copy so the 8-second wait feels shorter
Show trip-complete at once and move receipt, email and points to background jobs
Buy larger servers so the receipt and email steps finish in under 2 seconds
Remove the email receipt entirely, since the PDF is already in the app
quiz.explanation: None of those steps needs to finish before the rider can be told the trip is complete, so they belong on a queue as async jobs, with retries if the email fails. Bigger servers might shave seconds off but keep slow, failure-prone work in the user's critical path.

quiz.question: Ops wants a live view of restaurants that are slow to accept orders during dinner peak. Finance wants a daily GMV report that matches payment settlements. An engineer proposes one real-time streaming pipeline for both. What is the most sensible recommendation?
options: Stream everything, since fresher data is always better for every team
Batch everything nightly, since one simple pipeline is easier to maintain
Stream the finance data and batch the ops data, since finance needs precision
Stream the ops view and keep finance on reconciled daily batch loads
quiz.explanation: Ops needs minutes-fresh data to act during the peak, which justifies streaming. Finance needs complete, reconciled numbers once a day, which batch handles more cheaply and simply. "Fresher is always better" ignores the extra cost and complexity of streaming when nobody acts on the data in real time.

quiz.question: You are the PM at an 8-engineer SaaS startup that is still searching for product-market fit. A senior engineer proposes splitting the single codebase into 12 microservices "so we can scale". What is the strongest PM response?
options: Support it, since microservices are needed eventually and cheaper to do early
Approve splitting only the user-facing parts now to get half the benefit sooner
Defer to engineering entirely, since architecture is outside a PM's remit
Ask which current pain it fixes, and weigh it against the ops overhead for 8 people
quiz.explanation: Microservices solve specific problems (independent deploys, team scaling, hot spots that need separate scaling), but they add operational overhead that a small, fast-pivoting team feels heavily. Martin Fowler's "Monolith First" argument makes a similar point. Deferring entirely is tempting, but the PM owns the speed-of-learning trade-off and should test the rationale, not dictate the design.

quiz.question: You are speccing a wallet transfer in a fintech app: debit the user's wallet and credit the merchant's. Which data-store property matters most to confirm with engineering?
options: The store can scale horizontally to absorb festival-sale traffic spikes
Both updates run in one atomic transaction, so a failure rolls back both
The schema is flexible enough to add wallet fields without migrations
Balances are cached so the wallet screen loads in under 200 ms
quiz.explanation: Money movement needs all-or-nothing behaviour: a debit without its matching credit is a serious bug. That is the transactional guarantee relational databases are known for (some NoSQL stores also offer it). Horizontal scale matters too, but losing money is worse than slowness.

quiz.question: Customers report occasional double charges. Investigation shows the app automatically retries "Place order" when the request times out on a weak network, and sometimes the first request had in fact succeeded. What fix should you push for?
options: Disable automatic retries so a timed-out request is never sent twice
Add a dialog asking users not to tap "Place order" more than once
Send a unique idempotency key per checkout so retries reuse the first result
Auto-refund duplicates in a nightly batch job that scans all payments
quiz.explanation: An idempotency key lets the server recognise a retried request and return the original order instead of creating a new charge. Retries stay safe and failed requests can still recover. Disabling retries looks simple, but it turns network blips into failed orders and still leaves users tapping again by hand.

quiz.question: Engineers ask for 30% of next quarter's capacity to refactor the order service, calling it "a mess". You also have a revenue feature planned that touches the same service. What is the best next step?
options: Ask what the debt costs today in incidents and delivery speed, then size it vs roadmap
Reject it for now and promise a dedicated refactor quarter once targets are met
Approve it in full, since engineers are best placed to judge code-quality priorities
Split the difference at 15% so the feature and the refactor both get some time
quiz.explanation: Debt becomes prioritisable once it is expressed in product terms: incidents, slower or riskier changes, and especially its effect on the planned feature in the same service. That makes a joint trade-off possible. A blind 15% split feels fair but is not based on the actual cost or benefit.

quiz.question: Illustrative scenario: your cloud bill rose 40% month over month while orders and active users stayed flat. As the PM who owns the platform's cost metric, what should you analyse first?
options: Whether to migrate to a cheaper cloud provider before next month's bill
Which features to shut down to cut compute by 40% and restore the baseline
A cost breakdown by service to find what grew without matching traffic
Whether a reserved-capacity discount would lower the per-hour compute rate
quiz.explanation: Cost that grows without traffic usually points to a specific driver, such as an over-provisioned autoscaling floor, a new pipeline, data transfer or log volume, so you diagnose by service first. A discount or migration is tempting, but it treats the symptom without knowing what changed.

quiz.question: Illustrative scenario: your 6-engineer quick-commerce team self-runs PostgreSQL on cloud VMs. Last quarter, patching, backups and a 3 a.m. failover took about 30% of two engineers' time. A managed database would add roughly Rs 1.5 lakh a month to the bill. What is the strongest PM recommendation?
options: Stay self-run, since the managed database adds Rs 1.5 lakh a month to the bill
Weigh the Rs 1.5 lakh against freed engineer time and outage risk, likely go managed
Hire a dedicated DBA so the team keeps full control without extra cloud spend
Move the database to a cheaper region abroad to offset the managed premium
quiz.explanation: For a small team, managed services trade a higher unit cost for less ops toil: 0.6 of an engineer's time plus failover risk is usually worth more than the premium, and that time can go to roadmap work. Staying self-run is tempting because the bill is visible, but it ignores the hidden cost of engineer time; a region abroad adds latency and can break data-residency rules for Indian payment data.

keyTakeaways: Every arrow in a system diagram is a promise that can break. Your job is to ask what the user sees when it does.

Keep the user's critical path short. Do synchronously only what the user must wait for, and move the rest to queues. When a slow third party is involved (e.g. a payment gateway), show a clear pending state and take the result by webhook.
Architecture choices like microservices, streaming or NoSQL fix specific problems. Ask "which pain does this remove?" before "how modern is it?"
Technical debt gets prioritised when you express it in product terms: incidents, slower delivery and the user impact behind them.

lessons.label: Module 10
lessons.title: Building LLM Products: RAG, Agents, Model Choice and AI Product Metrics
lessons.description: Building on Day 29 (AI PM intro) and Day 35 (evals, prompts, guardrail basics), this deep dive covers the architecture and economics decisions behind LLM features (prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning, agent autonomy, model selection, AI UX, misuse risks) and the metrics that show whether a launched AI feature is worth what it costs.
learningObjectives: Choose between prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and fine-tuning for a given feature, and justify the choice by what the feature needs: private or changing facts, citations, consistent behaviour at scale, or speed to ship
Pick the lowest autonomy level (suggest, draft, act with undo, act alone) that solves a job, and list the actions that must always need human confirmation
Calculate cost per successful task for two candidate models, including the cost of human fallback, and explain why a model that is cheaper per request can cost more per successful task
Define a launch metric set (task success, acceptance/edit rate, cost per successful task, latency p50/p95, escalation rate, guardrail incidents) with targets and kill criteria set before launch

readingArticles.title: Emerging Patterns in Building GenAI Products
keyPoints: Shows the pattern sequence teams actually use: direct prompting, then embeddings and RAG, then improvements such as hybrid retrieval, query rewriting and reranking
Explains when fine-tuning is worth its cost and why most teams should exhaust prompting and retrieval first
Covers guardrails and evals as part of the architecture rather than an afterthought (skim the evals section, which Day 35 already covers)
Grounded in real client engagements, which makes it useful for explaining trade-offs to engineers

readingArticles.title: Building Effective AI Agents
keyPoints: Separates workflows (LLM steps in fixed code paths) from agents (the LLM decides its own steps and tool calls)
States plainly that agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and that errors can compound across steps
Recommends starting simple: optimise a single LLM call with retrieval and examples before adding agents
Describes reusable workflow shapes (prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) that a PM can name in specs

readingArticles.title: Prompt injection: What's the worst that can happen?
keyPoints: Prompt injection happens when untrusted text (emails, web pages, documents) is mixed into the prompt and the model follows instructions hidden in it
Risk is lower when output is only shown to the user (though rendered links or images can still leak data), and high once the model has tools that can send email, call APIs or read private data
Walks through concrete attacks: a hijacked email assistant, search index poisoning and data exfiltration
No reliable fix exists, so the product mitigations are to show users what the AI will do and require confirmation before consequential actions

videos.title: RAG vs. Fine Tuning
videos.creator: IBM Technology
keyPoints: RAG adds up-to-date or private knowledge at query time without retraining the model
Fine-tuning changes how the model behaves (style, format, domain language) using labelled examples
The two can be combined, and the right choice depends on how often the data changes and how specialised the task is
A useful whiteboard explanation to share with stakeholders who are not engineers

videos.title: How We Build Effective Agents: Barry Zhang, Anthropic
videos.creator: AI Engineer
keyPoints: Don't build an agent for everything. Use one only when the task is complex and valuable enough to justify the extra cost and latency
Keep the agent loop simple (model, tools, instructions) and add complexity only when evals show you need it
Look at the task from the agent's point of view: what context and tools would it really need?
A practical companion to the Anthropic 'Building Effective AI Agents' article

practicalTools.name: AI Feature Decision Memo
practicalTools.description: A one-page memo that turns an AI feature idea into concrete decisions: build approach, autonomy level, model choice with unit economics, human-in-the-loop design, misuse risks and launch metrics. It is the AI-specific add-on to your PRD (Day 15) and the eval plan you wrote in Day 35.
practicalTools.exercise: 1) Pick an AI feature for a real product you use, for example AI replies for a food delivery support console, a 'where is my refund' assistant for a fintech app, or AI-written product descriptions for e-commerce sellers. 2) Write the user problem in two lines: who has it, how they handle it today, and what 'done well' looks like. 3) Use the build-approach grid to choose prompting, RAG or fine-tuning, and justify it in two lines. 4) Choose the lowest autonomy level that solves the job, and list the actions the AI must never take on its own (refunds, payouts, account changes, messages sent to customers). 5) Fill in the economics table for two candidate models. Estimate tokens per request, look up current public prices, and assume success rates until your evals give you real ones. Label every number ILLUSTRATIVE. Then work out cost per successful task, including the cost of a human handling each failure. 6) Design the UX: streaming, citations, editable draft, limitations message, review step and escalation path. 7) List the untrusted inputs the model reads and the worst action an injected instruction could trigger, then add a mitigation (remove the tool, require a confirmation step, or filter the output). 8) Set launch metrics with targets and kill criteria before launch (use Day 13 for metric frameworks and counter-metrics, and Day 20 for experiment design, sample size and guardrail metrics). Keep it to one page.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page AI Feature Decision Memo with a justified build approach, an autonomy level and a never-alone action list, an economics table comparing two models (all figures labelled illustrative), a human-in-the-loop design, at least one injection or data-leakage mitigation, and 6-7 launch metrics with targets and kill criteria.
practicalTools.template:

6. SAFETY + MISUSE

7. LAUNCH METRICS (targets set BEFORE launch)

quiz.question: A fintech app wants its support assistant to answer questions about fee schedules. The fees change every month and live in internal policy documents. Which build approach fits best?
options: Fine-tune the model on last year's policy documents so it memorises the fee schedule
Write a longer system prompt telling the model to be careful and accurate about fees
Use RAG: retrieve the current policy passages at query time and cite them in answers
Switch to the largest available model, since it has more general financial knowledge
quiz.explanation: RAG is built for private, frequently changing facts. Updating the documents updates the answers, and the retrieved passages can be cited. Fine-tuning is the tempting wrong choice: it bakes in a snapshot that goes stale next month and gives you nothing to cite.

quiz.question: A SaaS CRM launches AI-drafted follow-up emails. Which metric best shows whether the feature is actually saving users work?
options: Total number of drafts generated per day across all customer accounts
Share of drafts sent with light or no edits, compared with drafts discarded
Average length of the generated drafts, measured in tokens per draft
Median model response time measured on the server for each draft
quiz.explanation: Acceptance and edit rate measure whether the output was good enough to use, which is the value the feature exists to create. Drafts generated is a vanity activity metric: users can generate many drafts and throw every one away.

quiz.question: You are the PM for a food delivery app. Leadership wants an AI agent that issues refunds automatically when customers report missing items, with full autonomy from day one. What is the best v1 design?
options: The agent drafts each refund with evidence, auto-approves below a small cap, and sends the rest to a human
The agent approves every refund itself, and a weekly audit reviews a random sample after payouts
The agent auto-approves any refund for customers with a clean order history, with no cap on amount
The agent approves every refund itself, guided by a system prompt telling it never to over-refund
quiz.explanation: Refunds move money and invite abuse, so a small cap bounds the damage from any single error or fraud while still automating the common case. A clean-history rule is the tempting option, but it does not limit the amount: a taken-over account or a model error can still pay out large sums. A weekly audit only finds problems after the money has gone, and a prompt instruction is not a control.

quiz.question: Illustrative numbers for a support bot: Model A costs $0.01 per request and resolves 80% of tasks on its own. Model B costs $0.001 per request and resolves 50%. Every task the model fails goes to a human agent, who resolves it at a cost of $0.40, so every task ends up resolved. Counting both model and human cost, which model has the lower cost per resolved task?
options: Model A, at about $0.09 versus about $0.20 per resolved task
Model B, because its cost per request is ten times lower than Model A's
Model B, at about $0.002 versus about $0.0125 for each task the model resolves
They are roughly equal at about $0.10 each once the human fallback is included
quiz.explanation: Every task is eventually resolved, so cost per resolved task = model cost + failure rate x human cost. Model A: $0.01 + 0.2 x $0.40 = $0.09. Model B: $0.001 + 0.5 x $0.40 = about $0.20. The $0.002 vs $0.0125 option is the trap: it divides only the API cost by the success rate and leaves out the humans who handle the failures.

quiz.question: A ride-hailing driver-support assistant reads drivers' uploaded documents and emails. It also has a tool that can change a driver's payout bank account. Security review flags prompt injection. What is the strongest mitigation?
options: Add a system prompt line telling the model to ignore any instructions found inside documents
Upgrade to a larger, more capable model that is harder to trick with injected text
Scan uploaded documents and block any containing the phrase 'ignore previous instructions'
Remove the bank-change tool from the assistant and require an authenticated, user-confirmed flow
quiz.explanation: There is no reliable prompt-level defence against injection, so the robust fix is least privilege: the model simply cannot take the high-impact action. A system-prompt instruction is tempting, but attackers routinely get around it, and around phrase filters and larger models too.

quiz.question: On an e-commerce site, the AI product Q&A assistant takes 8 seconds to return a full answer and many users leave before it appears. Engineering says total generation time cannot be cut this quarter. What is the best first move?
options: Add a 'thinking' animation while waiting, and keep returning the full answer all at once at the end
Cut the retrieved context to a single document so that answers become shorter and generate faster
Offer a 'notify me when ready' button so shoppers can keep browsing while the answer is generated
Stream the answer token by token and show the retrieved sources first, so users see progress in about a second
quiz.explanation: Streaming improves perceived latency (time to first token) without changing total generation time, and showing sources early builds trust. A thinking animation is the tempting option, but users still see nothing useful for 8 seconds. Cutting context reduces answer quality, and a notification moves the shopper away from the product page.

quiz.question: A SaaS support team classifies tickets by prompting a large model. It scores 94% accuracy on evals, but at 2 million tickets a day the cost and latency are too high. The team has 200,000 historical tickets labelled by agents. What should you do next?
options: Add RAG over the help centre so the classifier sees more context for each ticket
Keep the large model and add more few-shot examples to the classification prompt
Turn the classifier into an agent that looks up each customer's account first
Fine-tune a smaller model on the labelled tickets and compare it on the same evals
quiz.explanation: A narrow, high-volume task with plenty of labelled examples is the classic case for fine-tuning: a small tuned model can often match quality at a fraction of the cost and latency, and the existing eval set gives a fair comparison. More few-shot examples or an agent would add tokens and steps, raising cost and latency instead of cutting them.

quiz.question: A food delivery support console launched AI reply suggestions. Agents accept 85% of them, but CSAT on AI-assisted tickets has fallen and the ticket reopen rate has risen. What is the most likely explanation and next step?
options: The model is too slow; measure p95 latency and move to a faster model to fix CSAT
Agents accept drafts unchecked; audit a sample of accepted replies and add review for risky types
Customers dislike AI replies; add a visible label saying that the reply was AI-generated
Acceptance is high, so the feature works; the CSAT dip is most likely seasonal noise
quiz.explanation: High acceptance alongside worse outcomes is a sign of automation bias: people approve output they haven't checked. Acceptance is a proxy, so you have to audit quality on the outcome metrics. Calling it seasonal noise ignores that the reopen rate moved in the same direction.

quiz.question: A fintech feature will summarise customers' KYC documents using an LLM from an external vendor. Three vendors are on the shortlist. Which question should you settle first?
options: Which vendor ranks highest on public leaderboards for document summarisation benchmarks
Which vendor's model offers the largest context window for long, multi-page documents
Whether each vendor's data retention, training use and data region meet regulatory requirements
Which vendor offers the lowest price per million output tokens at the expected volume
quiz.explanation: KYC documents are sensitive personal data, so data handling is a pass/fail gate: a vendor that fails it is out, however good or cheap it is. Leaderboard rank, context window and price are trade-offs to weigh only among the vendors that pass.

quiz.question: An e-commerce team proposes skipping retrieval and pasting the whole 400-page seller policy manual into every prompt, because the new model's context window can hold it. What is the strongest PM objection?
options: Each time the manual is updated, the model would need to be fine-tuned again before its answers changed
Answers drawn from a long context cannot cite specific sections, so sellers would have no way to verify them
Every request pays for and waits on the full manual, and details deep in long prompts can be missed
Sending the full manual to the provider needs a fresh legal review that would delay launch by a quarter
quiz.explanation: Putting hundreds of pages of input tokens into every request multiplies cost and latency, and models can miss details buried deep in very long prompts. Retrieval sends only the relevant passages. Prompt caching can cut the repeated input cost, but not the latency on cache misses or the risk of missed details. The fine-tuning objection is the tempting mix-up: a document in the prompt updates as soon as you edit it, so no retraining is needed, and long-context answers can also be prompted to cite sections.

keyTakeaways: Start with prompting, use retrieval for facts, and fine-tune only for behaviour you need at scale. Change one layer at a time.
Every bit of autonomy adds risk. Give the model the least power that still does the job, and make every consequential action reversible or confirmed by a person.
Measure the cost of the outcome, not the API call. Cost per successful task includes retries, wasted calls and the humans who fix failures.
Any text the model reads can try to give it instructions. Design its tools and permissions on the assumption that some of that text will be hostile.

lessons.label: Module 11
lessons.title: Product Leadership & Product Operations
lessons.description: How senior PMs communicate with executives, run product reviews, resolve cross-functional conflict, influence teams they do not manage, and use product operations to scale themselves and their teams.
learningObjectives: Write a one-page executive update (under 400 words) that opens with the decision or ask, then gives options, trade-offs, a recommendation and risks, and answer "why is this late?" in under 30 seconds with the new date, your confidence, the root cause and the recovery plan, without blaming anyone
Pick the right resolution path for a cross-functional conflict (direct conversation, disagree and commit, or a joint escalation with a written options doc) and explain why

Diagnose whether a product org needs product operations by spotting at least three symptoms (scattered tooling, data-access bottlenecks, slow planning, lost customer feedback) and name what product ops would own and what product leaders keep
Run a product review that uses a 24-hour written pre-read, frames each agenda item as a decision, and ends with an owner and a date for every decision
Scale yourself by writing down strategy and decision principles so the PMs you lead can make calls within them without you

readingArticles.title: BLUF: The Military Standard That Can Make Your Writing More Powerful
keyPoints: BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) is a military writing convention: state the conclusion or ask first, then the supporting detail
In emails, lead with your ask; when revising, move your concluding sentence to the top
Find the "so what" the reader needs before you write anything else
Caveat: BLUF is a poor fit for sensitive news, for cultures that expect indirectness, and for topics that need context first, so adapt it to your audience

readingArticles.title: 2016 Letter to Shareholders (see "High-Velocity Decision Making" and "Disagree and Commit")
keyPoints: Many decisions are reversible two-way doors, so make them quickly with a lightweight process and correct course if wrong
Bezos suggests deciding with about 70% of the information you wish you had, because waiting for 90% is usually too slow
"Disagree and commit": once a direction is chosen without consensus, people who disagreed back it fully instead of half-heartedly
Escalate real misalignment early. Without escalation, disputes are settled by exhaustion: whoever has more stamina wins, not whoever is right.

readingArticles.title: Product Ops Overview
keyPoints: "Product Ops" means very different things at different companies, so ask what it actually owns before you assume
Anti-patterns: a renamed command-and-control PMO, splitting the PM job into two roles, or using product ops to cover for weak product leadership
Cagan argues for product ops as a force multiplier that bundles quantitative insights, qualitative research and tools and best practices
Its job is to enable product teams, not to control them

videos.title: How to Influence Without Authority by BestBuy Sr Product Manager
videos.creator: Product School
keyPoints: Watch for how a practising PM gets buy-in from teams they do not manage
Note the techniques that rely on trust and on what the other team needs, rather than on escalation
Compare the talk with this module's advice: learn the other team's goals first, then link your request to a metric they own
Pick one tactic to try in your next cross-team request

videos.title: 5 Rules for Communicating Effectively with Executives
videos.creator: Dr. Grace Lee
keyPoints: A short video on how to talk to senior leaders with confidence and earn their trust
Map each rule onto the one-page update template in the exercise
Note the business-acumen tips covered near the end of the video
Look for habits that waste an executive's time so you can cut them from your own updates

practicalTools.name: One-Page Executive Update: The Slipping Launch
practicalTools.description: This exercise practises a senior PM skill: turning a messy delivery slip into a short decision document that an executive can act on in five minutes. Day 19 covered mapping stakeholders and RACI. Here you are the person who has to bring the bad news, frame the options and ask for a decision. It is a best-practice format, not a fixed standard; many companies have their own memo template.
practicalTools.exercise: 1) Read the scenario and status table in the template. All numbers are illustrative. 2) Work out the decision you actually need. It is probably not "approve a new date"; it is a choice between scope, date and operational risk. Name who decides and by when, for example before the campaign's notice period runs out. 3) Fill in the options table for A, B and C. For each, write the customer impact, the business impact (campaign fee, lost festive orders, ops cost), the main risk and whether it can be reversed. Add an option D if you see a better one. 4) Recommend one option and give 2-3 reasons. Make it a real recommendation, not "all options have merit". 5) List the top two risks of your recommendation with a mitigation and an owner for each. 6) Write the update in BLUF order and keep it to one page (about 300-400 words). Put no jargon in the first two lines. 7) Write a 2-sentence verbal answer for when the CEO stops you in the corridor and asks "why is this late?". It should give the new date, your confidence, the root cause and the plan, and blame no one. 8) Self-check: could a busy executive decide after reading only the subject line and section 1? If not, rewrite them.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page executive update (300-400 words) with the decision needed, an options table with trade-offs, one clear recommendation, the top risks with mitigations and owners, one specific ask, and the next update date. Add a 2-sentence verbal answer to "why is this late?".
practicalTools.template:
SCENARIO (all numbers are illustrative)
You are the PM for "Scheduled Orders" on a food delivery app: customers can
book a meal up to 48 hours ahead. You committed a 1 Nov launch to the CEO.

5. RISKS AND MITIGATIONS

   1.

   ...

quiz.question: You are a PM at a fintech app writing a weekly update to your VP. The UPI autopay integration is behind schedule, and you need the VP to approve cutting it from v1 so you can hold the 15 Nov launch date. Which opening line is best?
options: Decision needed by Thursday: approve cutting UPI autopay from v1 so we can hold the 15 Nov launch date.
Context: over the last six weeks the team explored three integration approaches with the gateway partner.
Status: 9 of 12 tickets are done across four squads, and payments has the most work still open.
Heads up: we have hit some challenges with the gateway partner and wanted to flag them early.
quiz.explanation: Executive updates should lead with the decision or ask (BLUF) and put the evidence after it. The context-first opening is the tempting choice, but it makes the VP read through history before learning what you need from them.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the core purpose of a product operations function?
options: To set each team's priorities centrally so every squad's roadmap stays aligned with company goals and OKRs.
To track delivery dates and approve release plans so leadership gets one reliable view of progress across teams.
To remove operational friction in tools, data access and customer insight so PMs can focus on product decisions.
To write PRDs and acceptance criteria for every team so that PMs have more time to spend on strategy.
quiz.explanation: Product ops is a force multiplier: it removes operational friction in tooling, data and customer insight so PMs spend their time on product decisions. Tracking dates and approving release plans is the tempting choice, but that turns product ops into a PMO that adds control instead of enabling teams.

quiz.question: You are a PM at a ride-hailing company. Instant driver payouts were promised for this month and have slipped two weeks. The CEO stops you in the corridor and asks, "Why is this late?" What is the best response?
options: Walk through each engineering blocker in turn so the CEO sees how hard the team has worked to recover the schedule.
Give the new date and your confidence in it, the one main root cause, and how you are protecting the new date; offer a written note.
Explain that engineering underestimated the work and say you will push the team harder to make up the lost time.
Avoid naming any date until the team finishes re-estimating, so that you do not overcommit and slip a second time.
quiz.explanation: A good answer to "why is this late?" is short, owns the problem and looks forward: date, confidence, cause and plan. Refusing to give a date sounds prudent, but it leaves the CEO with nothing to plan around. You can give a date with a stated confidence level and update it later.

quiz.question: You and the design lead disagree on e-commerce onboarding. Design wants a three-screen tutorial; you want users to land straight on the home feed. You have both made your case, the data is inconclusive, and the Head of Product (the decision owner) chooses the tutorial. What should you do now?
options: Commit fully: build it well, agree the metric that would show it is wrong, and revisit at a set checkpoint.
Build the tutorial, but tell your engineers you disagreed so they know it was not your call.
Ask for one more week of user research before committing the team to either onboarding design.
Escalate to the CPO, since onboarding is in your area and the PM should own the final call on it.
quiz.explanation: Disagree and commit means arguing your case before the decision and backing the decision fully after it, ideally with a metric and a checkpoint so it can be revisited on evidence. Asking for more research sounds rigorous, but the decision owner has already decided with inconclusive data, so it only reopens the debate and delays the team.

quiz.question: Your food delivery team needs the central data platform team, which sits in a different org with its own roadmap, to build a new real-time event pipeline for your feature. You have no authority over them. What is the best first move?
options: Learn their goals and constraints, then show how the pipeline helps a metric their team owns.
Ask your VP to ask their VP to put the pipeline on the data platform roadmap for this quarter.
Send them a detailed PRD for the pipeline and ask for an engineering estimate by Friday.
Log the request in their intake queue and wait for it to come up in their next planning cycle.
quiz.explanation: Influence without authority starts with understanding what the other team is measured on and framing your request so it advances their goals. Going manager to manager may work once, but as a first move it damages trust and is better kept as a last resort.

quiz.question: At a B2B SaaS company, the Head of Sales has promised a large prospect custom SSO by Q1. It is not on the roadmap, and the engineering lead says it would push back a committed reliability project. You have talked it through with both of them and there is still no agreement. What should you do?
options: Side with engineering, since leadership already approved the roadmap and sales should not override it.
Tell sales the request must wait for next quarter's planning, and keep the current roadmap until then.
Escalate to your own manager first, on your own, so you can frame the issue before the others do.
Escalate together to the shared decision-maker with one doc setting out the options and the cost of each.
quiz.explanation: When peers cannot agree, a clean escalation means going together to the person who owns the trade-off, with one neutral options doc that both sides accept as fair. Siding with engineering because of an earlier approval is tempting, but it dismisses new business information that the trade-off owner should weigh.

quiz.question: A fintech has grown from 3 to 18 product teams in two years. PMs use five different tools to log customer feedback, analysts get about 40 ad-hoc data requests a week, and quarterly planning now takes six weeks. What is the best response?
options: Hire enough analysts that every PM has a dedicated analyst for their ad-hoc data pulls and reporting.
Standardise all teams on one feedback tool now, and revisit data requests and planning next half.
Set up a PMO that reviews and approves every team's roadmap so that quarterly planning closes faster.
Set up product ops to own shared tools, self-serve data and feedback intake, so planning gets lighter.
quiz.explanation: Scattered tooling, data-access bottlenecks and slow planning are classic signs that the org has outgrown informal processes, and product ops tackles their shared root cause while product leaders keep the planning decisions. Hiring analysts is tempting, but it scales the bottleneck linearly, and a PMO that approves roadmaps adds control instead of enabling teams.

quiz.question: You run a monthly product review for a ride-hailing app. It has turned into a 90-minute status show-and-tell where executives redesign screens on the spot and few decisions get made. What is the most effective change?
options: Invite fewer engineers and designers so that executives feel freer to give candid feedback.
Send a pre-read 24 hours ahead, frame each item around a decision, and use the time for debate.
Move the review from monthly to weekly so that issues surface earlier and each meeting is shorter.
Show only finished, polished designs so that executives have less room to redesign screens.
quiz.explanation: Good product reviews move status updates into a written pre-read and spend the meeting on the decisions and risks that need leaders' input. Showing only polished designs is tempting, but it moves the review too late: feedback then arrives after the team has invested, and the meeting still lacks a decision focus.

quiz.question: You were promoted to group PM at an e-commerce company and now lead three PMs. Every pricing, scope and launch call comes to you, and you have become the team's bottleneck. What is the best way to scale yourself?
options: Run a daily sync where each PM brings their pending decisions to you for a quick approval.
Take over the riskiest team's work yourself and let the other two PMs run on their own.
Ask the PMs to copy you on all stakeholder emails so you can step in before a problem grows.
Write down the strategy and decision principles, let PMs decide within them, and review the outcomes together.
quiz.explanation: Writing strategy and decision principles down lets other people make good decisions without you, and reviewing outcomes keeps quality high. A daily approval sync feels efficient, but every decision still waits on you, so the bottleneck stays and the PMs do not develop their judgement.

quiz.question: Your food delivery launch has just slipped by about three weeks. Marketing has a paid campaign booked for launch week, which can be moved with two weeks' notice. You are about 70% confident in the new date. When and how should you involve marketing?
options: Wait until engineering confirms the new date, so marketing only has to replan the campaign once.
Tell marketing to keep the campaign as booked, and plan to launch a reduced scope on the original date.
Tell marketing now, with the slip, your confidence level and the options, so they can decide before costs lock in.
Mention the slip in your regular weekly status email so that every stakeholder hears it the same way.
quiz.explanation: Partner teams need early, honest information, including how uncertain it is, while they can still act on it. Here that means before the campaign's notice window closes. Waiting for certainty sounds considerate, but it can push marketing past the deadline for moving the campaign and turn a manageable change into wasted spend.

keyTakeaways: Assume an executive may read only the first two lines. Put the decision or ask there, with the evidence under it. The same goes for product reviews: they are for decisions, not status, so put status in a pre-read and spend the meeting on the decisions and risks that need leaders.

Disagree openly before the decision and commit fully after it; when you cannot agree, escalate together with one shared doc, not separately with two stories. Influence without authority comes from trust and from knowing what the other team is measured on, so you can show how your request moves their metric. Escalating manager to manager is a last resort.

Product ops is a force multiplier: it gives PMs data and customer insight, shared tools and good practices, so they spend their time on product decisions. Models differ: Cagan keeps planning with product leaders, while Perri and Tilles also give product ops process and governance. Either way it should enable teams, not approve their work.
Once you lead other PMs, write down the strategy and decision rules, let them decide within those rules, and review outcomes rather than approving each call.

lessons.label: Module 12
lessons.title: Case Study: Food Delivery Orders Are Declining
lessons.description: A hands-on diagnosis case in which you work through a fictional food-delivery app's weekly topline, funnel, platform, city and release data to explain an 8% week-over-week drop in orders, find its most likely root cause and propose a fix with guardrails.
learningObjectives: Break a week-over-week drop in orders into sessions x conversion, and name which factor moved, using the case's Table 1
Find the single funnel step and the platform segment that account for at least 90% of the lost orders, and size the weekly impact to within about 10%
Test each candidate cause (a release, a backend change, a city-level event) against the data, and write down the specific evidence that confirms or rules it out
Write a one-page diagnosis covering the root-cause statement, confidence level, the top 3 verification checks with their data sources, an immediate fix and at least 2 guardrail metrics

readingArticles.title: How to answer metric drop questions in PM interviews
keyPoints: Before building product hypotheses, confirm the drop is real: rule out tracking bugs, pipeline failures and dashboard errors.
Work through technical causes in order: deployments, broken instrumentation, problems at third parties such as payment processors, and infrastructure incidents.

Segment by platform, browser, geography and device. A drop isolated to one platform or version usually points to a technical cause (a release, an SDK, an OS update), though platform-specific marketing or store changes can do the same.
Weigh user-behaviour and market explanations (competitors, seasonality, UX) alongside the technical checks, but give the technical causes priority because they are quicker to confirm or rule out.

readingArticles.title: Conversion funnel analysis for product managers: How to spot drop-offs
keyPoints: Define each funnel around one user goal and one success outcome before you measure anything.
Compare step-to-step conversion, not only end-to-end conversion, to find exactly where users drop off.
Aggregate rates blend very different behaviours. Segmenting by device or user type shows problems that the headline number hides.
Pair the numbers with qualitative context (support conversations, feedback, session insights) before you decide why users leave.

videos.title: Product Manager Metrics Interview: "Engagement Drops 10%"
videos.creator: IGotAnOffer (with an ex-Meta PM)
keyPoints: A full mock interview on diagnosing a sudden metric drop: the same skill this case practises
Pause before the candidate answers and write your own first three steps
Map each step they take to: confirm the data, decompose, segment, internal vs external causes, hypotheses
Compare their structure with your answer to this case, then refine your write-up

practicalTools.name: Metric-Drop Diagnosis: TiffinGo Orders -8% WoW
practicalTools.description: A fictional but internally consistent data pack for a food-delivery app: 4 weeks of sessions, orders and conversion; a 5-step funnel for last week vs the week before, overall and by platform; a city table with each city's Android share; conversion by city x platform; and a release log with ops notes. One cause explains the drop. At least one other item in the data looks guilty but is not. This case applies the metrics thinking from Day 13 and the funnel/segmentation practice from Day 31, the funnel thinking from Day 22 (AARRR) and the 5 Whys from Day 6.
practicalTools.exercise:
Use only the data in the template. Show your arithmetic.
1. Confirm the drop is real. Where do the order counts come from? Is the drop large compared with normal weekly variation in W36-W38?
2. Decompose: write orders = sessions x conversion for W38 and W39. Which factor moved, and by how much (in % and pp)?
3. Locate the step: using Table 2, find the funnel step whose step conversion changed. Are the other steps stable?
4. Locate the segment: using Table 3, compare Android and iOS at that step. Roughly what share of the lost orders comes from each platform?
5. Size it: estimate the orders lost per week as checkouts x the fall in checkout-to-order conversion on the affected segment. Does that roughly match the topline drop?
6. Test the suspects: for (a) the W38 restaurant-ranking model, (b) the Mumbai rain and rider shortages, and (c) Android 7.4.0, give the data point that supports or rules out each one. Explain why Mumbai shows the largest % and absolute drop (hint: Tables 4 and 5).
7. State the most likely root cause in one sentence, give 3 pieces of evidence and a confidence level (high/medium/low) with the reason.
8. List the top 3 checks you would run before the review, each with its data source (e.g. app-version split, payment-method split, payment gateway/SDK error logs, support tickets).
9. Propose a fix: what to do today and what to do this sprint. Remember that you cannot uninstall an Android update users already have, and that iOS 7.4.0 is waiting in App Store review.
10. Propose 2-3 guardrails (metrics, alerts or release rules) that would have caught this within hours rather than a week.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page diagnosis memo for the VP. A strong answer: (1) shows that sessions are flat (+0.0%) and conversion fell from 10.70% to 9.86% (-0.84 pp), and that orders come from the order database, so the drop is real and not a tracking artefact; (2) places the drop at checkout -> order placed (83.6% -> 76.9%) with every earlier step flat; (3) shows it is entirely Android (82.0% -> 71.0% at that step; Android orders -13.2%, iOS +0.2%; Android lost 16,928 orders, about 101% of the net -16,742, because iOS gained 186) and roughly uniform across cities in Table 5; (4) sizes it at about 156,908 x 11 pp, roughly 17,000 orders per week, which matches the topline -16,742; (5) names the root cause as the Android 7.4.0 payment change (new payments SDK / rebuilt UPI hand-off) causing payment failures or abandonment, rated high confidence that 7.4.0 is the cause, medium confidence that the payment SDK/UPI change (rather than the new checkout copy) is the mechanism, until the payment-method split and error codes confirm it; (6) rules out the ranking model (restaurant -> cart is flat, W38 orders are flat) and the Mumbai rain (Mumbai sessions are flat, Mumbai iOS conversion is flat, and Mumbai's larger drop is explained by its 75% Android share); (7) lists verification steps: split Android checkout -> order by app version 7.4.0 vs 7.3.x, by payment method (UPI vs card vs cash) and by device/OS, check payment-SDK and gateway error codes and the daily trend from 21 Sep, and read support tickets about failed or double-debited payments; (8) gives a fix: today, flip the payment flow back to the old path with a remote-config or feature-flag kill switch if one exists, or halt the release and ship a 7.4.1 hotfix; hold iOS 7.4.0 until the fix is confirmed; tell customer support about any failed or pending debits; (9) gives guardrails: a payment-success (checkout -> order) metric by platform and app version with an alert threshold, staged rollouts (e.g. 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%) gated on that metric, and new payment code shipped behind a feature flag.
practicalTools.template:
CASE: "Orders are down 8% and nobody knows why"
Company and all data below are FICTIONAL and illustrative.

THE SITUATION
You are the PM for ordering at TiffinGo, a food-delivery app in four
Indian cities. It is Monday 28 Sep 2026. The weekly business review shows
orders fell ~8% last week (W39) while app sessions were flat. Your VP asks:
"What happened, how sure are you, and what are we doing about it?"
You have 45 minutes before the review.

Definitions
- Session  = one app open (client event).
- Orders   = confirmed orders counted from the ORDER DATABASE (backend),
             not from app analytics events.
- Conversion = orders / sessions.
- Funnel counts = sessions reaching each step (client analytics events),
  except "Order placed", which is taken from the order database.
