RELEASE LOG AND OPS NOTES
Thu 17 Sep (W38)  Backend: new restaurant-ranking model on the home
                  feed, 100% of users, all platforms.
Mon 21 Sep (W39)  Android app 7.4.0 published to 100% on Play Store.
                  Changes: payment screen moved to a new payments SDK;
                  UPI "pay by app" hand-off rebuilt; new checkout copy.
                  Auto-update: ~70% of Android sessions on 7.4.0 by
                  Sun 27 Sep (version split available in analytics).
Mon 21 Sep (W39)  iOS app 7.4.0 (same payment change) submitted; still
                  in App Store review, NOT live. Planned release: W40.
Wed 23-Thu 24 Sep Ops note: heavy rain in Mumbai; city team reported
                  longer delivery times and some rider shortages.
No pricing, delivery-fee or marketing-campaign changes in W38-W39.

YOUR ANSWER (fill in)
1. Decomposition: orders = ____ x ____ ; which factor moved? ______
2. Funnel step where the drop sits: ____________ (W38 __% -> W39 __%)
3. Segment where it is concentrated: platform ____  city ____ (why?)
4. Orders lost per week attributable to it (estimate): ____________
5. Most likely root cause: _________________________________________
   Evidence (3 bullets): ____________________________________________
   What rules out the red herrings: _________________________________
6. What to verify next (top 3, with the data source for each): ______
7. Fix now / fix next: ______________________________________________
8. Guardrails so this cannot recur silently: ________________________

quiz.question: You are the PM at TiffinGo. Weekly orders fell 7.8% WoW (213,970 to 197,228) while sessions were flat (2,000,000 to 2,000,880). What is the most useful first step?
options: Break orders down by city first, since a local event is the most common cause of a sudden week-over-week dip
Compare average order value WoW to see whether customers are ordering smaller baskets than before
Survey customers who ordered in W38 but not in W39 to ask them why they stopped ordering
Decompose orders into sessions x conversion, check which factor moved, and then investigate that half
quiz.explanation: Orders = sessions x conversion. Sessions are flat, so the whole drop is in conversion (10.70% to 9.86%), and that tells you where to dig. Cutting by city first is tempting, but it jumps to a hypothesis before you know which factor moved, and city cuts can mislead because of mix. AOV affects revenue, not order count.

quiz.question: Using Table 2 (all platforms), at which funnel step did step conversion clearly change between W38 and W39?
options: Opened app -> Restaurant page
Restaurant page -> Added to cart
Reached checkout -> Order placed
Added to cart -> Reached checkout
quiz.explanation: Checkout -> order placed fell from 83.6% to 76.9%, while every earlier step moved by 0.1 pp or less. Restaurant -> cart is the tempting answer because a ranking model changed the week before, but that step held at 40.7%.

quiz.question: Mumbai shows the largest order drop of any city (-9.8%, -5,440 orders), and ops reported heavy rain and rider shortages there on 23-24 Sep. What is the best reading of the data?
options: Rain is the main driver: Mumbai has both the largest % drop and the largest absolute drop of any city
Rain explains Mumbai's drop and an Android issue explains the other cities, so both need fixing separately
Rain explains about half of the drop, because Mumbai is roughly half the size of the total order decline
Rain is not the driver: Mumbai sessions and iOS conversion are flat, and its bigger drop comes from its 75% Android share
quiz.explanation: Table 5 shows Mumbai's Android conversion fell by the same ~1.3 pp as every other city's, and Mumbai iOS was flat (11.91% to 11.89%). Mumbai simply has more Android users, so it loses more. Rain would have hit both platforms and the upper funnel, which did not happen.

quiz.question: A teammate suspects the new restaurant-ranking model that went live on Thu 17 Sep (W38). Which evidence most directly argues against it?
options: Early funnel steps are flat, W38 orders stayed normal, and iOS on the same model is unaffected
It is a backend change, and backend changes cannot hurt checkout conversion the way app releases can
It shipped to all platforms, yet the order drop appeared in some cities and not in others
Ranking models usually need several weeks of data before they change user behaviour measurably
quiz.explanation: A ranking problem would hit the home feed -> restaurant -> cart steps, on both platforms, from 17 Sep. Instead those steps are flat, W38 (4 days on the model) was normal, and iOS is fine. Saying backend changes cannot hurt conversion is wrong; they often do. The 'some cities' claim is also false, because every city dropped.

quiz.question: Which root-cause statement is best supported by the case data?
options: New users on Android are less familiar with digital payments, so more of them abandon at checkout
Android 7.4.0's new payment SDK / UPI hand-off is making Android orders fail or be abandoned at checkout
Users across the board are seeing higher prices at checkout and abandoning their carts more often
The new checkout copy confuses users on both platforms, which lowers the checkout -> order rate
quiz.explanation: The drop is at checkout -> order, only on Android, starts in the week Android 7.4.0 changed the payment flow, and is roughly uniform across cities. The checkout-copy option is tempting, but iOS does not have the release live and is flat, and there were no pricing changes. Note that the new checkout copy also shipped in Android 7.4.0, so on this data alone it is not excluded; the payment-method split and SDK/gateway error codes are what separate a payment failure from copy-driven abandonment.

quiz.question: Android checkouts in W39 were 156,908, and Android checkout -> order conversion fell from 82.0% to 71.0%. Roughly how many orders per week does this account for?
options: About 5,400
About 11,000
About 17,300
About 45,500
quiz.explanation: 156,908 x 11 pp is about 17,260 lost orders, which matches the topline drop of 16,742 (iOS was slightly up). 45,500 is the total number of Android checkouts that did not convert in W39, including the ~28,000 that would have failed normally. That figure is not the incremental loss.

quiz.question: Before the review, an engineer suggests the drop might just be a broken 'order placed' analytics event in Android 7.4.0. What is the strongest response based on the case?
options: Unlikely: orders are counted from the order database, not app events, so the 16,742 lost orders are real
Likely: a release that changes the payment screen often breaks the analytics events that fire on it
Unclear: there is no way to separate a tracking bug from a real drop without running a controlled A/B test
Unlikely: iOS numbers are fine, which shows that the analytics pipeline as a whole is working correctly
quiz.explanation: Ruling out instrumentation is the right instinct, and the definitions answer it: orders and the 'Order placed' step come from the backend order database. The iOS option is tempting, but a healthy pipeline on iOS says nothing about an Android-only event bug.

quiz.question: You have high but not yet proven confidence that Android 7.4.0 caused the drop. Which check would most efficiently confirm or refute it?
options: Run a two-week A/B test comparing the old and new payment flows to measure the effect precisely
Interview 10 Android users who abandoned checkout last week to understand their motivations
Split Android checkout -> order conversion by app version (7.4.0 vs 7.3.x) and payment method
Re-pull the city-level data at a daily grain to see whether the Mumbai rain days stand out
quiz.explanation: By the end of the week about 30% of Android sessions were still on 7.3.x, so you can pull this comparison today. If 7.3.x holds near the ~82% W38 baseline while 7.4.0 is far lower, especially on UPI, the cause is confirmed. A two-week A/B test is the tempting 'rigorous' option, but it would delay the fix by two weeks at roughly 17,000 lost orders a week.

quiz.question: The version split confirms it: 7.4.0 users fail mostly on UPI payments. What is the best immediate action?
options: Disable the new payment flow via a remote-config kill switch or a 7.4.1 hotfix, and hold iOS 7.4.0
Re-publish the 7.3.x code to Android as a rollback, and let iOS 7.4.0 go live as planned in W40
Offer Android users a checkout discount to win back lost orders while engineering builds a fix
Keep 7.4.0 live, file a P1 bug for the payments team, and fix UPI in the next sprint's release
quiz.explanation: Stopping the Android leak today (server-side switch or fast hotfix) and holding the iOS release keeps the bug off the healthy platform. The rollback option is tempting because it does fix Android, but letting iOS 7.4.0 ship would spread the same payment bug to the platform that is still converting normally.

quiz.question: Which guardrail would most likely have caught this problem within hours rather than at the weekly review?
options: A weekly orders target with an alert whenever orders fall more than 5% below the previous week
Payment success rate (checkout -> order) by platform and app version, alerted during staged rollouts
A daily sessions dashboard by city, reviewed by each city's operations team every morning
A post-launch review meeting held two weeks after every app release to discuss its impact
quiz.explanation: The failure was in one step, on one platform, in one version, so a guardrail cut at that level fires early, especially if rollouts are staged and gated on it. A weekly orders alert is the tempting choice, but it catches the problem only after a week of losses, and sessions never moved at all.

keyTakeaways: Decompose before you hypothesise: orders = sessions x conversion tells you which half of the business to investigate.
A drop that sits in one funnel step and one segment is usually a change someone shipped, so read the release log next to the data.
Check every suspicious-looking segment for mix: a segment can look worst simply because more of the affected users are in it.
A diagnosis is not finished until it has a size, a confidence level, a fix and a guardrail that would catch the problem next time.

lessons.label: Module 13
lessons.title: Case Study: Checkout Conversion Is Falling
lessons.description: Diagnose a 2.5-point drop in cart-to-order conversion at a fictional Indian e-commerce company by working through a step-by-step funnel, device, city-tier and payment-method data, then sizing the cause and planning the next three actions.
learningObjectives: Use step-to-step conversion rates for two periods to find the one checkout step whose rate actually changed, and tell a falling rate apart from flat order counts that mask it
Cut a funnel by device, city tier and payment method to find the segment that drives a decline, and reject a segment that converts poorly in both periods but did not change
Size how much of a conversion gap one segment explains with a counterfactual (attempts x change in success rate x downstream rate), and account for the rest (small rate changes and traffic-mix shift)
Write a one-sentence root-cause hypothesis and three next actions, each with an owner, a timeline and a result that would prove the hypothesis wrong

readingArticles.title: 50 Cart Abandonment Rate Statistics 2026
keyPoints: Baymard compiles many studies to give an average documented online cart abandonment rate of about 70%, so checkout leakage is normal. Your job is to find what changed.
Separates 'just browsing' abandonment from preventable causes such as extra costs, slow delivery, trust or security concerns, forced account creation and a complicated checkout.
Compares checkout form length against best practice, a reminder that some funnel loss is structural (always there) and some is a regression (new).
Useful for building a hypothesis list for each checkout step before you open the data.

readingArticles.title: Optimising authorisation rates: How to reduce network declines
keyPoints: Explains how a payment request travels through the gateway, the network and the issuing bank, and where it can be declined.
Explains why you should group failures by decline reason (insufficient funds, outdated card details, suspected fraud) because each needs a different fix.
Covers levers that raise success rates, such as better payment flows, smart retries, digital wallets and network tokens.
Includes a glossary (authorisation rate, decline code, dunning) that helps a PM talk to payments engineers and gateway partners.

videos.title: Flipkart Product Manager Mock Interview: Root Cause Analysis (Razorpay PM)
videos.creator: Aced (formerly Exponent)
keyPoints: Shows a full worked root-cause analysis (RCA) of a metric drop, out loud, in an Indian e-commerce setting.
Asks clarifying questions first (metric definition, time window, how big and how sudden the drop is) before forming hypotheses.
Splits the problem into internal causes (releases, bugs) and external causes (seasonality, competitors, partners), then narrows it with segmentation.
Ends with a clear hypothesis and next steps, the same structure this case asks you to produce.

practicalTools.name: Checkout Conversion Diagnosis Worksheet
practicalTools.description: A complete, fictional data pack for KartNest, an Indian e-commerce marketplace. It covers a five-step checkout funnel for two 14-day periods, the same funnel by device and by city tier, payment attempts and success rates by device and method, context notes from the team, and a fill-in worksheet. All numbers are illustrative and internally consistent. Recheck any derived figure with a calculator. Funnel and segmentation basics are covered on Day 22 (AARRR drop-offs) and Day 13 (metrics); this case is about applying them under pressure.
practicalTools.exercise:
Work through the template in order and write each answer down before reading the next table.
1. Headline check (Table 1): work out cart-to-order conversion for A and B, the change in points, and the % change in orders and in carts. Explain in one line why 'orders are roughly flat' is misleading.
2. Locate the step (Table 1): compare A% and B% for each step. Which step's rate moved? Which steps did not move, and what does that rule out (for example address or serviceability problems, or confirmation-page bugs)?
3. Device cut (Table 2): which device's funnel changed, at which step, and by how many points? Are the other two devices stable?
4. City-tier cut (Table 3): which tier converts worst? Did its conversion change much between A and B? Which step makes it low in both periods? Decide whether it is the cause or a distraction, and propose why Tiers 1 and 2 fell more than Tier 3 and name the cut (tier x device x method) that would confirm it.
5. Payment cut (Table 4): find the device x method with the largest success-rate (SR) change. Check whether the same method on other devices also fell. What does that tell you about whether the problem is the payment network or KartNest's own integration?
6. Size it: (a) orders expected in B at A's conversion = carts B x conversion A; (b) gap = expected - actual orders B; (c) orders recovered if your segment had kept A's SR = attempts B x (SR A - SR B) x PaySucc->Confirm rate; (d) share of the gap explained.
7. Explain the rest: estimate the effect of any other SR change (hint: desktop cards) and of the traffic-mix shift toward Tier 2 and 3 (hint: carts B per tier x conversion A per tier, compared with carts B x overall conversion A).
8. Use the context notes to write a one-sentence root-cause hypothesis that names the step, the segment and the likely trigger.
9. Write the next 3 actions. For each, give an owner, a timeline, and a result that would prove your hypothesis wrong. Also estimate roughly how many orders per day are at stake.
practicalTools.deliverable: A one-page diagnosis memo with: (1) Headline: conversion fell from 71.2% to 68.7% (-2.5 pts, about -3.5% relative) while carts rose 2.9%, so orders fell only 0.7% (142,341 to 141,296). The rate is the real signal. (2) Step: only payment-method-selected -> payment-success moved (92.3% to 89.1%). Address (85.2% vs 85.1%), method selection (91.5%) and confirmation (99.0%) are flat. (3) Segment: mobile web, whose payment step fell from 90.8% to 78.8% and whose conversion fell from 64.2% to 55.6%. Desktop (88.7% to 88.3%) and app (93.9%) are essentially stable. (4) Distractor dismissed: Tier 3 converts worst (68.9% and 67.8%) because its address step is about 80% vs about 86.5% elsewhere (serviceable pincodes), and that is unchanged. Tier 3 fell least (-1.0 pt vs about -2.8 and -3.0 pts in Tiers 1 and 2) likely because a smaller share of its payments are mobile-web UPI (confirm with a tier x device x method cut). (5) Cause located: mobile-web UPI SR fell from 91.0% to 68.0% on 21,969 attempts, while UPI on app (94.0%) and desktop (90.0%) held. That points to KartNest's mobile-web integration, not the UPI network. (6) Sizing: expected orders = 205,800 x 71.17% = about 146,469; gap = about 5,173 orders; recovered = 21,969 x 23 pts x 99% = about 5,000 orders, so about 97% of the gap. That is about 2.4 of the 2.5 points, or about 357 orders per day. (7) Remainder: the desktop card SR dip (86% to 85%) is about 90 orders, and the tier-mix shift from the Tier 2/3 campaign is about 100 orders (about 2% each). Note them and monitor, but don't chase them first. (The mix effect depends on the cut: by device it is about +60 orders because app grew fastest, and the pieces overlap rather than sum exactly.) (8) Hypothesis: the 16 Sep move to payment-gateway SDK v4 on mobile web broke or degraded the UPI flow (for example the intent or collect hand-off to UPI apps), causing failed payments, consistent with the rise in payment-issue tickets. (9) Actions, for example: a) Today, with Payments engineering: pull daily mobile-web UPI SR and error codes, split by SDK version, browser/OS and UPI app, to confirm that the break starts on 16 Sep. If SR fell before 16 Sep, or (if the rollout was staged) also fell on v3 traffic, or the fall is spread across all UPI apps and browsers with no v4-specific error codes, the hypothesis is wrong. b) Within 24-48 h, with engineering and the gateway partner: roll back to v3 or put the UPI flow behind a feature flag. Meanwhile, as a mitigation, show working alternatives (app deep link, other methods) after a UPI failure. Success = mobile-web UPI SR back near 91% and the payment step near 91%. c) This week, with the PM and Customer Support: reconcile 'money debited, order not placed' cases and refunds, add an automated alert on SR by device x method (for example a drop of a few points within a day), and add payment-SR checks to the release checklist for SDK upgrades. Strong answers also state what they did NOT prioritise (Tier 3 serviceability, desktop cards) and why.

KartNest is an Indian e-commerce marketplace. You are the PM for Checkout.

points. Orders are roughly flat, so is this real?" You have two 14-day

Definitions
  Cart      unique carts that started checkout
  Address   carts that saved a delivery address
  PayMeth   carts that selected a payment method and attempted payment
  PaySucc   carts with a successful payment (for COD: order accepted)
  Confirm   carts that reached the order-confirmation screen
  Crt       Table 4 carts, by the LAST method attempted. A cart that failed
            on UPI and then paid by COD counts under COD, so UPI SR here

  Each cart is counted once per step; Table 4 uses the last method the
