quiz.question: At KartNest, carts rose from 200,000 to 205,800 and orders went from 142,341 to 141,296. A director says, 'Orders are only down 0.7%, so this is noise.' What is the best reply?
options: Agree: a 0.7% dip in orders over two weeks is within normal variation, so keep monitoring
Disagree: carts grew 2.9% while orders fell, so cart-to-order conversion dropped about 2.5 points
Disagree: the drop is only real if Period B's average order value also fell
Agree: the festive campaign brought lower-intent traffic, so a lower conversion rate is expected
quiz.explanation: More traffic can hide a broken funnel. Conversion fell from 71.2% to 68.7%, so the right comparison is rates, not order counts. The campaign explanation is tempting, but traffic mix accounts for only about 100 orders, and the whole drop sits in one payment step, not across the funnel.

quiz.question: In Table 1, which step should you investigate first?
options: Cart -> address, which is the largest absolute drop-off in both periods
Address -> payment method, because it comes before the payment step
Payment success -> confirmation, because confirmation is where orders are counted
Payment method selected -> payment success, which fell from 92.3% to 89.1%
quiz.explanation: You are diagnosing a change, so look for the step whose rate moved. Only the payment-success step did; the others are flat to within 0.1 points. Cart -> address has the biggest leak overall, but it is the same in both periods, so it cannot explain the decline.

quiz.question: Using Table 2, which device-level finding best explains the drop at the payment step?
options: Desktop: it had the lowest payment-step rate in Period A (88.7%) and slipped again to 88.3% in B
App: its carts grew most (+4,400), so its share of total payment failures must have grown
Mobile web: its payment step fell from 90.8% to 78.8%, and its conversion fell from 64.2% to 55.6%
All three devices fell by a similar amount, which points to a company-wide payments issue
quiz.explanation: Mobile web's payment step fell 12 points while app held at 93.9% and desktop moved only 0.4 points. Desktop had the lowest payment rate in Period A, but it barely changed. That is a level, not a change, so it cannot explain the decline.

quiz.question: Tier 3 has the lowest conversion in both periods (68.9% then 67.8%). How should you treat it in this investigation?
options: Make it the priority: as the lowest-converting tier, it offers the largest recovery opportunity
Make it the priority: the festive campaign hit Tier 2 and 3 on 15 Sep, the day Period B began
Exclude Tier 3 from the analysis, because serviceability problems distort the overall funnel
Note it as a separate opportunity: its gap comes from a steady ~80% address step, and it fell least
quiz.explanation: Tier 3 is low because of an unchanged serviceability constraint at the address step (80% in both periods), and it fell only about 1 point vs about 3 in Tiers 1 and 2. The campaign timing is tempting, but Tier 1 had no campaign and fell as much as Tier 2, so the campaign cannot be the cause.

quiz.question: How many orders is Period B short of what Period A's conversion rate (71.2%) would predict?
options: About 1,045: Period A orders minus Period B orders (142,341 - 141,296)
About 4,130: the 5,800 extra carts in Period B converted at A's 71.2%
About 4,295: the fall in successful mobile-web payments (37,457 - 33,162)
About 5,173: B's 205,800 carts at A's 71.2% (about 146,469) minus 141,296
quiz.explanation: The fair counterfactual applies A's conversion to all of B's traffic: 146,469 - 141,296 = about 5,173 orders. The raw 1,045 difference ignores the 2.9% traffic growth, and 4,130 counts only the orders the extra carts should have added, not the full expected total.

quiz.question: Mobile-web UPI success rate fell from 91.0% to 68.0% on 21,969 Period B attempts, and 99% of successful payments reach confirmation. About what share of the roughly 5,173-order gap does this explain?
options: About 28%: scale the ~5,000 recovered orders by mobile web's 29% share of carts
About 50%: scale the ~5,000 recovered orders by UPI's ~52% share of mobile-web attempts
About 97%: 21,969 x 23 points x 99% = about 5,000 recovered orders
About 66%: 21,969 x 23 points x 68% (B's success rate) = about 3,440 orders
quiz.explanation: The counterfactual uses absolute volume: about 5,053 extra successful payments x 0.99 = about 5,000 orders, which is about 97% of the gap. Scaling by mobile web's or UPI's share double-counts, because the 21,969 attempts already reflect those shares. The downstream factor is the 99% payment-to-confirmation rate, not B's success rate.

quiz.question: Desktop card success rate slipped from 86.0% to 85.0% on about 9,250 attempts. A teammate wants to open a second investigation stream on it now. What do you advise?
options: Log and monitor it: about 9,250 x 1 point is ~90 orders (~2% of the gap); fix mobile-web UPI first
Open the stream now: card orders carry higher order values, so these losses may outweigh UPI's in revenue
Open the stream now: it is the only other segment whose rate fell, so it must share the same root cause
Fold it into the mobile-web UPI fix, because one SDK rollback will fix both payment issues
quiz.explanation: Sizing drives priority: about 90 orders vs about 5,000 from mobile-web UPI, and even a higher order value cannot close a 50x gap. Folding it into the SDK fix is tempting, but desktop never moved to SDK v4, so a rollback would not touch it. Watch it on a dashboard instead.

quiz.question: The context notes show that mobile web moved to payment-gateway SDK v4 on 16 Sep. Mobile-web UPI is losing about 350 orders a day. What is the best first action?
options: Run a two-week A/B test of SDK v3 vs v4 on mobile web to establish causality before acting
Pull daily mobile-web UPI success rate and error codes by SDK version, and line up a rollback with engineering
Survey mobile-web shoppers who failed at payment to understand why they dropped off
Send push notifications nudging mobile-web users to switch to the app for payment
quiz.explanation: A fast, cheap check (a break on 16 Sep, isolated to v4 traffic and UPI) can confirm the hypothesis within hours, and a ready rollback limits ongoing losses. A two-week 50/50 A/B test is rigorous, but it would knowingly lose about 2,500 more orders on a likely regression that the daily data can already confirm.

quiz.question: A stakeholder claims, 'The UPI network was unreliable in late September; it's not our problem.' Which data point most directly contradicts this?
options: App UPI held at 94.0% and desktop UPI at 90.0%; only mobile-web UPI fell (91.0% to 68.0%)
The overall UPI success rate fell from 92.8% to 86.6% across all devices
COD success stayed at 98.0% on every device in both periods
Payment-issue support tickets rose from 1,120 to 1,890 between the periods
quiz.explanation: A network-wide UPI problem would hit every device. A failure confined to one surface points to KartNest's own mobile-web integration. The overall UPI decline is consistent with both explanations, so it cannot tell them apart.

quiz.question: Tier 2 and 3 carts grew faster in Period B because of the campaign. Holding each tier's Period A conversion constant, how should you describe the effect of this traffic-mix shift?
options: It is the main driver: Tier 3 carts grew 11.5%, which explains most of the 2.5-point drop
It is small, about 100 orders (about 2% of the gap); the rate drop inside segments dominates
It cannot be estimated without user-level data, so leave it out of the memo
It pushes conversion up, because Tier 2 converts better than Tier 1
quiz.explanation: Sum of B carts x A conversion for each tier = about 146,367, vs 146,469 at the blended rate, so mix costs about 100 orders. Tier 3's 11.5% growth sounds large, but its conversion is only about 3 points below the others, so the mix effect stays small.

keyTakeaways: Compare rates, not counts: when traffic grows, a flat order count can hide a broken funnel.
Usually find the step first, then the segment: break the change down by step before you slice by device, city or method.
Lowest is not the same as worst-hit. Day 22's "fix the biggest drop-off" is for optimising a stable funnel; when diagnosing a decline, ask what changed between periods.
A diagnosis isn't finished until it's sized. Check what share of the gap your cause explains before you act on it.

lessons.label: Module 14
lessons.title: Case Study: Prioritize Six Feature Requests
lessons.description: Score six competing feature requests for a fictional B2B invoicing SaaS with RICE, then adjust the ranking for strategy, dependencies and uncertainty, and defend the call to a stakeholder whose request did not make the cut.
learningObjectives: Calculate RICE scores for six feature requests correctly, then rank them and check the total effort against a fixed quarterly capacity (RICE basics are on Day 11)
Find where a pure RICE ranking leaves out strategic value, such as revenue concentrated in a key segment or renewal and deal risk, and justify any change you make to the ranking
Turn a low-confidence, high-impact idea into a time-boxed discovery step with a clear go/no-go threshold, and show how a change in confidence would move its score
Sequence work around external dependencies, then write a trade-off rationale and a stakeholder message that explains a deprioritization using goals and data, not the formula alone

readingArticles.title: 5 Tips for Saying No to Stakeholders
keyPoints: Saying no is a core part of product work, so do not apologize for doing it
Understand the stakeholder's underlying interest before you give the decision
Move the conversation away from the feature and toward the user problem and the product goals
Look for common ground without splitting the difference and weakening the plan

readingArticles.title: A product manager's guide to saying no
keyPoints: A five-step sequence: listen actively, find the value, summarize, explain the cost, then say no
Make the cost explicit: effort, opportunity cost, poor fit with strategy, technical debt
Point to data and agreed strategy rather than personal opinion, and offer workarounds where you can
A careful, empathetic no stops rejected ideas from coming back again and again

videos.title: Top 4 Prioritization techniques in Product Management explained simply
videos.creator: David Pereira
keyPoints: A walk-through of RICE, ICE, the value matrix and MoSCoW, with simplicity as the guiding idea
Shows how each technique frames the value-versus-effort trade-off in a different way
Useful for comparing RICE with lighter alternatives before you do the case
Stresses that a technique supports the conversation and does not replace judgment

practicalTools.name: Ledgerly Quarterly Prioritization Case
practicalTools.description: A fictional B2B invoicing SaaS has 8 person-months of product team capacity (design, engineering and QA) next quarter and six competing requests. Each request comes with Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort estimates, plus notes on strategic fit, revenue at stake, dependencies and which stakeholder is pushing for it. You score them with RICE, decide where judgment should overrule the score, and defend the plan.
practicalTools.exercise:
Step 1 - Score: for each of A-F, compute R x I x C, then divide by Effort to get the RICE score. Write both numbers in the worksheet and rank A-F by RICE.
Step 2 - Pure-RICE plan: go down the RICE ranking and add items until the next one no longer fits in 8 person-months, skipping any item that does not fit. Which items ship, and how much capacity is left unused?
Step 3 - Stress-test the inputs: for each item, which input are you least sure of? Compare R x I x C (value before effort) with the final RICE score. Which items rank high mainly because of a tiny effort or a large but low-impact reach? Reach counts every user equally. How does that treat D, whose users sit in (or would join) mid-size accounts that bring in ~41% of revenue? Estimate the ARR that D protects or unlocks and compare it with the ARR exposure of C.
Step 4 - Adjust for strategy: re-read the company goal and the quarter OKR. Name at least one item where you would overrule the RICE ranking, and explain why in terms of the goal, revenue or deal risk.
Step 5 - Handle uncertainty: E has high impact but 30% confidence. Design a time-boxed discovery step (what you will test, on what data, for how long, and the accuracy or usage threshold that means 'build'). Recompute E's RICE assuming confidence rises to 80%, and say where it would then rank.
Step 6 - Handle dependencies: decide how the outside wait on A (WhatsApp approval) and the beta API on F should change sequencing or commitment. What do you start in week 1?
Step 7 - Final plan: give each item a decision (Build now / Time-boxed discovery / Next quarter / No). Keep total committed effort within 8 person-months and state the buffer you keep.
Step 8 - Rationale: write a 5-8 sentence trade-off rationale for leadership.
Step 9 - Stakeholder message: pick the stakeholder whose item you deprioritized or scaled down (the CEO for E, the Head of Design for C, or the Customer Success lead for F). Write the message using the four-part prompt in the worksheet.
practicalTools.deliverable: A strong answer contains: (1) a RICE table with every calculation shown and the arithmetic correct, plus a pure-RICE ranking; (2) the capacity a pure-RICE fill uses and the capacity it leaves unused; (3) at least one explicit override of the RICE order, justified by the stated goal, segment revenue or renewal and deal risk (with an estimate of the ARR at stake), not by who shouted loudest, and an acknowledgment that reach in users undercounts account-level value; (4) a concrete discovery plan for the low-confidence item, with a time-box, the data it will be tested on, a success threshold and a recomputed score; (5) dependency handling that starts outside lead-time work early and does not commit firmly to work blocked by a beta API; (6) a final plan of no more than 8 person-months with a buffer and a clear decision on each of the six items; (7) a rationale that names what you are giving up and why; and (8) a stakeholder message that restates their goal, explains the decision with goals and data, offers a specific next step with a date, and says what evidence would change the decision. It must not hide behind 'the formula says so'. Several final plans can be defended; the quality of the reasoning is what is graded.
practicalTools.template:
CASE: "Ledgerly" - prioritize six feature requests for next quarter
(Fictional company. All names, people and numbers are illustrative.)

1. CONTEXT
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Ledgerly is a B2B SaaS invoicing and collections app for Indian
small and mid-size businesses (SMBs).

  Paying accounts ............................ 4,000
  Monthly active users (all accounts) ........ ~15,000
  Mid-size accounts (20-200 employees) ....... 360 (9% of accounts)
  Mid-size share of annual recurring revenue . ~41%

  Company goal this year : "Win and keep mid-size businesses."
  Quarter OKR            : Reduce mid-size account churn.
  North Star metric      : Invoices paid on time.
  Capacity next quarter  : 8 person-months of product team time
                           (design + engineering + QA, after bug
                           fixes and maintenance).

2. THE SIX REQUESTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Reach  = users who will touch the feature in one quarter
Impact = 3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal
Conf.  = confidence in the Reach and Impact estimates
Effort = person-months (design + engineering + QA)

ID  Feature                       Reach   Impact  Conf.  Effort
                                 (users)           (%)    (p-m)
--  ---------------------------  -------  ------  -----  ------
A   WhatsApp payment reminders     9,000     2      80     2
B   Bulk CSV invoice import        3,500     1      90     1
C   Dark mode                     12,000   0.25     90     0.5
D   SSO (SAML) login                 400     3      90     3
E   AI bank reconciliation         6,000     3      30     6
F   Partial payments on invoices   2,500     1      80     2

3. NOTES ON EACH REQUEST
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A  WhatsApp payment reminders
   - Directly moves the North Star (invoices paid on time).
   - DEPENDENCY: needs WhatsApp Business verification and approval
     of message templates. Lead time is outside the team's control;
     the team guesses 3-5 weeks. The effort figure excludes the wait.

B  Bulk CSV invoice import
   - Top request from accountants who manage many client businesses.
   - Well understood, low technical risk.

C  Dark mode
   - Most-upvoted idea on the public feature board and in app-store
     reviews. The Head of Design is enthusiastic.
   - No link to this year's goal or the North Star.

D  SSO (SAML) login
   - Reach = ~400 users: ~250 at 10 existing mid-size accounts plus
     ~150 expected at the 3 late-stage deals if they close this
     quarter. All require SSO to pass their IT security review.
   - STAKEHOLDER PUSHING HARD: Head of Sales. 3 late-stage mid-size
     deals list SSO as a blocker; 2 existing mid-size customers
     raised it ahead of their renewals.
   - Money at stake: the 3 deals total ~Rs 54 lakh ARR; the 2
     renewals total ~Rs 30 lakh ARR (avg mid-size account ~Rs 9
     lakh ARR vs ~Rs 1.3 lakh for a small account).

E  AI bank reconciliation
   - Would auto-match bank statement lines to invoices, removing
     hours of manual work per week for finance users.
   - STAKEHOLDER PUSHING HARD: the CEO, after a competitor announced
     an "AI accountant" feature.
   - No prototype yet. Statement formats vary by bank and matching
     accuracy is unknown, hence 30% confidence. Largest effort.
   - A 3-week prototype on real bank statements would take ~1
     person-month.

F  Partial payments on invoices
   - Customer Success lead's top ask: many customers' clients pay
     in instalments, and today this is handled in spreadsheets.
   - DEPENDENCY: the payment gateway's split-payment API is in beta;
     the partner "expects" general availability in month 2.

4. YOUR WORKSHEET (fill in - nothing is precomputed)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
RICE score = (Reach x Impact x Confidence) / Effort

ID  R x I x C   / Effort  = RICE   RICE rank  Final rank  Decision*
--  ---------   --------   ------  ---------  ----------  ---------
A   ________    ________   ______  _________  __________  _________
B   ________    ________   ______  _________  __________  _________
C   ________    ________   ______  _________  __________  _________
D   ________    ________   ______  _________  __________  _________
E   ________    ________   ______  _________  __________  _________
F   ________    ________   ______  _________  __________  _________

* Decision = Build now / Time-boxed discovery / Next quarter / No

Capacity check: total effort committed = ____ of 8 person-months
Buffer kept for surprises = ____ person-months

Trade-off rationale (5-8 sentences):
____________________________________________________________________

Message to the stakeholder whose item was deprioritized:
  To: ______________   Item: ____
  1. What I heard (their goal, in their words): ____________________
  2. What we decided and why (goal + data): ________________________
  3. What we will do instead / next step and date: _________________
  4. What would change the decision: _______________________________

quiz.question: In the Ledgerly case, what is the RICE score for A (WhatsApp payment reminders: Reach 9,000, Impact 2, Confidence 80%, Effort 2)?
quiz.explanation: 9,000 x 2 x 0.8 = 14,400, and 14,400 / 2 person-months = 7,200. 14,400 is the tempting slip: it is the value before you divide by effort.

quiz.question: Using the Ledgerly data, which request ranks LAST on pure RICE score?
options: E - AI bank reconciliation
D - SSO (SAML) login
F - Partial payments on invoices
B - Bulk CSV invoice import
quiz.explanation: D scores 400 x 3 x 0.9 / 3 = 360, below E (900), F (1,000) and B (3,150). Many people guess E because of its 30% confidence, but its large reach and impact still put it above D.

quiz.question: You fill Ledgerly's 8 person-months strictly in RICE order and skip any item that no longer fits. Which set ships?
options: A, C, B, F, D - 8.5 person-months
A, C, B, D - 6.5 person-months
A, C, B, F - 5.5 person-months
A, C, E - 8.5 person-months
quiz.explanation: The RICE order is A (7,200), C (5,400), B (3,150), F (1,000), E (900), D (360). After A, C, B and F (5.5 person-months), E needs 6 and D needs 3, and neither fits. A pure-RICE plan therefore leaves 2.5 person-months unused and skips the item tied to the company goal. D cannot be added because 8.5 is over capacity.

quiz.question: Ignoring effort, compare the expected value (Reach x Impact x Confidence) of C (dark mode) and E (AI reconciliation). What do you find?
options: They are equal at 2,700 each
quiz.explanation: E: 6,000 x 3 x 0.3 = 5,400. C: 12,000 x 0.25 x 0.9 = 2,700. C's high RICE score (5,400) comes from dividing by a tiny 0.5 person-month effort, not from large value. Swapping the two figures is the common mistake.

quiz.question: D (SSO) scores only 360 on RICE, yet you are considering building it this quarter. Which argument best justifies overruling the score?
options: The Head of Sales is the most senior voice pushing for it, and requests from sales usually carry revenue
Its confidence should be raised to 100%, because the Head of Sales is certain the deals depend on it
Reach counts users equally, but D's users sit in mid-size renewals and deals, the segment the goal targets
Its effort is probably padded, and cutting it to 1.5 person-months would double the score to 720
quiz.explanation: RICE reach weights every user the same. D's value sits in mid-size accounts (~41% of ARR), in ~Rs 30 lakh of renewals and ~Rs 54 lakh of late-stage deals, and that ties directly to the company goal. Deferring to the loudest senior voice, or bending the confidence or effort inputs until you get the answer you want, hides the real reason for the override instead of stating it openly.

quiz.question: E (AI bank reconciliation) has Impact 3 but 30% confidence, needs 6 of the 8 person-months, and the CEO wants it. What is the best way to handle it this quarter?
options: Commit the full 6 person-month build, because impact is the highest on the list and the CEO is sponsoring it
Drop it entirely, because its RICE score of 900 ranks fifth out of six requests
Run a stakeholder workshop to agree on a higher confidence figure so that it ranks near the top
Run a time-boxed prototype on real bank statements with an accuracy bar before deciding on the build
quiz.explanation: Low confidence with high impact calls for buying information cheaply: a small, time-boxed test against a clear threshold, so you can decide whether the 6 person-month build is worth it. Committing the full build risks most of the quarter on an unknown, and dropping it ignores a potentially large upside.

quiz.question: After discovery, E's confidence rises from 30% to 80%, while reach, impact and effort stay the same. What is its new RICE score, and where does it rank?
options: 3,600 - 3rd, above B
2,400 - 3rd, above B
1,200 - 4th, above F
2,400 - 4th, below B
quiz.explanation: 6,000 x 3 x 0.8 / 6 = 2,400. That puts E between B (3,150) and F (1,000), so it ranks 4th. The tempting error is to assume a big jump in confidence lifts E above B, but B's 1 person-month effort keeps it ahead.

quiz.question: A (WhatsApp reminders) needs WhatsApp Business verification and template approval, with a 3-5 week lead time the team does not control. How should you sequence it?
options: Submit verification and templates in week 1, build in parallel, and launch once approval lands
Build the feature first, then submit for approval once QA is complete
Move A to next quarter so that it no longer depends on an external approval
Swap A for dark mode this quarter, because C has no external dependencies
quiz.explanation: Start the outside wait as early as possible so that it overlaps with the build. Then the dependency delays launch as little as possible, and A, the top RICE item and the one that moves the North Star, still ships this quarter. Submitting after QA adds the full 3-5 weeks onto the end of the work.

quiz.question: Your plan commits 7 of the 8 person-months. The Customer Success lead asks you to also commit F (partial payments, 2 person-months) for month 3, 'in case the gateway API lands'. What is the best response?
options: Commit F for month 3 and absorb the 1 person-month overrun, since the partner expects general availability in month 2
Put F first in line for next quarter, triggered by the API reaching general availability, with no firm date now
Start building F against the beta API now, so that it is ready the day general availability arrives
Swap F in for D this quarter, because F's RICE score of 1,000 is almost three times D's 360
quiz.explanation: Adding F would take the plan to 9 of 8 person-months, and F depends on a beta API whose date is only 'expected'. Queuing it first for next quarter, with an explicit trigger, is honest and keeps momentum. Building against the beta now spends capacity the plan does not have and risks rework if the API contract changes. Swapping F for D gives up the goal-linked mid-size item for one whose timing the team does not control.

quiz.question: You have scaled E (the CEO's request) down to a 3-week discovery spike. Which message to the CEO is strongest?
options: I hear the worry about the competitor's AI launch. We're testing matching on real statements for 3 weeks and will bring a build decision.
RICE ranks E fifth of six at 900, so the framework rules it out this quarter. We can revisit it next quarter.
We'll add AI reconciliation to the roadmap for later this year, so it stays visible and nobody feels blocked.
Let's build a lighter version of the full feature in about 3 person-months, so we have something to announce.
quiz.explanation: The strong message acknowledges the CEO's underlying goal, explains a concrete next step tied to evidence, and promises a dated decision. Pointing to the formula reads as hiding behind the score instead of engaging with the competitive concern.

keyTakeaways: A RICE score is where the debate starts, not the decision. Do the arithmetic first, then explain every place where you overrule it.
Look at what is driving each score. A tiny effort or a large but low-value reach can push an item up a ranking it does not deserve.
Low confidence and high impact means: buy information cheaply before you commit the big build.
A useful structure for saying no: show you understood their goal, tie the decision to agreed goals and data, offer a next step, and say what would change your mind.

lessons.label: Module 15
lessons.title: Case Study: Launch a New Product
lessons.description: Work through a fictional fintech launch brief and turn research, competitor and constraint data into a scoped MVP, a metrics tree, a staged launch plan and a test of the riskiest assumption.
learningObjectives: Use research findings, engineering estimates and a capacity budget to sort candidate features into an MVP in/out list, with a one-line reason for each
Define a North Star metric for a new product, with 3-4 input metrics and 2-3 guardrails, and explain how each one connects to user value or user harm
Check a leadership target against funnel maths (exposure x step conversions) and propose a target you can defend, along with the levers that must move to reach it
Pick the riskiest assumption by weighing impact if wrong against the strength of the evidence, then design a time-boxed experiment with a pass/fail bar set in advance

readingArticles.title: The Four Big Risks
keyPoints: Cagan names four product risks to tackle before building: value, usability, feasibility and business viability
Business viability covers legal and compliance, go-to-market, cost to acquire and monetisation, so the Stash regulatory constraint belongs here
The PM is accountable for value and viability, the designer for usability and the tech lead for feasibility
Strong teams take on these risks early, during discovery, not after launch

readingArticles.title: What is a Minimum Viable Product (MVP)? How to Get Started
keyPoints: Defines an MVP as the most basic version that satisfies early adopters and tests the idea in the market
Links the MVP to Eric Ries and Lean Startup, who popularised it (the term was coined by Frank Robinson): the most validated learning for the least effort
Walks through choosing core features, testing with users and iterating on what you learn
Uses examples such as Amazon starting as a single-category online bookstore

videos.title: Michael Seibel - How to Plan an MVP
videos.creator: Y Combinator
keyPoints: Treat the MVP as the first step in learning from real users, not a smaller copy of the final product
Time-box the build and cut features hard so you launch quickly
After launch, talk to users and let their behaviour decide what you build next
Early versions are meant to feel incomplete, so don't let that delay the launch

practicalTools.name: Stash Launch Case: MVP, Metrics, Launch and Riskiest-Assumption Test
practicalTools.description: You are the PM at Zentra Pay, a fictional UPI payments app, launching an auto-savings product called Stash. The brief has the research, a fake-door test, a benchmark funnel from an older feature, engineering estimates, constraints, competitors and a target from leadership. Your job is to turn this data into launch decisions you can defend.
practicalTools.exercise:
Work through the steps in order and show your maths.
1. Problem and users: In 3-4 sentences, describe who Stash is for and what job it does for them. Use at least two findings from section 3, and say which finding should most shape the design.
2. MVP scope: Use the estimates and the ~27 usable engineer-weeks to list MVP IN and MVP OUT. Give each feature a reason that refers to the data (survey, interviews, round-up maths, platform constraint). Say how much buffer you keep and why. Name any feature that is in for trust rather than delight. If you need a refresher, see Day 11 for MoSCoW.
3. Success metrics: Define one North Star (see Day 13), 3-4 input metrics that mirror the funnel stages and 2-3 guardrails that protect users and the core payments business. For each metric, give its definition and time window.
4. Target check: Use the benchmark funnel (section 3D) and the planning assumption (section 7) to estimate active savers at the end of month 6. Compare your estimate with the 100,000 ask. Then write a short note to leadership: agree, reset or reframe, and list the 2-3 levers that would have to move.
5. Positioning: Use the competitor table to write one positioning line for Stash. Make sure it plays to Zentra's advantage and stays inside the regulatory constraint (no promised returns). See Day 12 for competitive analysis.
6. Launch strategy: Choose the first segment and explain why. Lay out stages (for example dogfood, closed beta, % rollouts, full launch) with a go/no-go gate between each. Say how you would spend, or hold back, the Rs 40 lakh budget. See Module 8 for launch mechanics.
7. Riskiest assumption: List 4-5 assumptions across value, usability, feasibility and viability. Rate each on impact if wrong and on strength of evidence, then pick the riskiest. See Module 2 for assumption mapping.
8. Experiment: For that assumption, write a hypothesis, method, sample and segment, primary metric, pass/fail threshold set in advance, timebox and the decision each result would trigger. Explain how your test fits between the closed-beta start (week 12) and the week-20 go/no-go - about 8 weeks, or two monthly pay cycles. See Module 6 for test design.
practicalTools.deliverable:
A strong answer is a 1-2 page launch memo that:
- Frames the problem around the 'save what is left' behaviour and the trust and lock-in worries, with the survey and interview data quoted accurately.
- Has a scope that adds up: something like KYC 3 + payday auto-save 4 + dashboard 3 + withdrawal 3 + analytics 1 = 14 engineer-weeks, plus small habit features, with a visible buffer below 27. Round-ups and save-with-friends are deferred, with stated reasons (about Rs 81/month vs Rs 1,000 intent; 9 engineer-weeks; batched-debit constraint) and the signal that would bring them back. Instant withdrawal is kept as a trust feature.
- Has a North Star built on repeated saving behaviour, not sign-ups or AUM. Its inputs match the funnel (KYC completion, mandate set-up, first successful save, cycle-2 continuation), and its guardrails cover user harm (failed payments after a debit, complaints, mandate cancellations) and the core app.
- Does the funnel maths and states its proxies: 3,600,000 x 4.7% (banner click as a proxy for KYC start) x 39% x 72% x 35% = about 16,600 active savers, roughly 6x short of 100,000 (about 1.02M KYC starts, ~17% of MAU, would be needed). Using the 1.88% waitlist rate instead gives about 6,650. Either way the ask is out of reach. A strong memo notes that auto-save may retain better than manual gold deposits and that the 120,000 KYC'd users skip the 39% step, then proposes a reset target or reframe and names its levers.
- Has a positioning line that leans on 'already where you pay' and on quick access (instant withdrawal up to a limit, stated honestly), with no return promises.
- Has a staged launch that starts with an already-KYC'd segment, with explicit gates and most of the budget held until the habit metrics pass.
- Picks a riskiest assumption backed by an impact x evidence argument, and an experiment with real behaviour (not stated intent), a pass bar set in advance, a sample size and a decision rule that fits the timeline.
- Bonus: a pre-build test (e.g. a concierge payday-save nudge to KYC'd gold users) that de-risks the habit before week 12.
practicalTools.template:
CASE BRIEF: ZENTRA PAY LAUNCHES "STASH" (AUTO-SAVINGS)
All companies, people and numbers below are FICTIONAL and ILLUSTRATIVE.
Regulatory details are simplified for teaching; real rules need legal review.

1. COMPANY SNAPSHOT
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Zentra Pay       UPI payments + bill-pay app (India), 4 years old
Monthly actives  6,000,000 MAU
Core users       salaried, age 22-32, median age 26
Usage            18 UPI payments per active user per month (average)
Full KYC done    120,000 users (2% of MAU) via an older gold-savings feature;
                 this KYC can be reused for Arcadia with one consent tap
Why now          Leadership wants a savings product to deepen engagement and
                 earn distribution revenue from a partner fund house.

2. TARGET USERS (hypothesis)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Young salaried users who intend to save but "save whatever is left" at
month-end, have no recurring savings habit, and already pay daily on Zentra.

3. THE PROBLEM: RESEARCH FINDINGS
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A) In-app survey, n = 1,500 MAU
   "I want to save more than I do"                       72%
   "I already have a recurring savings habit (SIP/RD)"   24%
   "I would try auto-save inside Zentra"                 41%
   Median amount willing to auto-save per month       Rs 1,000

   Biggest barrier to saving (pick one)       Share
   No money left at month-end                  46%
   Don't trust apps with my savings            28%
   Process too complicated (KYC, forms)        18%
   Other                                        8%
   Total                                      100%

   Most wanted feature (pick one)             Share
   Payday auto-save (fixed amount on payday)   38%
   Round-ups on every UPI payment              31%
   Named goals ("Goa trip")                    19%
   Save together with friends                  12%
   Total                                      100%

B) User interviews, n = 14
   9 of 14  "save what is left"; most months nothing is left
   7 of 14  said they would pause an auto-save "in a tight month"
   6 of 14  had abandoned a savings or investing app at the KYC step
   5 of 14  worried their money would be locked in

C) Fake-door test (7 days): "Save automatically with Zentra - join the
   waitlist" banner
   Users shown banner     200,000
   Clicked                  9,400    4.70% of shown
   Joined waitlist          3,760   40.00% of clickers   1.88% of shown

D) Benchmark: Zentra's older gold-savings feature (manual deposits)
   Stage                           Users   Step conv.   From start
   Started KYC                    50,000         -        100.0%
   Completed KYC                  19,500     39.0%         39.0%
   Made first deposit             14,040     72.0%         28.1%
   Still depositing at day 90      4,914     35.0%          9.8%

E) Round-up maths: 18 payments x average round-up Rs 4.50
   = about Rs 81 saved per user per month (vs Rs 1,000 median payday intent)

4. PROPOSED PRODUCT: "STASH"
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Payday auto-save: user picks an amount; it is moved on salary day
- Round-ups: spare change from each UPI payment is saved
- Savings sit in a liquid mutual fund via a licensed partner
- Dashboard: balance, history, returns; instant withdrawal (up to a limit)
- Named goals; streaks and reminders; save-with-friends

5. CONSTRAINTS
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Team       1 PM, 1 designer (50%), 2 mobile engineers, 1 backend engineer,
           1 QA (shared with another team), partner's compliance contact
Timeline   Closed beta in 12 weeks; go / no-go for full launch at week 20
Budget     Rs 40 lakh launch marketing for 6 months (incentives max 10 lakh)
Regulatory Zentra cannot hold savings itself: money goes to a liquid fund
           via licensed partner "Arcadia AMC" (fictional). Full KYC is
           required before the first investment. Each recurring debit needs
           a mandate the user approves once. Ads must not promise returns.
Platform   Partner API supports weekly or monthly mandates only - no debit
           per transaction. Round-ups must be batched into one weekly debit.

Rough engineering estimates (engineer-weeks, illustrative)
   KYC via partner SDK                       3
   Payday auto-save (mandate + schedule)     4
   Savings dashboard                         3
   Instant withdrawal                        3
   Round-ups (batched debit + reconcile)     9
   Named goals                               2
   Streaks + reminders                       2
   Save with friends                         6
   Analytics instrumentation                 1
   Total                                    33
Capacity: 3 engineers x 12 weeks = 36 engineer-weeks; about 25% goes to
testing, bug fixes and partner integration -> about 27 usable.
(Simplification: treat engineer-weeks as interchangeable. In reality the one
backend engineer is the bottleneck for mandate, debit and withdrawal work.)

6. COMPETITORS (fictional)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SaveSprout  Standalone round-up savings app
  + Polished habit features (streaks, goals); strong with students
  - Separate app; needs bank linking; withdrawals take 2 working days
BigBank Digital RD  A large bank's recurring deposit inside its app
  + High trust; fixed, guaranteed returns
  - Fixed monthly amount; penalty for breaking early; clunky UX
CoinCrate   Micro-investing in digital gold from Rs 10
  + Very low minimum; gamified; fast onboarding
  - Price swings; buy/sell spread; users question safety

7. LEADERSHIP ASK
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
"100,000 active savers by the end of month 6 after launch."
(Active saver = at least one successful auto-save in the last 35 days.)
Planning assumption: about 60% of MAU will see a Stash entry point within
6 months (3,600,000 users).

8. YOUR ANSWER TEMPLATE
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
MVP IN  (feature | why it is needed for the core job or for trust)
MVP OUT (feature | why later | what would bring it back)
Engineer-weeks used: ___ of ~27 (buffer kept: ___)
North Star: ___      Inputs (3-4): ___      Guardrails (2-3): ___
Target check: funnel maths vs 100,000 ask -> agree / reset / reframe
Launch: segment -> stages -> gates to move to the next stage
Riskiest assumption: ___ (why: impact if wrong + how little evidence)
Experiment: hypothesis | method | sample | metric | pass/fail | timebox

quiz.question: In the Stash fake-door test, 4.7% of users who saw the banner clicked it and 1.88% joined the waitlist. What does this result best support?
options: Users will save about Rs 1,000 a month once Stash launches
There is real interest in the idea, but no proof people will keep saving
Stash has reached product-market fit with young salaried users
Round-ups are more popular than payday auto-save with Zentra users
quiz.explanation: A fake door measures curiosity and stated intent. It says nothing about KYC completion or sustained saving. Product-market fit is shown by retained behaviour over time, not by a 7-day banner test.

quiz.question: Round-ups would save about Rs 81 per user per month (vs Rs 1,000 median payday intent) and cost 9 of the ~27 usable engineer-weeks because debits must be batched. What is the best MVP call?
options: Ship round-ups first, since 31% picked them and they feel effortless
Ship payday auto-save; defer round-ups and track demand for them
Ship both, and cut instant withdrawal to keep a buffer in the plan
Ship round-ups only, as they don't ask users to commit a fixed amount
quiz.explanation: Payday auto-save was the top-ranked feature (38% vs 31%), moves about 12x more money and costs less than half as much to build (4 vs 9 engineer-weeks). Cutting withdrawal to keep a buffer is tempting, but withdrawal answers the 28% trust barrier and the 5/14 lock-in worry, so it is a trust-critical MVP feature.

quiz.question: Which is the best North Star metric for Stash?
options: Active savers: users with a successful auto-save in the last 35 days
Total rupee balance (AUM) held in Stash across all users
Number of users who completed KYC through the partner flow
Number of waitlist sign-ups from the in-app savings banner
quiz.explanation: A North Star should reflect repeated delivery of the core value, which here is actually saving. AUM is tempting, but it is a lagging business output that a few large savers can inflate even while most users quit. The 35-day window gives a monthly payday debit some slack so the metric doesn't flicker.

quiz.question: Using the case data, 3.6M exposed x 4.7% x 39% x 72% x 35% comes to about 16,600 active savers, while leadership asked for 100,000 by month 6. What should the PM do?
options: Accept the 100,000 target and raise incentive spend to hit it
Drop the Stash launch, since the target can't be met in 6 months
Keep the target but count anyone with KYC done as an active saver
Share the funnel maths and agree a reset target tied to key levers
quiz.explanation: The plan is about 6x short. Hitting 100,000 would need around 1.02M KYC starts (17% of MAU), so the PM should make the gap visible and agree a realistic target plus the levers that must move (KYC reuse, habit continuation). Redefining 'active' is tempting, but it games the metric and breaks the link to real value.

quiz.question: Which Stash assumption is the riskiest one to test first?
options: Users will keep payday auto-save on across several pay cycles
Enough users are interested in saving inside a payments app
The partner's KYC SDK can be integrated within three weeks
Users will prefer Stash's interface over SaveSprout's interface
quiz.explanation: Sustained saving drives the North Star but has the weakest evidence: the gold benchmark used manual deposits, 46% say nothing is left at month-end and 7/14 would pause in a tight month. Interest is tempting to pick, but the fake door already gives some evidence for it.

quiz.question: You will run a 3,000-user Stash closed beta to test whether people keep auto-saving. The beta opens at week 12 and the go/no-go is at week 20. Which experiment plan is strongest?
options: Count auto-save sign-ups in the first week and judge success on that
Survey beta users at week 4 on whether they plan to keep saving
Measure the share still saving after the 2nd payday, then set the bar from results
Measure the share still saving after the 2nd payday, against a bar set beforehand
quiz.explanation: Continuation after the second payday measures the real habit with real money, and if users are enrolled quickly at week 12 it can be read by about week 20. The tempting distractor uses the same metric but picks the pass/fail bar after seeing the data, which lets almost any result pass, so the bar must be fixed in advance.

quiz.question: Which guardrail matters most for payday auto-save?
options: Average Stash balance per active saver, measured every week
Number of named goals created per active saver each month
UPI payment failures from low balance in the days after an auto-save
Click-through rate on Stash banners on the app home screen
quiz.explanation: A guardrail catches harm: an auto-save that leaves users unable to pay bills hurts them and Zentra's core payments business. Average balance is tempting, but it is an output metric you want to grow, not a harm signal.

quiz.question: Which first launch segment fits the Stash data best?
options: All 6M monthly users at once, to maximise learning speed
Waitlist sign-ups plus a paid campaign for brand-new users
Students first, to take on SaveSprout in its strongest segment
Users who already have full KYC, then widen in gated stages
quiz.explanation: The 120,000 users who already have full KYC skip the 39% KYC bottleneck, so the first stage tests only the habit question, at low risk, before money goes into scale. The waitlist is tempting, but most of it would hit the KYC wall, and paying to acquire users before the habit is proven wastes budget. These users already chose a savings feature once, so treat their habit rate as an upper bound and add a small non-KYC cohort before widening.

quiz.question: The MVP (core features plus streaks and named goals) uses 18 of ~27 usable engineer-weeks. A stakeholder wants save-with-friends (6 weeks) added, saying 24 of 27 still leaves a buffer. What is the best response?
options: Add it, since 24 of 27 still leaves a 3-week buffer for any slips
Add it, since social saving will spread Stash quickly among friends
Defer it: only 12% want it and it fixes none of the top saving barriers
Swap it in for streaks and goals, as social features retain users better
quiz.explanation: Save-with-friends had the lowest demand (12%) and does nothing for the top barriers (no money left, trust, KYC). Adding it would also cut the buffer to 3 weeks, while partner integration is the least predictable work. The thin-but-positive buffer is the tempting argument, but fitting into capacity is not a reason to build a low-value feature.

quiz.question: Given the competitor table, which positioning gives Stash the most defensible edge?
options: Saving inside the app users already pay with, plus quick access to cash
Higher guaranteed returns than BigBank's recurring deposit
A lower minimum than CoinCrate, starting at Rs 1 per save
More gamification than SaveSprout, with streaks and leaderboards
quiz.explanation: Zentra's daily payment habit and 6M MAU are an advantage that SaveSprout (separate app, 2-day withdrawals) and BigBank (breakage penalty) can't easily copy. Promising higher guaranteed returns is tempting, but liquid funds don't guarantee returns and the ads must not promise them.

keyTakeaways: Interest is not behaviour. A click on a banner shows curiosity, not that someone will keep a habit going.
Size the MVP to the core job and the trust basics, then leave buffer. A plan that books 100% of capacity has no room for partner or compliance surprises and will very likely slip.
Do the funnel maths before you accept a target, because multiplying the step rates can turn a bold goal into an impossible one.
Test the assumption that would hurt most if wrong and has the least evidence, not the one that is easiest to test.

lessons.label: Module 16
lessons.title: Case Study: Fix a Retention Problem
lessons.description: Diagnose a sudden drop in new-user retention at a fictional micro-savings app by reading a weekly cohort table, separating a channel-mix shift from a product change, and proposing experiments to confirm and fix the cause.
learningObjectives: Find the first cohort where a retention break appears and classify it as a signup-cohort (row) pattern or a calendar-week (diagonal) pattern, ruling events in or out by their timing fingerprint
Split a blended retention drop into a channel-mix effect and a within-channel effect using share x rate arithmetic, and explain why the split is approximate
Use activation-funnel step rates, absolute counts of activated users and the W1/W0 ratio (a proxy for retention among activated users) to find the step where users are lost
Write a root-cause statement with a confidence level and stated caveats, then design a holdout experiment with a hypothesis, a primary metric and a guardrail to confirm it

readingArticles.title: Cohort Retention Analysis in 2026: How to Separate Real Users From AI Tourists
keyPoints: Blended retention averages hide the differences between cohorts. The useful insight is in comparing segments, not in the overall average.
Acquisition cohorts (grouped by signup date) show the effect of timing and channel. Behavioural cohorts (grouped by an action such as finishing activation) show which actions predict retention.
The shape of the curve tells you more than the headline percentage: it may keep declining, flatten and hold, or curve back up (a 'smile').
Measuring later retention against an early baseline filters out casual users who try the product once and leave.

readingArticles.title: Why Retention Is The Silent Killer
keyPoints: Retention is often deprioritised because its payoff compounds over years, which clashes with quarterly goals, even though better retention eventually beats faster acquisition.
A wrongly defined retention metric (wrong unit, wrong frequency or wrong core action) can hide real problems. Check the definition before you trust a trend.
Retention measures breadth (how many users stay) and engagement measures depth (how intensely they use the product). Read the two together.
Deeper engagement supports monetisation and defensibility through switching costs and network effects.

videos.title: How To Keep Your Users | Startup School
videos.creator: Y Combinator (David Lieb, YC Group Partner)
keyPoints: How to define cohorts and decide what counts as an 'active' user for retention
How to choose the right core action and time frame to measure, and what good retention looks like
A chapter on the ways teams fool themselves when they read retention data
Ways to improve the retention curve once you know where it breaks

practicalTools.name: PaisaJar Retention Diagnosis
practicalTools.description: A realistic, fictional case. New-user W1 retention at a micro-savings app fell from about 46% (July cohorts) to about 31% for every cohort that signed up from 3 Aug onward. Three things changed at around the same time: a paid-social campaign, a new onboarding flow and a withdrawal fee. You get a weekly cohort table (8 signup cohorts x weeks 0-6), a breakdown by acquisition channel, and an activation funnel. All numbers are illustrative and have been checked for internal consistency. This module assumes you already know how to read a basic cohort table and calculate retention (see Day 24) and how funnels and AARRR work (see Day 22). For A/B test design and sample sizing, see Day 20.
practicalTools.exercise:
Work in order, and do not open Exhibits B and C until you have finished Step 3.

Step 1 - What would you investigate first? Before forming any opinion, write the first three checks you would run, in order, and explain why. (For example: Is the drop real, or did the onboarding release change event tracking or the definition of a 'save'? Which cohort does the break start in? Does it follow signup week or calendar week?)

Step 2 - Read Exhibit A. (a) Which cohort does the break start in? Is the change in C4 the same size as the change in C5? (b) Is the pattern a row pattern (it follows signup week) or a diagonal pattern (it follows calendar week)? (c) Find the cells in the calendar week of 17 Aug (C1 W6, C2 W5, C3 W4, ...). For each one, compare the drop from the previous week with the drop at the same age in a cohort that reached that age BEFORE 17 Aug. Is the decay faster after the fee?

Step 3 - For each of the three events (channel shift, onboarding v2, withdrawal fee), write a hypothesis and its 'fingerprint': exactly what Exhibits A-C should show if that event were the cause. Then choose which analysis to run first: cohort by channel, or activation step completion. Justify your choice.

Step 4 - Open Exhibit B (cohort by channel). (a) Compare C4 with C1-C3. Did any channel's W1 fall, or did only the channel mix change? (b) Pool C1-C3 and pool C5-C7. For each pool, calculate each channel's share and W1. Then calculate the blended W1 the new mix would produce at the OLD channel rates. Split the total drop into a mix effect and a within-channel effect. (c) Did every channel fall, or only paid social?

Step 5 - Open Exhibit C (activation funnel). (a) Which step's conversion changed at C5, and which steps stayed flat? (b) Compare the absolute number of first savers in C4 and C5, alongside started signups. (c) Calculate the W1/W0 ratio (a proxy for retention among activated users) for each channel before and after the change. What does this tell you about the core product?

Step 6 - Write a one-sentence root cause, give your confidence level, and list what you cannot yet conclude (for example, onboarding v2 shipped without a control group, and the channel mix was changing at the same time).

Step 7 - Propose two or three experiments or actions. For each, give the hypothesis, the variant, a primary metric, a guardrail metric, and what result would change your mind. Say how the creator campaign should be judged from now on.

Step 8 - Write a five-line update for the CEO that responds to each stakeholder claim.
practicalTools.deliverable:
A strong answer contains:

(1) First checks, in order: confirm the data is valid (onboarding v2 did not change the 'save' event or the cohort definition); find the first broken cohort; test row versus diagonal. A strong answer does not jump to a fix. Note that v2 lets more marginal users complete signup (Organic users +8% from C4 to C5 with no change in organic acquisition), so the denominator grew. Also compare first savers per STARTED signup: 42.0% in C4 vs 33.9% in C5.

(2) Timing read: C4 shows a small dip (W1 43.2% vs about 45.8% for C1-C3), and C5 shows a large step change (W1 about 31%) that persists in C6-C8. This is a row pattern. The step into the fee week is not steeper than the pre-fee steps at the same age (C2 W4->W5 -2.1 vs C1 -1.6; C3 W3->W4 -2.3 vs -3.0 for C1/C2). C1 W6 has no pre-fee comparator. C7 (signed up in the fee week) looks the same as C5 and C6. With only 1-3 post-fee weeks, the data shows no clear fee effect yet, but it cannot rule out a lagged one. Keep monitoring.

(3) Mix analysis: in C4, within-channel W1 is unchanged (Organic 45.5 vs 45.1 pooled, Referral 54.5 vs 54.9, Paid social 30.2 vs 30.2). The C4 dip is therefore purely a mix shift, with paid-social share rising from 10.5% to 26.0%. Pooled C1-C3 vs C5-C7: shares went from 66.6/22.9/10.5 to 50.1/17.1/32.8, and W1 went from 45.8% to 31.0% (-14.8 pts). The new mix at the old rates gives 41.9%, so the mix effect is about -3.9 pts and about -10.9 pts is within-channel. Every channel fell by roughly a quarter (Organic 45.1 to 33.6, Referral 54.9 to 41.1, Paid social 30.2 to 21.7). The answer should note that the split depends on calculation order: at the old mix and new rates, the result is 34.1%.

(4) Funnel analysis: signup completion rose from about 70% to about 77%. Bank linking within the signup week fell from about 75% to about 54% of completed signups. First save given a linked account stayed roughly flat at about 81-83% (C8 80.6%). From C4 to C5, started signups rose 4% (6,886 to 7,173) but first savers fell about 16% (2,889 to 2,435). The W1/W0 ratio (a proxy for retention among activated users) within each channel is flat (Organic 73.1 vs 72.4, Referral 78.5 vs 78.8, Paid social 60.3 vs 59.7), so activated users still retain as before. The leak is in getting users to activation, not in ongoing value.

(5) Root cause, with medium-high confidence: onboarding v2's optional 'Link later' step reduced bank linking and therefore first saves. This accounts for most of the drop. The paid-social mix shift is a real but secondary and separate effect. Caveats: there was no control group; the timing could also coincide with an unseen change; the analysis cannot show whether paid-social users skip linking more often (the funnel needs a split by channel to check); we have not yet checked how many link-later users make a first save in week 1 or later (logs show fewer than 2% link that late, so the effect on W1/W0 should be small); and the within-channel 10.9 pts also includes the bigger v2 denominator (more marginal completers) and post-fee weeks for C6-C7, so it is an upper bound on the pure onboarding effect.

(6) Experiments: (a) A holdout A/B test that randomises users at signup START between mandatory linking (v1) and link-later (v2). Primary metric: % of users who start signup and make a first save within 7 days of starting. Secondary metric: W2 retention on the same base. Guardrails: signup completion and complaints/support tickets. (b) A v2 variant that asks the user to link at the moment they create their first goal, tested against v2 control on the same metrics. (c) Judge the creator campaign on cost per activated or retained user, using its own channel cohort curves, not blended retention. Also report retention by channel and track an activation metric alongside signup completion.

(7) A CEO update that names the cause, gives the mix-versus-product numbers, responds to each stakeholder claim with evidence, and states the next step and the date a decision will be made.
practicalTools.template:
CASE: PaisaJar -- "Why did new-user retention fall?"
(Fictional company. All numbers are illustrative, made up for practice.)

THE PRODUCT
PaisaJar is a micro-savings app in India. Users set a goal ("Goa trip"),
link a bank account via a UPI autopay mandate, and save small amounts into
a goal jar. Nobody can save until a bank account is linked.

RETENTION DEFINITION (unchanged during the period)
Cohort = calendar week (Mon-Sun) in which the user completed signup.
Wn     = % of the cohort who made >= 1 savings deposit in the n-th
         calendar week after the signup week. W0 = the signup week itself,
         so W0 is NOT 100%: it is the share who made a first save.
Data as of Monday 7 Sep 2026. "-" = week not finished yet.

WHAT CHANGED RECENTLY
27 Jul  Marketing launched a creator campaign on Instagram (paid social).
        Paid-social budget roughly tripled from this week.
03 Aug  Onboarding v2 shipped to 100% of new users (no A/B test). In v1,
        signup ended on a full-screen "Link your bank" prompt that users
        could only dismiss by closing the app. In v2 that prompt is
        replaced by an optional "Link later" card on the home screen.
        'Completed signup' (account + KYC) means the same in both
        versions. Design reports signup completion rose from ~70% to ~77%.
17 Aug  Pricing change for ALL users: Rs 10 fee on instant withdrawals.
        Standard 2-day withdrawals stay free.

WHAT PEOPLE ARE SAYING
Head of Growth: "Creator-campaign users are low intent. That's all it is."
Design lead:    "Onboarding v2 is a clear win -- completion is up 7 pts."
Finance:        "Fee complaints are all over social media. That's the churn."

quiz.question: The PaisaJar CEO tells you W1 retention fell from about 46% to about 31%. Onboarding v2 shipped on 3 Aug. What should you do first?
options: Ask Growth to pause the creator campaign while you dig into which channels are dropping
Roll back onboarding v2 for all users, since it is the most recent change to the product
Check that v2 did not change the save event or cohort logic, then find the first broken cohort
Survey users who stopped saving to ask why, so you start from their stated reasons
quiz.explanation: Before you form hypotheses, check that the data is valid and find where the break starts, because an instrumentation change shipped with v2 could create a fake drop. Rolling back v2 is tempting, but it acts before any diagnosis, and the channel mix was changing at the same time, so a rollback alone would not prove anything.

quiz.question: The Rs 10 instant-withdrawal fee started on 17 Aug for ALL users. If the fee were driving churn, where in Exhibit A would you expect to see its effect?
options: In the rows for C7 and C8, the cohorts that signed up in or after the fee week
Starting on the diagonal of 17 Aug cells (C1 W6, C2 W5, C3 W4, ...) and in every later week
In the W0 column of every cohort, because users would meet the fee when they sign up
In the cohorts with the highest paid-social share, because those users are more price-sensitive
quiz.explanation: A change that hits every user at the same calendar moment starts as a diagonal across cohorts and, if it persists, continues in every later calendar week; it does not show up as a row. 'C7 and C8' is the tempting mistake: it treats a calendar-time change as a signup-cohort change and misses the effect on existing users.

quiz.question: C4's blended W1 is 43.2%, compared with about 45.8% for C1-C3. Exhibit B shows C4 channel W1 of Organic 45.5, Referral 54.5 and Paid social 30.2 (C1-C3 pooled: about 45.1, 54.9 and 30.2), while the paid-social share rose from about 10% to 26%. What best explains C4?
options: Onboarding v2 reached some C4 users early and lowered their retention
The creator campaign brought lower-intent paid-social users, so that channel's retention fell
The withdrawal fee reduced saving across the whole C4 cohort
A mix shift: more users came from a lower-retaining channel, and no channel got worse
quiz.explanation: Every channel's W1 in C4 matches its C1-C3 level, but the blended rate fell, so the cause is composition (mix), not behaviour. The 'lower-intent paid-social users' option is tempting, but paid-social W1 in C4 (30.2) equals its C1-C3 level, so that channel did not get worse.

quiz.question: Pooled W1 was 45.8% for C1-C3 and 31.0% for C5-C7. Applying the C5-C7 channel shares to the C1-C3 channel rates gives 41.9%. What does this tell you?
options: About 3.9 points come from the mix shift; most of the rest comes from lower retention within every channel
The mix shift explains about 11 of the 14.8 points, so the product is mostly fine
The mix shift explains the whole drop, because paid social now makes up a third of signups
The data cannot separate the mix effect from the product effect without an A/B test
quiz.explanation: The new mix at the old rates loses only 45.8 - 41.9 = 3.9 pts, so about 10.9 pts come from rates falling inside each channel. The split is approximate because it depends on calculation order, but it clearly shows that mix is the smaller part. Option A reverses the two effects.

quiz.question: Exhibit C: signup completion rose from about 70% to 77%, bank linking in the signup week fell from about 75% to 54% of completed signups, and first save given a linked account stayed at about 82%. Where did the loss happen?
options: At signup start, because paid social is sending more low-intent visitors into the funnel
After linking, because linked users are saving less often than before
In weeks 2 and later, because users are not forming a saving habit
At the bank-linking step, which v2 made optional
quiz.explanation: Bank linking is the only step whose conversion fell sharply, and it is the step v2 changed. Completion went up and save-given-linked stayed flat. The 'after linking' option is ruled out because first save among linked users is unchanged at about 82%.

quiz.question: The design lead says onboarding v2 is a win because signup completion is up 7 points. Which response is best supported by the data?
options: Agree: more completed signups means bigger cohorts, and a bigger base will grow the number of savers over time
First savers fell from 2,889 (C4) to 2,435 (C5) while started signups rose, so v2 adds completions, not savers
The completion rise comes from the paid-social campaign, not from v2, so v2 should be judged as neutral
Completion moves week to week, so ask Design for four more weeks of data before judging v2 either way
quiz.explanation: Completion is an intermediate step metric. The outcome that matters is users reaching the value moment, and that number fell even as started signups rose about 4%. The campaign option is wrong because completion jumped at C5 (the v2 cohort), not at C4 (when the campaign started).

quiz.question: Within each channel, the W1/W0 ratio (a proxy for retention among activated users) is about the same before and after 3 Aug (for example, Organic 73.1% vs 72.4%). Why does this matter?
options: It shows users who reach a first save still get value, so the leak is before activation
It shows the channel mix explains the drop, since each channel's savers behave as before
It rules out the withdrawal fee as a cause of churn for every user, new or existing
It shows the drop is in habit formation, so the fix is better reminders after the first save
quiz.explanation: A flat W1/W0 ratio means users who reach a first save behave as before, so the leak is earlier, at activation. It does not mean mix explains everything, because within-channel W0 fell sharply. It does not clear the fee: W1/W0 looks only at the first week after signup, and fee-driven churn would most likely appear in later weeks, after users have tried to withdraw.

quiz.question: Onboarding v2 shipped to 100% of users with no control group, and the channel mix was changing at the same time. What is the strongest way to confirm v2 is the cause?
options: Randomise users at signup start between mandatory linking (v1) and link-later (v2), and compare 7-day first saves
Wait three more weeks, then compare C5-C8 with C1-C3 again with the extra cohorts' data
Roll back v2 for everyone and attribute any later recovery in retention to the rollback
Interview 10 users who skipped bank linking to learn why they never came back to save
quiz.explanation: Randomisation separates the onboarding effect from the changing channel mix and any other change happening at the same time. Use the % of users who start signup and make a first save within 7 days of starting as the primary metric, with signup completion as a guardrail. A full rollback is tempting, but a before/after comparison is still confounded by the mix shift.

quiz.question: The Head of Growth wants to keep scaling the creator campaign. Paid-social W1 is about 30% before v2, compared with about 45% for Organic. How should the campaign be judged?
options: Cut it, because it pulls blended retention down and makes the product look worse
Scale it freely, because paid-social retention did not change when the campaign began
By cost per activated or retained user and its own channel cohort curves, not its effect on blended retention
Leave it to Marketing, because channel performance is not a product question
quiz.explanation: A lower-retaining channel can still be profitable if the cost per retained user works. Blended retention penalises it simply for being different. 'Cut it' is the tempting mistake: it treats a mix effect as if it were a quality failure.

quiz.question: Which experiment most directly targets the main cause found in the PaisaJar data?
options: Waive the Rs 10 instant-withdrawal fee for new users in their first month, against a fee control, and compare W1
Prompt users to link their bank when they create their first goal, against current v2, and compare 7-day first saves
Raise referral rewards to shift signups back toward the highest-retaining channel, against current rewards, and compare blended W1
Send push reminders to users who have not saved for two weeks, against a no-push control, and compare return rates
quiz.explanation: The loss happens at bank linking, which v2 made optional. The fix should raise linking and first saves (within 7 days of starting signup) without undoing v2's completion gain. Boosting referrals is plausible, but it only addresses the smaller mix effect (about 4 of the 15 points) and leaves the within-channel drop untouched.

keyTakeaways: Find where the break starts first. A change that follows signup week shows up as a row; a change that follows calendar week starts on a diagonal and persists in every later calendar week.
A blended average can fall even when no segment gets worse. Split by channel before you blame the product, and split by channel before you clear it.
A better step metric is not a win until more users reach the value moment. Count activated users, not only rates.
Two events that happen at the same time give you a hypothesis, not proof. Confirm the cause with a holdout before you announce it.

lessons.label: Module 17
lessons.title: The PM Toolkit: Templates & Calculators
lessons.description: A guided tour of the course's PM Toolkit page, covering what each template and calculator is for, when to use it, and how to avoid the common ways people misuse them.
learningObjectives: Pick the right toolkit template for a given moment in the product lifecycle (problem statement, interview script, journey map, OST, PRD, user story, metrics tree, experiment brief, launch checklist or post-launch review) and explain why it fits
Score at least 3 real backlog items with the RICE calculator, write the evidence behind every input, and name the one input that would change the ranking if it were wrong

Turn a baseline conversion rate and minimum detectable effect (at alpha 0.05, 80% power) into a sample size per variant and a test duration in whole weeks using the A/B sample-size calculator, and record both in an experiment brief before launch
Work out LTV, LTV:CAC and CAC payback with the unit-economics calculator and state the assumptions that limit the result (LTV: constant churn, no expansion, undiscounted; payback: ignores churn)

readingArticles.title: PM Toolkit: Templates (PRD, problem statement, user story, interview script, journey map, OST, metrics tree, experiment brief, launch checklist, post-launch review)
keyPoints: Use the templates in the order you need them: discovery (problem statement, interview script, journey map, opportunity solution tree), then delivery (PRD and readiness checklist, user story, launch checklist), then measurement and learning (metrics tree, experiment brief, post-launch review). Deeper coverage: Day 4 interviews, Day 5 journey maps, Day 6 problem statements, Day 13 metrics trees, Day 15 PRDs, Day 16 user stories, Day 20 experiments.

The PRD is a one-pager whose sections run from problem through goal and metrics, users, scope, requirements, experience, technical/data, launch and risks. Run the readiness checklist before engineering starts. A common failure is a PRD that has requirements but no baseline, no target and no out-of-scope list.

The opportunity solution tree (Teresa Torres) links one measurable outcome to customer opportunities, then to solutions, then to assumption tests. The metrics tree breaks a North Star into levers that each team owns, with guardrails. Use both to explain why you are working on something.

The experiment brief makes you write the hypothesis, the MDE, guardrails, sample size and decision rules before launch. The post-launch review then compares target against actual and ends in an explicit keep, iterate or roll-back decision with owners.

readingArticles.title: PM Toolkit: Calculators (RICE, ICE, WSJF, A/B test sample size, unit economics)
keyPoints: RICE = Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort. Impact uses Intercom's scale, from 3 (massive) down to 0.25 (minimal), and Effort is in person-months. A common heuristic: if Confidence is below 50%, do discovery before committing (see Day 11 for RICE basics). ICE (commonly attributed to Sean Ellis) rates Impact, Confidence and Ease from 1 to 10. It is faster and rougher, which suits growth experiments. The toolkit averages the three scores; some teams multiply them instead, which usually gives a similar ranking.

WSJF (as used in SAFe) = Cost of Delay / job size, where Cost of Delay = business value + time criticality + risk reduction/opportunity enablement, each scored relatively on a 1-2-3-5-8-13-20 scale. It favours small, urgent jobs, so sanity-check any large strategic bet that ranks low.

The sample-size calculator uses a standard normal approximation for conversion metrics. Fix n before you start, do not stop early because the result looks significant (peeking inflates false positives), and run whole weeks (see Day 20).

Unit economics: LTV = ARPU x gross margin / monthly churn, which assumes constant churn, no expansion revenue and no discounting. Payback = CAC / monthly gross profit per customer, which ignores churn during the payback period. A 3:1 LTV:CAC ratio is a rule of thumb, not a law.

readingArticles.title: My favorite product management templates
keyPoints: A curated list (Lenny's favourites plus reader picks from Twitter) of 1-pager/PRD, strategy, vision and go-to-market templates, plus extras such as a roadmap template and decision frameworks (SPADE, Coinbase).

Includes widely used formats such as Amazon's working-backwards press release, Geoffrey Moore's positioning statement and decision-making frameworks. Compare them with the toolkit's versions and borrow what fits your team.
Our takeaway: compare 2-3 of the PRD/1-pager templates listed (for example, Kevin Yien's, with its 'Non-Goals' section) with the toolkit's PRD, and keep only the sections your team actually uses.

keyPoints: An experienced PM explains what goes into product requirements and why to start from the customer problem.
Shows how requirements documents support alignment across engineering, design and stakeholders.

practicalTools.name: Three-Lens Prioritisation, Unit Economics + Experiment Brief on a Real Backlog Item
practicalTools.description: Take one real backlog item from your work, or from a product you use every day such as a food delivery, ride-hailing, fintech or SaaS app. Score it against two competing items with three of the toolkit's prioritisation calculators (RICE, ICE and WSJF) and explain where they disagree. Then check the unit economics of the product, and write a pre-registered experiment brief for your item, using the sample-size calculator to set the test length. The worked example at the bottom of the template is illustrative only; replace every number with your own.
practicalTools.exercise: Part A - prioritisation. 1) Enter the same 3 backlog items into RICE (toolkit.html#rice), ICE (#ice) and WSJF (#wsjf). Note where the rankings disagree and explain why in one line each (for example, WSJF rewards small, time-critical jobs). For every RICE input, write one line naming its source (analytics, tickets, interviews or a guess). 2) Replace the input you are least sure about with its plausible low and high values (Confidence stays at or below 100%; Impact moves one step on the 0.25-3 scale) and note whether the ranking flips. That input is your sensitivity point. 3) Choose a verdict for your item: build next, discovery first (if Confidence is below 50%), or park. Part C - unit economics. 4) For your product (or a subscription app you use), enter ARPU, gross margin, monthly churn and CAC into toolkit.html#unit-economics. Record LTV, LTV:CAC and payback months, and list two assumptions that make the result optimistic. Part B - experiment brief. 5) For your item, copy the experiment brief from toolkit.html#experiment-brief. Write a falsifiable hypothesis with an MDE. Name one primary metric, at least one guardrail with a threshold, and one diagnostic metric. 6) Put the baseline and MDE into toolkit.html#sample-size and record n per variant. Duration in days = (n per variant x number of variants) / daily eligible users, rounded up to whole weeks. As a rough heuristic, if this is more than about 6 weeks, revisit the MDE or choose a higher-traffic metric. 7) Write the ship, iterate and stop rules before looking at any data. 8) Submit the filled template below.
practicalTools.deliverable: The filled template, in three parts. Part A is a RICE / ICE / WSJF comparison for 3 items with a one-line explanation of each ranking disagreement, an evidence line for every RICE input of all 3 items, a sensitivity note and a verdict. Part B is a complete experiment brief with a hypothesis, metrics, sample size, duration in whole weeks and pre-agreed decision rules. Part C - unit economics: LTV, LTV:CAC and payback months with the inputs used and two assumptions that make the result optimistic.
